plectis.label: Plectis
plectis.preview: Plectis is an open-source mathematics project, with checked proofs, research papers and software that people and agents can build on.
plectis.card: The Lean repository holds the mathematics: formal proofs, short notes, longer working records and open questions. A separate software repository holds reusable research components. This site connects both. Older paths, package names, and URLs still say Microcosm; those are this same project under the name it used before.
plectis.rule: Read Plectis as the public project name. If you see Microcosm in a path, package, or old link, treat it as the same project, not a second one.
plectis.deep: The name comes from Latin plectere, to weave. It names the public cut. What the system actually is lives in the source files, standards, and validators; renaming the public identity did not rename every package id or old URL.

component.label: component
component.preview: A component is one bounded unit of machinery with a defined job, explicit inputs and outputs, and a limit on what it may claim.
component.card: The system is built as a set of these units rather than one large program, and each one is presented on its own card. A component card names the unit, says what it does, gives the evidence line that backs it, links to its source route, and marks where its scope stops. Each component can be opened and inspected on its own.
component.rule: Take a component as one bounded unit doing one job, and read its evidence line and scope limit to see what it is responsible for and where that responsibility ends.
component.deep: Component is a naming boundary, not a separate object: it lets the object model be read on the public pages without inheriting the internal working vocabulary, and the source registry, atlas, object map, and evidence profiles decide what each component is allowed to claim.

scope_limit.label: scope limit
scope_limit.preview: A scope limit is the explicit boundary between what a unit's evidence establishes and what that unit is not allowed to assert.
scope_limit.card: Every component, evidence class, and published packet on this site carries a scope limit. It marks the edge of what the supporting evidence covers, so that a real result stays a claim about exactly what was checked and does not stretch into launch readiness, whole-system correctness, hosted-service behaviour, professional advice, or private runtime state. A local fixture can pass while the scope limit still rules out any wider guarantee.
scope_limit.rule: When a result is shown, read its scope limit to see how far the evidence reaches. The result holds only within that boundary, and nothing beyond it is being claimed.
scope_limit.deep: A scope limit does not weaken evidence; it protects it by blocking unsupported elevation. The component digest, the claim-ceiling index, the question routes, and the evidence pages all check this boundary before an answer is permitted to make a broader claim.

evidence_class.label: evidence class
evidence_class.preview: An evidence class names the kind of support behind a result, without treating that support as proof of every claim drawn from it.
evidence_class.card: When a card or result on this site is marked as backed, its evidence class is the category of that backing. The classes distinguish, for example, a result whose support is a link to a source row, one whose support is a fixture that passed, one whose support is a tool that ran locally, and one whose support is a recorded review. Each class carries its own ceiling on what may be claimed from it, so two results can both be supported while resting on very different kinds of evidence.
evidence_class.rule: Check which evidence class a result carries, and read it as a statement about the kind of support, not the strength of every conclusion. A class sits next to a scope limit that names what that support does not establish.
evidence_class.deep: The governing list of classes is kept in the source slice and the site builder's claim-ceiling projection, so a class is a fixed vocabulary entry rather than a free-form label, and it keeps a local fixture or a generated record from being read as wider authority.

record.label: record
record.preview: A record is a durable file or row you can reopen later to see what was checked, produced, or routed.
record.card: A record is the inspectable object a page points to when it refers to something more solid than a sentence. Each record carries what produced it and where its authority stops, and it sits below its owning source rather than replacing it. Records are how narrative pages connect to source authority: a reader can open the actual result row, receipt, ledger, or generated projection behind a statement.
record.rule: When a page points you to a record, open it and read what it actually preserves and where its scope ends. A record holds a checkable object; it does not make a claim true merely by existing.
record.deep: In this system a record may be a source row, a generated projection, a receipt, a ledger entry, or a public packet. Each is durable and reopenable, and each ranks below the source that produced it.

substrate.label: substrate
substrate.preview: A substrate is the underlying body of files, routes, recorded state, and tools that the system operates on, distinct from the pages and summaries projected over that source material.
substrate.card: The substrate is everything the public pages are generated from: the source files, the standards, the recorded state, the validators, and the tools that act on them. It is the concrete, inspectable layer beneath any summary, route, or evidence view. A generated page can describe or point into the substrate, but it does not own the source records, package identifiers, or state transitions that live there.
substrate.rule: When something is called the substrate, treat it as the lower source layer that a page is reporting on, and look to it rather than the page when you need the actual file or record.
substrate.deep: The substrate is what keeps a generated page honest about its own status: the page makes a map, digest, or evidence view, while the substrate remains the authority that owns the source records, validators, identifiers, and state changes underneath.

source_authority.label: source authority
source_authority.preview: Source authority is the artifact, standard, tool, or ledger that owns a fact more strongly than anything generated from it: the place where the truth is held, beneath any page, summary, or AI answer that merely reports it.
source_authority.card: Every generated surface on this site, a page, a digest, an AI summary, is a projection of something lower down. The source authority is that lower thing: a source file, a standard, a validator, a ledger, or a generated sidecar with an ownership contract. When prose, HTML, or a summary may have drifted, the source authority is where the actual claim lives and where a fact is settled. A projection can route to its source authority, but summarising a fact does not make the summary the owner of it.
source_authority.rule: When a page makes a claim, the source authority is the artifact it stands below; treat that artifact, not the page, as the place the fact is owned.
source_authority.deep: This is the rule that keeps generated public surfaces honest: they are useful because they route, compress, and display, and they stay accurate by naming the lower artifact or tool that owns each claim and refusing to assert anything beyond it.

organ.label: organ (source identifier)
organ.preview: An organ is the source-code name for the same bounded unit that public pages call a component.
organ.card: The system is built as a set of these units rather than one large program. Each organ does one job, such as mapping a route, running a check, importing source material, or generating a page, and can be opened and inspected on its own. Each one carries its own boundary and a record of what it is allowed to assert, so a unit's reach is fixed and visible rather than implied.
organ.rule: When a source path or identifier names an organ, read it as one bounded unit doing a single job; the same unit appears on the public pages as a component.
organ.deep: Organ is the source-level and runtime name for these units, kept stable in file paths, identifiers, and compatibility records; component is the same thing under its public label.

witness.label: check result
witness.preview: A witness is the durable record that one specific check ran and what it found, shown in public copy as a check result or verification record.
witness.card: When a statement on this site claims it is supported, the witness is the concrete artifact behind that support: the output of a validator, a test, or a source-row check, naming exactly what was examined and what held. It is evidence for one bounded statement, not a verdict on the whole system.
witness.rule: Read what a witness actually checked before relying on it. It vouches for that one claim and nothing wider.
witness.deep: Each witness carries its scope limit with it: the command or record that produced it, the exact thing it examined, and the boundary of what that result does and does not cover.

navigable.label: navigable
navigable.preview: A navigable term, record, or page carries at least one concrete anchor, source reference, relationship link, command, or pointer that takes a reader from its summary to the underlying object or evidence.
navigable.card: Across Plectis, an object is treated as navigable when it can be opened, cross-referenced, checked, and traced back to its source instead of only being named. A navigable component, for example, links to the source file that defines it, the standards it answers to, and the check that confirms it. The opposite is a dead term: a word that sounds meaningful but offers no route to anything concrete.
navigable.rule: When something is described as navigable, expect a real link, anchor, or command behind it, and follow that route to the source if you want to confirm the claim yourself.
navigable.deep: Navigability is how the system separates a real surface from a decorative one: a navigable concept can be selected, opened, related to others, and bounded by what it is allowed to claim, while anything that cannot route to a source, record, or owner is counted as a gap.

above_and_beyond.label: above and beyond
above_and_beyond.preview: In ai_workflow, above and beyond means bounded follow-through that makes the requested result durable, then stops at a named boundary.
above_and_beyond.card: It describes a finished pass that did the immediately useful follow-through, not one that wandered off into new scope. When a task surfaces something that would otherwise go stale or be hard for the next person to find, the extra work is to make that one result durable: name the boundary, do the smallest improvement that prevents rediscovery, run a focused check, and leave evidence. The boundary is part of the trait: the work has a source case, a place it belongs, a check, and a clear stopping point.
above_and_beyond.rule: When a pass is described this way, take it to mean the result was made durable and was bounded, not that scope was expanded; the record of what was checked tells you how far the follow-through actually reached.
above_and_beyond.deep: It is the active form of care and standards held together: care protects whoever reads the result next, and the safety condition is that the extra work stays bounded, with a recorded stopping point rather than an open-ended campaign.

accept.label: accept
accept.preview: To accept something is to admit, approve, receive, or treat it as satisfying a stated condition.
accept.card: Acceptance may concern input validity, a proof step, a publication gate, or a proposed result. It should be tied to an actor or checker and a rule rather than treated as universal endorsement.
accept.rule: When something is accepted, identify the accepting authority, criteria, scope, and resulting permissions.
accept.deep: Acceptance under one interface or test does not establish correctness, safety, or approval outside that boundary.

access.label: access
access.preview: Access is the ability and permission to reach, open, or use a page, file, tool, or service.
access.card: Access answers whether a reader can get to something, not whether that thing is complete, correct, or safe to rely on. Public access, repository access, and tool access are separate permissions.
access.rule: Treat access as a reachability condition and check authority, evidence, and license separately.
access.deep: A route can exist without being accessible because it needs an account, network, local checkout, or permission that the current reader does not have.

accountability_layer.label: accountability layer
accountability_layer.preview: The accountability layer is the set of evidence records, result records, source links, and scope limits that lets a reader trace what a mechanism ran and where the resulting claim stops.
accountability_layer.card: This layer sits around a mechanism rather than replacing it. It connects the visible claim to the recorded run or replay, the source that owns it, the kind of evidence attached to it, and the boundary beyond which that evidence says nothing.
accountability_layer.rule: Use the accountability layer to follow a claim back to evidence and source; do not treat the page that presents those links as the authority itself.
accountability_layer.deep: The layer makes a claim inspectable by preserving provenance and limits together. A record without a source route or a scope limit is not enough to establish accountable public evidence.

action.label: action
action.preview: An action is a discrete operation performed by a person, agent, program, or tool that can change state or produce an observable effect.
action.card: Actions differ from intentions and suggestions because something actually happens. Their authorization, target, and result should be recorded when they affect durable state.
action.rule: Verify who or what acted, on which target, under what permission, and with what outcome.
action.deep: A multi-step task may contain many actions but become valid only when its transaction and closeout conditions are satisfied.

actor_axes.label: actor axes
actor_axes.preview: Actor axes keep separate how an actor accesses the system, what it can do, how it is invoked, and what role it plays.
actor_axes.card: Rather than ranking actors on one scale from weak to strong, the system measures them along several axes at once. The primary axis is substrate authority, which marks whether an actor has live, direct access to the system's own files and tools (Type A) or works from an interface, an API, an injected copy of context, or the public web without that direct access (Type B). The other axes, including capability tier, invocation surface, topology role, evidence access, purpose lane, and reasoning budget, are recorded separately so that being clever, being expensive, and being delegated never get confused with having authority over the real material.
actor_axes.rule: When an actor is described by where it sits on these axes, read each axis on its own. A capable or costly actor is not automatically one with direct authority over the system, and a delegated helper with live access can hold more authority than a powerful service that only sees a copy.
actor_axes.deep: The decisive axis is substrate authority: a tool-using agent with live access to the repository counts as Type A, while operator dashboards, bridges, hosted models, and anything reasoning over injected or public context count as Type B unless they too hold live access to the private material.

admitted_proof_step.label: admitted proof step
admitted_proof_step.preview: An admitted proof step is a gap left deliberately in a proof: a step assumed rather than proved, which the proof checker accepts on request and flags.
admitted_proof_step.card: It is the single most important number to check in any formal corpus. One admitted step in the wrong place can carry an entire result, so a large corpus with an admission may establish less than a small one without. Formal systems make this checkable rather than a matter of trust, because the checker records every admission.
admitted_proof_step.rule: Check the admitted-step count first. Everything downstream of an admission is assumed, not proved.
admitted_proof_step.deep: The reason to publish the count rather than the intention is that admissions are normal during development and easy to leave behind. The number is a fact about the corpus as shipped.

affordance_row.label: affordance row
affordance_row.preview: An affordance row is one selectable navigation entry that says what an artifact is, why to open it, and where its source evidence lives.
affordance_row.card: The system organises navigation as rows, not as monolithic documents. Each affordance row is the atomic unit of that navigation surface: it states one option, the next thing an agent or reader could open, along with enough structured detail to decide whether to open it. A row can be shown at different depths, from a one-line flag through a fuller card to a detailed view with the exact command that produced its evidence, so a choice can be made from a budgeted menu instead of by searching through source files.
affordance_row.rule: When you meet an affordance row, read it as one option on a menu: it tells you what the thing is, what opening it costs, and what backs it, so you can decide your next read without scanning the underlying files.
affordance_row.deep: The row compresses choice rather than content: it turns "what can I do with this artifact" into source-derived structure, with each row being projectable at several depths, linked to its evidence, marked with a lifecycle state, and typed by what it is allowed to claim.

agent.label: agent
agent.preview: An agent is a software-controlled worker that can interpret instructions, inspect context, use permitted tools, and produce or change artifacts.
agent.card: On this site, an agent is not a person and not an autonomous authority. It acts through a bounded tool and permission surface, and its outputs still require source checks and validation.
agent.rule: Judge an agent by the evidence and permissions attached to its actions, not by how fluent its explanation sounds.
agent.deep: Different agents may have different contexts, tools, runtimes, and mutation rights even when they use the same underlying model.

agent_reliability.label: agent reliability and safety
agent_reliability.preview: Agent reliability and safety is the question of whether an AI agent's report of what it did matches what it actually did, and whether it stays inside the limits it was given.
agent_reliability.card: An agent can say it committed a fix, ran a test, or finished a task, in fluent prose, with none of it having happened. Reliability work checks the report against the record the action would have left. Safety work checks the second half: whether the agent stayed inside its sandbox, refused what it should refuse, and did not quietly widen its own permissions.
agent_reliability.rule: A component in this area checks a specific failure it can reproduce. None of them establishes that an agent is reliable in general.
agent_reliability.deep: It is the largest area of the public release, with 20 components. The worked example on the landing page belongs to it: an audit that runs real git and pytest against notes carrying three planted forgeries, and is required to name each refusal.

agent_seed.label: agent seed
agent_seed.preview: An agent seed is the durable, attributed record of an AI agent's own observations, synthesis, and drift signals, kept separate from raw seed so agent interpretation cannot be mistaken for the operator's original words.
agent_seed.card: When a coding agent working inside this system learns something worth keeping, such as a pattern it noticed or a correction it made, it deposits that into an agent seed rather than into the operator's raw seed. The deposit is stamped with the agent that wrote it and the sources it drew on. It is treated as useful but lower authority than the operator's own statements of intent, so the system can retain what an agent learned without that material being mistaken for the operator's voice.
agent_seed.rule: Take an agent seed as an AI agent's recorded reasoning, attributed to that agent, not as the operator's intent. It carries who wrote it and what it drew on, so weigh it accordingly.
agent_seed.deep: Keeping agent-authored synthesis in its own seed is what lets the system absorb an agent's learning while the operator's raw seed stays the higher authority on intent, with neither layer impersonating the other.

agent_trace.label: agent trace
agent_trace.preview: An agent trace is the recorded sequence of what an AI agent actually did during a session: the calls it made, the files it touched, and the order it did them in.
agent_trace.card: An agent's own account of its work is a summary written by the thing being audited. The trace is the record underneath it, and the two can disagree. Keeping the trace separate is what makes it possible to check whether a reported action occurred, which is a different question from whether the report is plausible.
agent_trace.rule: Compare an agent’s closeout with the captured trace, but read the trace only within its instrumentation coverage: it is evidence for recorded events, not proof that every action was observed.
agent_trace.deep: This is the same discipline the rest of the site applies to itself: prose describing a run is not the run. An agent is simply a case where the prose is unusually convincing.

ai_native.label: AI-native
ai_native.preview: AI-native describes a system or workflow designed around AI agents doing bounded, inspectable work through explicit tools, records, permissions, and checks.
ai_native.card: The phrase describes architecture, not intelligence or correctness. Agents are expected to inspect, build, maintain, route, or validate artifacts, while human direction, source authority, and separate checks still constrain the result.
ai_native.rule: Read AI-native as a description of how the workflow is organized, never as proof that the workflow is autonomous, reliable, or correct.
ai_native.deep: The system makes agent context, tool access, durable state, handoffs, and validation first-class because agent work must survive beyond one chat and remain open to inspection.

algorithm.label: algorithm
algorithm.preview: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps for transforming specified inputs into outputs.
algorithm.card: An algorithm describes the procedure independently of one programming language or implementation. Correctness, termination, and efficiency are separate properties that need their own arguments or measurements.
algorithm.rule: Ask what inputs the algorithm accepts, what output it promises, and under which assumptions it terminates.
algorithm.deep: Two implementations can realize the same algorithm while differing in performance, numerical behavior, and failure handling.

allowed.label: allowed
allowed.preview: Allowed describes an action, value, or state that a governing rule or authority permits within stated conditions.
allowed.card: Permission can be conditional, role-specific, time-limited, or scoped to one target. Absence of an explicit prohibition is not always the same as an affirmative grant of authority.
allowed.rule: Before acting on an allowance, identify who grants it, the target, conditions, and any limits or required records.
allowed.deep: Allowed means permitted, not recommended, safe in every context, or guaranteed to succeed.

anchor.label: anchor
anchor.preview: An anchor is a stable reference point used to attach, locate, or route related material.
anchor.card: In web pages an anchor identifies a destination within a document; in evidence and explanation it can be the source fact or concept around which other claims are organized.
anchor.rule: Use an anchor only when its identifier and owning surface remain stable enough for the intended reference.
anchor.deep: Anchors improve reachability but do not strengthen the authority or truth of the material they locate.

annex.label: annex
annex.preview: An annex is a curated account of reusable patterns from an external framework, repository, or document, translated into this system's vocabulary without importing the outside source as local authority.
annex.card: Annexes live under the `annexes/` directory and hold shape-level notes about external sources: what problem each one solves and which patterns are worth borrowing. They exist so that before a piece of machinery is built from scratch, the system can check whether the same shape has already been solved elsewhere and translate the idea in, rather than re-deriving it or forking another project's structure. Each annex is a reference point for a pattern, never a binding rule the system must obey.
annex.rule: Treat an annex as a pointer to outside prior art, not as part of the system's own authority. It tells you where a pattern came from and how it was adapted, not what the system is required to do.
annex.deep: The governing discipline is adapt, do not adopt: an external primitive is compared against the local one and a more coherent version is synthesised when the evidence supports it, so the system can learn from open work without taking on its ontology.

answer.label: answer
answer.preview: An answer is a response intended to resolve or address a question, request, or problem.
answer.card: A useful answer matches the question's scope, distinguishes known facts from inference, and makes supporting evidence or uncertainty visible. It can be partial when the boundary is explicit.
answer.rule: Evaluate an answer by relevance, support, completeness for the stated scope, and honesty about what remains unresolved.
answer.deep: An answer can be correct yet unhelpful if it addresses a different question or hides the route needed to verify it.

apache_2_0.label: Apache-2.0
apache_2_0.preview: Apache-2.0 is a permissive open-source licence: anyone may use, modify, and redistribute the code, including commercially, provided they keep the required notices.
apache_2_0.card: It is one of the permissive licences, meaning it does not require anyone who redistributes the code to publish their own changes, which is what separates it from the copyleft family such as the GPL. What it does require is that the notices travel with the code: the licence text, the copyright line, and a statement of any file that was modified. It also grants every user a patent licence from the contributors, and withdraws that grant from anyone who brings a patent claim alleging the work infringes.
apache_2_0.rule: The licence governs what a recipient may do with the published files. It grants nothing over the private system those files were taken from, makes no warranty, and carries no claim that the code is correct.
apache_2_0.deep: The choice matters for a reader deciding whether they can build on this. Permissive terms plus an explicit patent grant is the combination most commonly accepted inside companies, so the published components can be run, modified, and embedded without a legal review of the kind a copyleft licence would trigger. The reference page states the terms, the authorship, the no-affiliation note, and the point where the public source slice ends.

appeal_lifecycle.label: appeal lifecycle
appeal_lifecycle.preview: An appeal lifecycle is the governed path for formally challenging a label or decision—from dispute, failure classification, and repair ownership through recorded reasoning to a resolution that either closes or reopens the judgment.
appeal_lifecycle.card: When the system makes a judgment, such as labelling a route or expecting a particular result, that judgment can be contested. The appeal lifecycle is the path that contest follows: the challenge is classified by cause, such as a model failure, a weak prompt, a lost packet, a wrong expected label, a stale projection, or a gap in the underlying scheme; it is handed to whichever plane is responsible for repair; it can hold back affected changes until it is settled; and it ends with a written rationale and, where needed, a test that proves the fix.
appeal_lifecycle.rule: Read where an appeal sits in its path before trusting the judgment it contests. A pending appeal means a judgment is under dispute and may be holding back the changes it touches; a closed one carries the rationale that settled it.
appeal_lifecycle.deep: The point of an appeal lifecycle is that disputed judgments turn into cumulative learning rather than one-off corrections: each appeal names the kind of error it found, so repeated challenges expose patterns in where the system gets things wrong.

apply.label: apply
apply.preview: An apply is the governed write step: it changes a named source target under a stated operation and validates the result.
apply.card: Apply is the execution half of the observe-then-apply pair: observing gathers candidate changes, applying is the only step permitted to alter the system's files and records. Each apply names what it touches and what operation it performs, validates the state before and after, and where possible records how to undo it. It is the disciplined gate through which any modification to the substrate must pass.
apply.rule: When something says it was applied, expect a specific target, a stated operation, and a before-and-after check behind it, not an unbounded edit. Observations alone do not change anything until an apply runs.
apply.deep: Apply exists to keep autonomous mutation disciplined: the system can surface many candidate insights, but only this lane is allowed to change source state, and only under explicit operation, validation, and rollback posture.

architecture.label: architecture
architecture.preview: Architecture is the high-level arrangement of a system's parts, responsibilities, boundaries, and connections.
architecture.card: Architecture explains why parts are separated and how information or control moves among them. It is more durable than one implementation detail but still concrete enough to constrain implementation.
architecture.rule: Read an architectural claim by locating the components, interfaces, ownership boundaries, and intended flows it names.
architecture.deep: A diagram becomes architectural only when its boxes and edges correspond to real responsibilities and relationships.

area.label: area
area.preview: An area is a bounded region of a subject, system, interface, or field of work.
area.card: Areas group related material so a reader can approach a large whole through a recognisable concern. Their boundaries may overlap when one artifact serves several concerns.
area.rule: Use an area as a navigation and scope boundary, not as proof that everything inside it is uniform.
area.deep: An area is broader than one page or component and narrower than the entire system it helps organise.

argument.label: argument
argument.preview: An argument is an ordered chain of reasons intended to support a conclusion from stated assumptions or evidence.
argument.card: In mathematics, an argument explains why a statement follows; it may be informal prose or a fully formal proof. In evaluation prose, an argument can also defend or challenge an interpretation.
argument.rule: Check each premise, inference, and conclusion rather than accepting the argument's overall plausibility.
argument.deep: A valid logical form can still yield an unusable conclusion when a premise is false, unstated, or outside the intended scope.

artifact.label: artifact
artifact.preview: An artifact is any durable file, row, packet, page, record, or other inspectable object produced, maintained, or consumed by the system.
artifact.card: Artifact is the broad category; its kind determines how it should be read. Source artifacts may own truth, generated artifacts project other sources, and result artifacts preserve what a run found, so the word alone says nothing about authority.
artifact.rule: When something is called an artifact, identify its kind, producer, authority posture, and freshness before relying on it.
artifact.deep: Treating every durable object as an artifact gives the system one inventory language while preserving the differences between source, generated, evidence, navigation, and compatibility roles.

artifact_kind.label: artifact kind
artifact_kind.preview: An artifact kind is the category an item belongs to—such as component, paper module, standard, principle, or doctrine card—used to choose the right collection before browsing its individual rows.
artifact_kind.card: The system is not one flat list of files. Its objects are grouped into a fixed set of kinds, and each kind has its own page where every member of that class is listed together. An artifact kind names one of those classes. Choosing a kind narrows the whole system to one type of thing, for example all components or all paper modules, before you open any single entry.
artifact_kind.rule: When you meet an artifact kind, read it as the category you are inside: it tells you what type of object every row on that page is, and the boundary of what that page can contain.
artifact_kind.deep: Each kind also carries a support status, recording whether its members can be browsed as full rows with source evidence or are only listed by name, so the kind sets your expectation of how much you can inspect.

atom_feed.label: Atom feed
atom_feed.preview: An Atom feed is a machine-readable list of a site's updates that a reader application can subscribe to.
atom_feed.card: A feed reader polls the file on a schedule and shows what has changed since the last look. That inverts the usual arrangement: nothing has to be handed over, no address is collected, and stopping is a local action rather than a request to a sender. It is the same idea as RSS, standardised later and more strictly.
atom_feed.rule: The feed carries what the site publishes and nothing about who reads it. Subscribing is not a signal to the author that anyone is reading.
atom_feed.deep: It is offered here in place of a mailing list, alongside GitHub Watch, releases, and discussions, which are the other routes for following the work. Each of those is a pull rather than a push, so the reader keeps the decision about when and whether to look.

audit.label: audit
audit.preview: An audit here is a check of whether a report matches what actually happened, rather than a check of whether the work itself was correct.
audit.card: It is a narrower thing than the word usually implies. An audit compares an account against a record, so it catches an action reported but not taken, or taken and not reported. Whether the action was a good idea is a separate question the audit does not touch.
audit.rule: An audit tells you whether a report was faithful, not whether the work was right.
audit.deep: This is the check most systems lack, because a component's own summary is normally the only account of what it did, and it is written by the thing under examination.

authority.label: authority
authority.preview: Authority is the recognized right of a particular source, rule, or actor to settle a stated kind of fact or permit a stated action.
authority.card: Authority is always scoped: a registry may own an identifier, a theorem checker may settle proof validity, and an operator may authorize publication. None of those roles automatically owns the others.
authority.rule: Ask who or what is allowed to settle this exact question before treating a statement as final.
authority.deep: A useful system keeps authority close to the artifact that can actually maintain the fact and prevents summaries or generated views from silently inheriting it.

axiom.label: axiom
axiom.preview: An axiom is a primitive, non-derived constraint the system treats as always binding, sitting above the principles that interpret it into behaviour for particular situations.
axiom.card: The doctrine is layered: axioms at the top, then principles, then standards and skills below them. An axiom is a formal declaration that holds across every context the system operates in, such as voice authority, projection discipline, or operator scope. A principle is derived from an axiom and judged against it in a bounded setting, whereas the axiom is the fixed point the rest of the lattice composes against. The system targets roughly seven such axioms, and they remain provisional.
axiom.rule: Read an axiom as the strongest, most general commitment on the page: if a lower rule appears to conflict with it, the axiom is what holds. It states an invariant, not a procedure.
axiom.deep: An axiom relates to a principle the way a mathematical axiom relates to a theorem: the principle is derived and judged against the axiom, while the axiom is taken as given. A well-chosen axiom makes the principles and standards beneath it easier to derive, because it captures a single design intuition the whole system holds constant.

back_end.label: backend
back_end.preview: The backend is the machinery a system runs on: the processing, storage and logic behind whatever a person sees.
back_end.card: Most of what is published here is backend. That is not an accident of scope, it is where the checkable claims live: a screen is demonstrated, whereas a routine that reads an input and writes a result can be run by anyone and compared.
back_end.rule: Backend claims are the ones you can test yourself. Weigh them accordingly.
back_end.deep: The asymmetry explains the shape of the release. What could be given away as evidence was given away; what could only be shown was recorded instead.

band.label: band
band.preview: A band is one named depth of description, from a one-word signal up to full evidence, that says what a short view must include, may omit, and must link onward to.
band.card: Many records on this site are written as a ladder of bands rather than a single block of text: word, phrase, flag, card, context, deep, and evidence, depending on the profile. The same item is available at each band, and the bands sit one inside the next like a telescope or a set of nested dolls, so a short browse can open into a working summary and then into full detail. A band is governed by a contract, not by a word count, so what appears at each level is fixed by rule rather than by how much someone happened to write.
band.rule: A band tells you the depth of what you are reading, not just its length. If a band does not answer your question, follow it down to the next band rather than assuming the detail is absent.
band.deep: The depth ladder belongs to a compression profile, which declares the full set of bands and what each one must hold; an individual record then fills those bands in. This is why a description can be expanded or collapsed in a predictable way, and why drift is flagged against one specific band rather than the whole file.

barrier.label: barrier
barrier.preview: A barrier is a proved result showing that a particular route to a problem cannot work, closing off an approach rather than advancing towards a solution.
barrier.card: Barriers are the most useful negative results and the easiest to overstate. One that closes two approaches can read as closing the subject, and the difference matters entirely: an approach still open after a barrier is where the remaining work is. Every barrier recorded here is required to state what it does not rule out.
barrier.rule: For any barrier, read what it leaves open. That is the part that decides what to do next.
barrier.deep: This requirement came from a real error rather than from caution. A parity obstruction was carried to the edge of publication as closing the certificate engines for one problem; a third, weaker engine in the same file was untouched by it and was found by accident. No surface recorded which engines existed, so nothing could have caught it.

base.label: base
base.preview: In these papers, a base is the number whose successive powers organize a numeral expansion or appear in the denominators of a series.
base.card: Base two gives powers 2, 4, 8, and so on, while base three-halves gives rational powers. Changing the base can change the arithmetic enough that a theorem at one base says little about another.
base.rule: Check which base a series or digit argument uses before transferring a result.
base.deep: Integer bases support ordinary positional digit expansions, while rational bases introduce extra denominator structure that can defeat arguments built for whole-number bases.

basis.label: basis
basis.preview: A basis is a smallest collection of building blocks from which everything in a space can be assembled, each thing in exactly one way.
basis.card: Exhibiting an explicit basis is stronger than knowing one exists, because it lets a computation replace an argument: every element becomes a finite list of coefficients.
basis.rule: A basis for one space says nothing about a different space until a map between them is given.
basis.deep: The Erdős #249 work gives an explicit rational basis for the dyadic sections of Euler's totient, with dimension one at level zero and exactly two to the e plus one at every level e at least one, which is Lean-checked. That is a theorem about the coefficients of the series, not about its irrationality.

benchmark.label: benchmark
benchmark.preview: A benchmark is a fixed set of tasks, inputs, metrics, and scoring rules used to compare performance under repeatable conditions.
benchmark.card: A benchmark makes comparison possible only inside its declared design. Its usefulness depends on representative tasks, protected answers, honest scoring, and resistance to leakage or gaming; a benchmark score is never a general measure of intelligence or safety.
benchmark.rule: Read a benchmark result together with its task set, metric, baseline, and leakage controls.
benchmark.deep: Benchmarks are measurement instruments whose validity can drift when systems train on the test set, optimize to the metric, or exploit quirks that do not transfer to the intended real-world task.

binary_expansion.label: binary expansion
binary_expansion.preview: A binary expansion is a representation of a number using powers of two and digits limited to zero and one.
binary_expansion.card: For numbers between zero and one, the digits appear after the binary point just as decimal digits appear after a decimal point. A rational number has an eventually repeating expansion, which turns some irrationality questions into questions about whether repetition is possible.
binary_expansion.rule: When an argument uses binary digits, ask whether it concerns the exact infinite expansion or only a computed prefix.
binary_expansion.deep: Finite computation can reveal a long prefix but cannot prove that no repeating tail ever begins, so digit evidence alone does not establish irrationality.

bind.label: bind
bind.preview: To bind two things is to record an explicit connection that later readers or checks are expected to preserve and follow.
bind.card: A binding is stronger than mentioning two things in the same paragraph. It names the relationship, identifies both sides, and makes the connection inspectable so later work can detect when one side changes or disappears.
bind.rule: When text says one object binds another, look for the recorded relationship and the rule that depends on it.
bind.deep: Bindings turn an implied association into system state: evidence can bind to a claim, a path can bind to an artifact, and a status can bind to the actions it permits.

blocked.label: blocked
blocked.preview: Blocked describes work or movement that cannot proceed because a named condition, dependency, permission, or obstacle prevents it.
blocked.card: A blocker should be actionable or at least observable: it identifies what cannot happen, why, and what change would permit progress. Delay or difficulty alone does not necessarily constitute a block.
blocked.rule: When something is blocked, verify the blocking condition and the exact re-entry condition rather than assuming the whole task is impossible.
blocked.deep: Blocks are scoped to paths through a process; an alternative safe route may remain open even when one path is blocked.

board.label: board
board.preview: A board is a shared visual or structured surface that organizes items, status, decisions, or controls for collective inspection.
board.card: Boards turn many records into an at-a-glance operational view. They are usually projections over underlying data, so freshness and update ownership determine how much reliance they deserve.
board.rule: Use a board to orient and select items, then follow its routes to the owning records for exact evidence.
board.deep: A board can coordinate action without becoming the source authority for every item it displays.

body.label: body
body.preview: A body is the main substantive content of a document, page, paper, or record, excluding its surrounding navigation and metadata.
body.card: The body carries what a reader is meant to read in full. Titles, menus, summaries, and indexes may point to a body without duplicating it.
body.rule: Follow the body pointer when a synopsis is too compressed to support the claim you need.
body.deep: Separating body content from navigation and metadata lets the site package, search, and deduplicate long texts without treating every presentation as a second copy.

bound.label: bound
bound.preview: A bound is a limit past which a quantity is shown not to go, in one direction or the other.
bound.card: Bounds are how finite work says something about an infinite question. Checking every case is impossible; proving that any failure must occur beyond a certain point, and then checking everything below it, is not. Much of the computation here has that shape.
bound.rule: A bound tells you where something cannot be. Whether the remaining region is searchable is a separate question.
bound.deep: The useful bounds are the sharp ones. A bound that leaves an infinite region unexamined converts a problem into a smaller problem rather than closing it.

bridge.label: bridge
bridge.preview: A bridge is a one-round transport that sends a bounded context-and-instruction packet to an external worker and returns its response, without giving that worker independent browsing, iteration, or mutation control.
bridge.card: A bridge carries one prompt packet out to an external worker, such as a separate reasoning model or research run, and carries one response packet back. The worker sees only what the controlling lane chose to send, and the response returns as candidate evidence that the owning lane then validates, imports, or discards. The same packet can be sent to many workers in parallel, which is what makes a bridge useful for research, parallel reasoning, and large population work.
bridge.rule: Treat anything a bridge returns as a worker's answer to a fixed packet, not as a decision the system has already acted on. The surrounding lane owns what was sent and what is done with the reply.
bridge.deep: The orchestration around a bridge, choosing the context, holding the schema, reading results back, validating them, and deciding on any change, belongs to the controller or mission runner, never to the bridge itself.

build.label: build
build.preview: A build is the process, or the resulting artifact set, produced by transforming source files through declared tools and configuration.
build.card: Building can compile code, render pages, package data, and validate invariants. A successful build proves that those configured transformations completed, not that every claim in the output is true.
build.rule: Distinguish the build process from its outputs and record the source revision and toolchain used.
build.deep: Reproducible builds make the same declared inputs yield equivalent outputs, which turns unexplained drift into a diagnosable difference.

bundle.label: bundle
bundle.preview: A bundle is a component's evidence packaged as files you can open: the source bodies it ran, the fixtures it read, and the result record it wrote, exported together so the run can be inspected without the private system.
bundle.card: A claim is easy to make and hard to check. The bundle is the checkable form: rather than describing what a component does, it ships the actual bodies, inputs, and outputs of a run in one place. That is the difference between reading an account of a check and holding the check. Bundles are metadata-only where the underlying data is private, so what you get is the shape and the verdict, not the substrate.
bundle.rule: When a component claims something, open its bundle. If there is no bundle, you are reading a description rather than evidence.
bundle.deep: Bundles exist because this site publishes components whose full source is not published. Without them a reader would have to trust the summary. With them the trust moves to something narrower and testable: that the exported bytes match the source they claim to come from, which the build checks by digest on every run.

call.label: call
call.preview: A call is an invocation that asks a function, command, service, tool, or person to perform a named operation.
call.card: Technical calls have inputs, a target, execution conditions, and an output or effect. In prose, called can also assign a name, so the surrounding grammar matters.
call.rule: For an operational call, identify the invoked target, arguments, authority, and result.
call.deep: Issuing a call does not guarantee successful completion; errors, timeouts, refusal, or partial effects may follow.

care.label: care
care.preview: Care is the judgment trait of treating correctness, human stakes, and future upkeep as part of the work, so a result is not merely produced but left findable, trustworthy, refreshable, and safe to extend.
care.card: Care is what turns a stake into upkeep. An agent acting with care makes maintenance, continuity, and the comprehension of whoever comes next into visible obligations: it fixes route gaps, preserves provenance, avoids bloating adapters, and leaves explicit closeout records of what was done. It is not a decorative value word. On this system it attaches to concrete actions such as running validators, probing routes, and recording receipts, so the care can be seen in evidence rather than merely asserted.
care.rule: When work here is described as done with care, look for the upkeep it left behind: a closeout record, a validator that ran, a preserved trail. Care that leaves no such trace is just a word.
care.deep: Care is one register within the broader judgment surface that governs how agents act on the system. It sits under the standards rather than floating free of them, so it can justify extra validation, clarity, and propagation work only when that work is anchored to evidence commands and recorded outcomes.

carry.label: carry
carry.preview: To carry something is to contain, transport, preserve, or make it operative across a boundary or transition.
carry.card: On this site, records carry fields, artifacts carry claims, and proof steps carry assumptions forward. The verb should identify what is conveyed and whether it remains unchanged.
carry.rule: When something carries information or authority, trace the source and the rule that permits the transfer.
carry.deep: Carrying a claim does not strengthen it; limitations and dependencies must travel with the claim if the transfer is faithful.

case.label: case
case.preview: A case is one particular set of conditions or inputs considered separately inside a larger question, test, or proof.
case.card: Dividing work into cases makes differences explicit: a rule may hold for one input class and fail for another. Covering several cases does not establish unexamined ones.
case.rule: Check which conditions define the case and whether the collection of cases is complete.
case.deep: In proofs a case is a branch of an argument; in tests it is a concrete input and expected outcome; in both uses its boundary must be stated.

certificate.label: certificate
certificate.preview: A certificate is a finite piece of data that makes a fact checkable by direct computation, so a machine can confirm the case rather than follow an argument.
certificate.card: Certificates are how a formal corpus grows to this size. Rather than proving each case by argument, a generator emits the data for each one and the proof checker confirms it. That is why declaration counts run to six figures while the number of distinct human ideas stays small: most of the corpus is checked, not written.
certificate.rule: A certificate establishes its own case. A family of them does not establish the general statement unless something proves the family covers it.
certificate.deep: This is the exact gap between a very large verified corpus and a solved problem, and it is where the remaining work on these problems sits.

change.label: change
change.preview: A change is a transition by which something becomes different in content, state, location, behaviour, or interpretation.
change.card: Changes should be described against a before-state and after-state. Their significance depends on the affected boundary, downstream consequences, and whether the transition was intended and authorized.
change.rule: Read a change through its target, delta, reason, authority, and validation.
change.deep: A visible file edit may be only one projection of a deeper source change, while a generated rewrite may alter many bytes without changing reader-visible meaning.

changelog.label: changelog
changelog.preview: A changelog is a chronological record of notable changes made to a project, product, document, or release.
changelog.card: A useful changelog tells readers what changed and often why, without reproducing every low-level edit. It supports orientation across versions but does not replace source history or validation evidence.
changelog.rule: Use a changelog to identify relevant changes, then inspect the linked source or release evidence for exact detail.
changelog.deep: Selection matters: a changelog is curated for readers, whereas a commit history records a finer-grained sequence of repository events.

check.label: check
check.preview: A check is a command you can run that tests one stated claim and writes down what it found.
check.card: Checks are the unit of evidence here. Each is a real command rather than a description of one, runs on your machine rather than a server, reads committed inputs, and leaves a result record behind. That is the whole mechanism: the claim says what should be true, the check finds out, and the record is what remains afterwards.
check.rule: Run the check. Reading about a check establishes nothing that running it would.
check.deep: A check is only as informative as its ability to fail, which is why the negative cases matter more than the passing ones. A check that cannot fail is a formality with the appearance of rigour.

checker.label: checker
checker.preview: A checker is a tool or procedure that evaluates an input against explicit rules and reports whether those rules are satisfied.
checker.card: Checkers make repeatable judgments over a bounded property such as syntax, links, types, or proof validity. Their result inherits both the strength and the blind spots of the encoded rules.
checker.rule: Read a checker result together with the rules it implements, the inputs it examined, and its failure behaviour.
checker.deep: A checker can be fully correct about its own rule set while that rule set remains incomplete for a broader real-world goal.

citation.label: citation
citation.preview: A citation names the exact work, version and author a claim or result comes from.
citation.card: The Lean repository's CITATION.cff gives the metadata for its citation anchor release. If Plectis materially helped a result, the request is to cite the release and say so. The credit policy separates citing the project from crediting a person.
citation.rule: Cite the pinned release, not the moving branch, so the cited object cannot change under the reference.
citation.deep: The problem notes cite Erdős's original statements and the prior work they build on, so each result's context can be checked independently of this site.

claim.label: claim
claim.preview: A claim is a stated assertion about what something does or establishes, written down separately from the evidence for it so the two can be compared.
claim.card: Every component here states its claim in one place and ships its check in another. Keeping them apart is what makes the pair checkable: a claim that drifts wider than its evidence becomes visible as a mismatch rather than blending into the surrounding description. The wording of a claim is treated as an artefact in its own right, and edits to it are checked.
claim.rule: Read the claim and the check together. A claim with no check behind it is a description.
claim.deep: The failure this guards against is gradual. Nobody rewrites a claim into a lie; wording widens a little at a time until it covers ground the evidence never did, which is why the relationship is registered rather than remembered.

claim_registry.label: claim registry
claim_registry.preview: The claim registry is the reviewed list of what the formal work is asserted to establish, kept separately from the proofs themselves.
claim_registry.card: A proof corpus does not say what it means. The registry is where each public assertion is written down with its status, which formal statement supports it, and how far it reaches. Keeping it separate is what allows a check that the wording still matches the mathematics after either changes.
claim_registry.rule: The registry states the claims. The corpus states the theorems. Compare them.
claim_registry.deep: Most of the corpus is deliberately not registered: checking a declaration does not promote it into a reviewed public claim, and treating those as the same thing would let unreviewed work inherit reviewed standing.

class.label: class
class.preview: A class is a category of things treated as sharing selected properties or, in programming, a definition for a family of objects and behaviour.
class.card: Plectis uses class in two explicit senses: a semantic or status class groups rows under one governed rule, while a software class defines instances and behaviour. The field or surrounding code must choose the sense; a label such as evidence class does not imply Python inheritance.
class.rule: Resolve class from the owning schema or code locus, then ask which properties membership guarantees and which other axes remain independent.
class.deep: Class membership is deliberately only one axis. An agent class, evidence class, or failure class does not silently confer authority, quality, status, or permission unless the governing contract says so.

clean.label: clean
clean.preview: Clean describes a condition with no detected unwanted residue, conflict, error, or modification under a stated check.
clean.card: The relevant check must be named: a clean worktree has no reported file changes, while a clean validation has no detected violations. Cleanliness is therefore bounded by the detector and target.
clean.rule: Read clean as shorthand for a specific observed condition and find the command or rule that established it.
clean.deep: A clean result does not prove the absence of defects that the check was not designed or able to detect.

clone.label: clone
clone.preview: To clone a repository is to copy it, with its full history, onto your own machine so you can run and inspect it locally.
clone.card: Cloning is the first step in every route on this site that produces evidence rather than description. It needs no account and no permission, which is deliberate: the checks are meant to be run by people with no relationship to the author.
clone.rule: Cloning is how you stop taking this site's word for anything.
clone.deep: A clone is a copy at a moment in time. It goes stale as the published repository moves, which is why a result from an old local copy can describe a version nobody else can obtain.

close.label: close
close.preview: To close something is to complete its required ending conditions or make it no longer open for further action in its current state.
close.card: Closing a task, question, claim, or route requires different evidence. The word should name the condition that changed and any residual work deliberately left outside the closure.
close.rule: Treat closure as scoped: verify exactly what is closed and which conditions establish it.
close.deep: A closed loop records the result and connects it back to the surface that requested or governs the work.

closed_route.label: closed route
closed_route.preview: A closed route is an approach that was tried and shown, by proof or exact computation, not to reach its target.
closed_route.card: The long working records list closed routes beside the results. A route is recorded as closed so that the next person does not spend time rediscovering the same dead end, and so that the reason it failed can point to a different approach.
closed_route.rule: Read a closed route as evidence about a method, not about the problem.
closed_route.deep: A route closed under one representation of the problem can reopen under another, so each closed route names the coordinates it was tried in.

closeout.label: closeout
closeout.preview: Closeout is the end of a unit of work: the point at which what changed, what is still open, and what was deliberately not done are recorded, before the work is handed on.
closeout.card: Work that ends without a closeout leaves the next reader to reconstruct it. The closeout records the landed change, the residue, and the boundary of what was attempted, so a session can be picked up without archaeology. It also names what was left alone on purpose, which is otherwise indistinguishable from what was forgotten.
closeout.rule: Read a closeout for what it says was not done. That is usually the part that matters.
closeout.deep: The hardest thing to record honestly is the deliberate omission, because it reads like a gap. Naming it is what separates a bounded piece of work from an unfinished one.

code.label: code
code.preview: Code is text written in a programming or formal language so a computer or proof checker can parse and act on it.
code.card: Code may implement a program, specify data transformations, or state formal proofs. Its presence does not show that it has been run, tested, or reviewed.
code.rule: Inspect the language, version, dependencies, and execution evidence before making claims from code.
code.deep: Source code is a readable input; generated code, compiled binaries, and runtime behavior are distinct artifacts connected by a toolchain.

coding.label: coding
coding.preview: Coding is the activity of expressing instructions, data structures, and behaviour in a programming or formal language.
coding.card: Coding turns an intended operation into source that a machine or checker can interpret. It includes design choices and validation, not only typing characters.
coding.rule: Judge coding work by the behaviour and constraints of the resulting source, together with focused checks.
coding.deep: Code can be syntactically valid yet fail its purpose, so implementation intent and observable behaviour remain part of the work.

coding_agent.label: coding agent
coding_agent.preview: A coding agent is an AI tool that can run commands on your machine, such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, as distinguished from a chat assistant that can only read and quote.
coding_agent.card: The distinction decides what a review can establish. A coding agent clones the repository and runs the checks, so its report rests on runs that happened. A browser assistant reads the same pages and cites them, which is useful orientation but establishes nothing about whether the code works. This site separates the two routes deliberately rather than letting a reader assume any AI review is equivalent.
coding_agent.rule: Ask which route produced a review. What an agent ran is evidence; what it summarised is not.
coding_agent.deep: The asymmetry is not about model quality. A capable assistant that cannot execute is still limited to restating what the repository says about itself, which is exactly the claim under test.

cofinal.label: cofinal
cofinal.preview: A property is cofinal when it keeps recurring however far out you go, so past any index you name there is always a later one that has it.
cofinal.card: Cofinal is the word that separates a computation from a theorem in this corpus. Checking a property up to index three hundred thousand shows it holds there. It does not show that the property keeps recurring past every bound, and that gap is usually the whole remaining difficulty.
cofinal.rule: A finite check never establishes a cofinal statement, however far the check reaches.
cofinal.deep: Several papers here isolate the missing step as exactly a cofinal supply: for Erdős #68 a cofinal step that no proof supplies, for Erdős #251 cofinal non-integrality for every fixed shift length, and for Erdős #249 no cofinal supply of certificates. Naming the missing statement exactly is what those papers deliver; proving it is not.

cold_agent.label: cold agent
cold_agent.preview: A cold agent is a capable software agent beginning with no conversation history or memory of earlier work, forced to orient entirely from the durable files and routes available on disk.
cold_agent.card: A cold agent is a coding or reasoning agent that opens this system fresh, without the context a previous session would have carried, and without any unwritten shared knowledge to fall back on. To act safely it has to read the source, the standards, and the recorded state, and from those work out what each thing does, what opens it, what proves it, and what comes next. The system is designed so that this is possible: orientation comes from the artifacts, not from folklore held in someone's head.
cold_agent.rule: When a page assumes a cold agent, it is assuming you arrive with no prior context and everything you need is on the page or one click away. Take it at face value: if something cannot be worked out from the written artifacts, that is a gap in the system, not knowledge you were expected to already have.
cold_agent.deep: The cold-agent frame is a deliberate test the system applies to itself: every artifact should name what it does, what opens it, what proves it, and what comes next, so that an agent with no memory can make the next safe decision without re-deriving the whole system. It is the discipline that lets work continue across a wiped session, a switch of machine, or a handover between people and agents.

cold_clone.label: cold clone
cold_clone.preview: A cold clone is a fresh copy of a repository on a machine that has never seen it, used to check that the published thing works for a stranger rather than only for its author.
cold_clone.card: Software usually works on the machine that built it. A cold clone removes that advantage: nothing is cached, no local configuration is present, and no undeclared dependency is quietly satisfied. It is the cheapest way to find out whether what was published is what was tested, and it routinely finds gaps that pass on the author's laptop.
cold_clone.rule: Use a cold-clone result as evidence that the named published revision and declared commands work without the author’s local state; do not extend it to environments or behaviors the probe did not exercise.
cold_clone.deep: This matters more here than usual, because local checkouts of a published repository drift quickly. A result taken from a stale working copy can describe a version nobody else can obtain, which is a claim about the author's disk rather than about the release.

combinatorics.label: combinatorics
combinatorics.preview: Combinatorics is the area of mathematics that studies finite or discrete arrangements, selections, counts, and structural patterns.
combinatorics.card: Combinatorial questions often ask how many configurations exist or whether a particular arrangement must occur. Proofs use counting, extremal arguments, probability, algebra, and graph structure.
combinatorics.rule: Identify the objects being arranged or counted and which configurations are considered distinct.
combinatorics.deep: Many problems associated with Erdős connect combinatorics with number theory, probability, and discrete geometry.

command.label: command
command.preview: A command is a concrete instruction submitted to a program, shell, or tool through its command interface.
command.card: A command names the program and arguments to run, but its effect also depends on the working directory, environment, permissions, and input files. Displaying a command is not evidence that it was executed.
command.rule: Record the command with its environment and result when reproducibility matters.
command.deep: Commands can read, create, change, publish, or delete state, so their authority and risk come from the invoked operation rather than the text alone.

commit.label: commit
commit.preview: A commit is one recorded change to a repository, carrying its own identifier, author, timestamp and complete contents.
commit.card: Commits are what make a history checkable rather than assertable. Each has a hash that identifies its exact contents, so citing a commit pins a claim to a specific state of the files rather than to whatever they say today. When something here reports a commit hash, that is the receipt.
commit.rule: When work is reported as done, look for the commit. The hash names exactly what changed.
commit.deep: A hash is not a signature. It proves which bytes, not who wrote them or whether they are correct.

common_sense.label: common sense
common_sense.preview: Common sense is governed, situation-aware judgment that combines the current state and surrounding rules to infer the right bounded action when no bespoke instruction spells it out.
common_sense.card: In this system common sense is the live judgment that connects fixed governance to the case in front of an agent. It reads the axioms, standards, routes, and recorded state, applies ordinary intelligence to the specific situation, checks whether the names and routes it assumes actually resolve, and acts on the cheapest truthful surface available. When the work reveals a reusable gap, such as a missing route, standard, or recorded fact, the lesson is folded back into the artifact that owns it, with the originating case cited. It is the non-brittle part of the system's intelligence: source-backed and testable rather than improvised.
common_sense.rule: When a result is described as reached by common sense, read it as a judgment derived from the system's stated rules and live state, not as a guess. It should be traceable back to the routes, facts, and standards it drew on.
common_sense.deep: Its defining discipline is that the judgment must stay reusable: routes are expected to resolve through the system's own lookups, facts that can change are projected or queried rather than frozen, and a durable local lesson is propagated up into the owning artifact so a later agent can rely on it.

compact.label: compact
compact.preview: Compact describes material reduced in size or detail while preserving the information needed for its intended use.
compact.card: A compact view omits lower-priority detail so a reader can scan or choose quickly. It should retain routes to fuller evidence and make its omissions or boundary understandable.
compact.rule: Treat compact material as a navigation or decision aid and open the deeper source when omitted detail matters.
compact.deep: Good compression preserves decision-relevant distinctions; merely making text shorter can erase the very boundary a reader needs.

comparator.label: Comparator
comparator.preview: Comparator is a tool from the leanprover organisation that checks whether a submitted Lean proof proves a statement declared separately from it.
comparator.card: The separation is what gives it force. The statement to be proved is written down independently, so a proof of some adjacent easier statement is rejected rather than quietly accepted.
comparator.rule: Comparator checks the match between a proof and a declared statement. It is not peer review, not a novelty assessment, and not a claim that any problem is solved.
comparator.deep: In this corpus Comparator is pinned to a fixed commit and run over nineteen propositions, using no axioms beyond propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice. The same job runs a second fixture built to fail, with one statement altered, and counts as passed only when the checker rejects it by name.

compatibility_route.label: compatibility route
compatibility_route.preview: A compatibility route is an old URL or identifier retained solely to redirect readers to the current Plectis surface, preserving access without reviving the retired name as the live one.
compatibility_route.card: When a site is renamed or reorganised, links and identifiers that people already hold would otherwise break. A compatibility route is the machinery that keeps those old paths resolving: a tombstone page, a redirect, an alias, or a manifest entry that takes the visitor to the current location. It names the old route, the new route, the behaviour, and the scope, so the move is visible rather than silent.
compatibility_route.rule: Treat a compatibility route as a forwarding link, not as a second live site. Where it leads is the current surface; the old address it came from is retired.
compatibility_route.deep: A compatibility route is public migration infrastructure: it prevents broken links and keeps the history of earlier addresses inspectable, while making the current identity, Plectis, unmistakable. It does not rewrite the past or imply that the old name is endorsed.

compiled_binary.label: compiled binary
compiled_binary.preview: A compiled binary is the executable file a build produces from source code, in the form the machine actually runs.
compiled_binary.card: Two builds of the same source can produce different binaries, so recording the hash of the binary that ran says more about what happened than naming the source alone.
compiled_binary.rule: A hash of a binary identifies the file that ran. It does not by itself say the source it came from was correct.
compiled_binary.deep: The external verification job records both exit codes, the pinned tool revisions, and the hashes of the built binaries in one receipt bound to the commit under review.

compression.label: compression
compression.preview: Compression is the governed reduction of larger source material into a smaller navigable view that records what it preserves, what it omits, which profile and band shaped it, and how to reopen the authoritative source.
compression.card: In this system compression is governed, not casual. Every compact summary is produced under a declared profile that fixes how much detail a given band carries, so a one-line entry, a card, and a full module are different rungs of the same material rather than arbitrary trims. Each row records what was preserved and what was omitted, and keeps a path back to the source it stands for, so a reader can always open the fuller layer beneath any summary.
compression.rule: Treat a compressed row as a faithful but partial view: it carries an omission record and a route back to source, so when detail matters, follow that route rather than relying on the short form alone.
compression.deep: Compression here is the write side of navigation: standards declare the readable shapes, profiles declare the band contracts, and the resulting summaries are generated surfaces that let later readers spend attention deliberately. Where no profile governs a row, the system records a profile gap instead of inventing an ad hoc summary.

compression_profile.label: compression profile
compression_profile.preview: A compression profile is the repeatable rulebook for shortening one artifact kind, specifying its depth bands, mandatory content, allowed omissions, and forbidden collapses.
compression_profile.card: Each profile is tied to a specific artifact kind, such as a voice record, a relational map, a peer-knowledge note, or a term definition. It names the bands the artifact can be projected into, the schema each band must follow, the evidence policy, and the validation check, so that a cheap automated worker, a larger model, and a person all shorten the same artifact into the same shape. Four profiles run today, covering voice records, relational maps, peer-knowledge notes, and vocabulary terms.
compression_profile.rule: When a piece of content here is shown at varying lengths, the compression profile is what fixed which details had to survive and which were allowed to fall away; read it to know what a short form is guaranteed to still carry.
compression_profile.deep: Profiles are registered together so that compression behaves as a governed primitive: the stated design target is that every artifact kind eventually names its own profile, so that any worker producing a band yields an identical row shape.

concept.label: concept
concept.preview: A concept is a curated vocabulary entry that gives a recurring object, abstraction, or class of meaning one stable identifier and definition for other system records to reference consistently.
concept.card: Concepts are the system's defined nouns, as distinct from its procedures. Each one fixes a single object or idea, gives it a stable identifier and a short description, links to where it is defined in the source, and connects to the mechanisms and principles that use it. Together they form the shared ontology that mechanisms act on and principles reason about, so that a recurring object keeps one settled meaning across the whole system.
concept.rule: Treat a concept as the settled meaning of one named object. When something else on the site refers to it, read the concept to learn exactly what that object is, not how to do anything with it.
concept.deep: A concept is curated and source-linked rather than improvised, which is how the system keeps its vocabulary from drifting as it grows. It names a thing; the steps that act on that thing live in mechanisms and skills, not in the concept itself.

conditional_reduction.label: conditional reduction
conditional_reduction.preview: A conditional reduction proves that one statement would follow from another that is not itself proved, converting a problem into a different problem rather than solving it.
conditional_reduction.card: Reductions are real work and are routinely mistaken for progress towards a solution. What a reduction establishes is that the target now rests on a named, unproved hypothesis; whether that is easier than the original is a separate judgement nobody has made. The registry records these separately from unconditional results for that reason.
conditional_reduction.rule: For a conditional result, find the hypothesis it rests on. Nothing is settled until that is proved.
conditional_reduction.deep: The honest accounting is that a reduction moves the difficulty and reports where it went. Counting reductions alongside proofs would make a portfolio of open problems look like a portfolio of results.

conditional_theorem.label: conditional theorem
conditional_theorem.preview: A conditional theorem proves that a conclusion follows from a hypothesis that has not itself been proved.
