conditional_theorem.card: The proof of the implication can be completely rigorous, and machine-checked, while the conclusion remains unavailable because nobody has established the hypothesis. Reading only the conclusion of a conditional theorem is the commonest way to misread this corpus.
conditional_theorem.rule: Always read the antecedent. A conditional theorem asserts nothing about its conclusion until the hypothesis is proved.
conditional_theorem.deep: The Lean repository holds 259 conditional theorems. Their hypotheses are lifted out as 101 standalone propositions, 23 of them substantial, with 144 implications between those proved in Lean. Seventeen of the 23 turn out to be equal in strength to the open problem they were meant to approach, so that list is one problem restated many times.

confirm.label: confirm
confirm.preview: To confirm something is to obtain additional evidence that supports an existing expectation, claim, identity, or result.
confirm.card: Confirmation reduces uncertainty by checking a proposition through an appropriate observation or independent route. Its strength depends on whether the new evidence is genuinely informative rather than a repeat of the same unverified source.
confirm.rule: When a check confirms a claim, identify the proposition tested and whether the evidence is independent or merely derivative.
confirm.deep: Confirmation supports a claim within the check's boundary but does not eliminate untested alternatives or future change.

conjecture.label: conjecture
conjecture.preview: A conjecture is a precise mathematical statement believed or suspected to be true but not yet proved or disproved.
conjecture.card: Conjectures are informed research targets, often supported by examples, computation, analogy, or partial theorems. Those supports do not change the conjecture's unproved status.
conjecture.rule: Treat a conjecture as an open claim until a valid proof or counterexample settles it.
conjecture.deep: A conjecture may be reformulated into equivalent statements or divided into cases without becoming solved, and a catalogue can update its status as the literature changes.

connect.label: connect
connect.preview: To connect two items is to give a reader or program a traversable route from one to the other, usually with a label explaining their relationship.
connect.card: Connections make the site usable as a map rather than a pile of pages. A useful connection says not only where the other item is but why it is relevant—for example, that one file generated another or that one result supports a claim.
connect.rule: Follow the relationship label as well as the link, because a connection does not by itself mean equivalence, support, or authority.
connect.deep: A connection may be a hyperlink, source reference, typed relation, dependency edge, or command route; its meaning comes from the recorded relation, not from adjacency alone.

contact.label: contact
contact.preview: Contact is a supported way to reach a person, team, or service or the act of doing so.
contact.card: A contact point may be an email address, form, profile, or named route. Publishing it says how communication can begin, not that every message will receive a reply or produce an agreement.
contact.rule: Use the contact method for the purpose it states and respect its audience and privacy boundary.
contact.deep: Reachability, consent, identity, and responsiveness are separate properties even when one contact address is public.

content.label: content
content.preview: Content is the human- or machine-readable material carried by an artifact, apart from the container, route, and permissions around it.
content.card: Content can be prose, data, code, diagrams, or structured records. Its format and location do not by themselves determine its authority.
content.rule: Separate what an artifact contains from what the artifact is allowed to establish.
content.deep: The same underlying content can be projected into several formats, so identity and source pointers matter when deciding whether two surfaces are copies or independent claims.

context.label: context
context.preview: Context is the surrounding information, conditions, and relationships needed to interpret something appropriately.
context.card: The same word, result, or action can mean different things under different goals, files, environments, or prior statements. Context supplies those constraints without necessarily becoming part of the thing itself.
context.rule: Before interpreting a term or result, identify the relevant audience, task, source, time, and surrounding claims.
context.deep: More context is not automatically better; useful context is selected for the decision while preserving the boundaries that prevent misinterpretation.

context_window.label: context window
context_window.preview: A context window is the amount of text a language model can hold in view at once.
context_window.card: It is a hard limit rather than a preference. Anything outside the window has no effect on what the model produces, whether or not the model behaves as though it remembers.
context_window.rule: Work larger than the context window has to be navigated rather than read whole, which is a constraint on the system, not on the reader.
context_window.deep: The stated reason this system exists is that its author cannot hold it in his head and no agent can hold it in its context window, so claims about it have to be checkable rather than remembered.

continuity.label: continuity
continuity.preview: Continuity is the problem of carrying work across a break, so that a session which stops mid-task can be resumed without reconstructing what was happening.
continuity.card: AI sessions end, contexts fill, and machines restart. Continuity is the discipline of writing enough to disk that the next actor can pick up safely rather than guessing, and of being explicit about what is unfinished. It is one of the seven areas the components are grouped into.
continuity.rule: Continuity work is judged by whether a stranger could resume from what was written down.
continuity.deep: The failure is subtle: a handoff that reads confidently but omits what was uncertain leaves the next actor repeating settled work or trusting an unchecked claim.

continuous_integration.label: continuous integration
continuous_integration.preview: Continuous integration is a service that runs a project's checks automatically on every change, on a machine other than the author's.
continuous_integration.card: The difference from running checks by hand is that nobody has to remember. A check inside continuous integration runs on changes its author never thought about, including the ones that break it.
continuous_integration.rule: A test that exists in a repository and a test that runs in continuous integration are different claims. Only the second one keeps holding.
continuous_integration.deep: A July 2026 rerun found one component's forgery lane silently skipping when run from the terminal. It was fixed, and its test module is now part of the normal public CI floor, so the same regression would be caught rather than noticed by chance.

contradiction.label: contradiction
contradiction.preview: A contradiction is an impossible conclusion—such as a statement and its negation both holding—derived from a set of assumptions.
contradiction.card: In a proof by contradiction, the target is established by assuming its opposite and showing that assumption forces an impossibility. The proof is only as strong as the chain from the assumption to the contradiction.
contradiction.rule: Identify the assumption being rejected and the exact impossible statement it produces.
contradiction.deep: Irrationality proofs commonly assume a series is rational, extract a finite denominator or repeating pattern, and then show the required arithmetic structure cannot exist.

contributor_credit.label: contributor credit
contributor_credit.preview: Contributor credit is the recorded acknowledgement of who supplied an idea, a proof, a review, a formalisation, software or compute to the project.
contributor_credit.card: The credit policy in the Lean repository keeps solvers, collaborators, prior work, tools and infrastructure distinct. If you solve a problem, the result and the credit are yours and your collaborators'. If the project materially helped, the request is that you cite the release and say so. Credit is not automatic paper coauthorship.
contributor_credit.rule: Expect credit that names your contribution as what it is; do not expect coauthorship by default.
contributor_credit.deep: Tool use is disclosed separately from credit, so a contribution made with an AI agent is credited to the person who directed and stands behind it.

control.label: control
control.preview: Control is the ability or mechanism used to direct behaviour, constrain choices, or authorize changes.
control.card: Control may be exercised by a rule, interface, permission boundary, feedback loop, or person. It differs from observation because it can affect what happens rather than merely report it.
control.rule: When a surface is called control, identify which decisions it can make and which state it is permitted to change.
control.deep: Good control has a bounded target and visible feedback; otherwise direction can be applied without knowing whether it had the intended effect.

convergence.label: convergence
convergence.preview: Convergence means the partial sums of an infinite series approach one fixed finite value as more terms are included.
convergence.card: A convergent series has a well-defined sum even though no finite stage contains every term. Convergence says that the value exists; it does not say whether that value is rational, algebraic, transcendental, or easy to compute.
convergence.rule: Separate the question of whether a series converges from the question of what kind of number its limit is.
convergence.deep: Proofs control the tail left after a partial sum to show that all later sums remain arbitrarily close to one value, replacing an informal picture of settling down with a quantified statement.

coprime.label: coprime
coprime.preview: Two integers are coprime when their greatest common divisor is one, meaning they share no prime factor.
coprime.card: Coprime does not require either number to be prime; 8 and 15 are coprime even though both are composite. The condition is what lets modular inverses and multiplicative orders exist.
coprime.rule: Check coprimality with respect to the exact pair of integers named in the result.
coprime.deep: When a base is coprime to a denominator, repeated multiplication by that base cycles among invertible residue classes rather than collapsing to zero.

copy.label: copy
copy.preview: A copy is a reproduction of material placed in another location or representation.
copy.card: A copy may preserve the source exactly or transform it during copying. Its usefulness depends on knowing what it copies, when it was made, and whether later source changes are expected to propagate.
copy.rule: Treat a copy as secondary material unless an explicit rule promotes it to authority.
copy.deep: Exactness is a claim about correspondence at a particular time, while freshness asks whether the source has changed since then.

corpus.label: corpus
corpus.preview: A corpus is a fixed body of material treated as one collection, so results can be quoted against a known set rather than an open-ended one.
corpus.card: In Plectis, corpus means an enumerated body against which a count, proof, or check is made: for example, the published PDFs, Lean declarations, or another manifest-backed collection. Fixing membership makes the claim reproducible; a result over one corpus does not extend to future files or excluded material.
corpus.rule: Locate the manifest, revision, or membership rule before reading a corpus-wide count or coverage claim.
corpus.deep: Corpus is a measurement boundary, not a claim of representativeness or completeness. Plectis reports both raw declaration counts and deduplicated statement counts because the same fixed corpus can support different legitimate units.

correctness.label: correctness
correctness.preview: Correctness is the property of satisfying the specification, rule, or truth condition relevant to the thing being judged.
correctness.card: Software correctness relates behaviour to a specification, mathematical correctness relates reasoning to accepted rules and premises, and factual correctness relates a claim to reality. Each requires its own evidence.
correctness.rule: Read a correctness claim together with the standard and scope against which it was established.
correctness.deep: Local correctness does not automatically compose into whole-system correctness because interactions, assumptions, and uncovered conditions can introduce failure.

count.label: count
count.preview: A count is the number of items, events, or occurrences in a defined collection or measurement boundary.
count.card: Counts look simple but depend on what qualifies as one item, how duplicates are handled, and which period or source is included. Those rules determine whether two counts are comparable.
count.rule: Read every reported count with its unit, inclusion rules, and measurement boundary.
count.deep: A precise count can still answer the wrong question if the collection omits relevant items or combines unlike units.

counterexample.label: counterexample
counterexample.preview: A counterexample is a single case that fails a general statement, which is enough to disprove it.
counterexample.card: The asymmetry is total: proving a general claim requires covering every case, while refuting it requires exactly one. Several results here work by narrowing what a surviving counterexample would have to look like, which is progress even when none is found, because each constraint shrinks where one could hide.
counterexample.rule: A constraint on counterexamples is a real result even when no counterexample exists.
counterexample.deep: Narrowing is the usual shape of progress on a problem that resists both proof and refutation: the space of possible failures gets smaller without closing.

coverage.label: coverage
coverage.preview: Coverage is the measured portion of a declared population, surface, or requirement set that a process has actually inspected, represented, or satisfied.
coverage.card: Coverage is meaningful only when the denominator is named. A count of linked declarations, tested routes, or reviewed claims can show completeness inside a known inventory while saying nothing about objects that were never included in that inventory.
coverage.rule: Ask what the total population is, how membership was determined, and what uncovered items remain.
coverage.deep: A coverage receipt pairs the numerator with the authoritative inventory and the method used to match items, preventing a large count from masquerading as completeness over an undefined universe.

critic_posture.label: critic posture
critic_posture.preview: Critic posture is a repeatable way of testing an emerging idea by asking which abstraction is weak, which route has no answer, and which governing standard is missing, rather than offering a one-off objection.
critic_posture.card: Critic posture is one of the system's named judgment traits, used when people and an agent are working an idea out together. Instead of agreeing and moving on, it pauses to test the idea: it names the candidate term being introduced, checks whether the system can actually route to it, and asks what a newcomer would miss. When a criticism holds up under that test, it is not left as a passing remark; it is turned into something durable, such as a refined definition, a recorded rule, or a standard.
critic_posture.rule: When you meet critic posture on this site, read it as the discipline of pressing on an idea's weak points and then recording what survives, not as a separate reviewer or a verdict on the whole system.
critic_posture.deep: Its characteristic move is the failure question: what would a fresh reader miss here, which route currently fails, which standard is absent, or which single case is being treated as a general rule. A criticism that stays stable is then converted into a governed artifact rather than remaining a chat objection.

data.label: data
data.preview: Data is recorded information represented in a form that people or programs can store, inspect, and process.
data.card: Data can be measured, declared, copied, computed, or generated, and those origins affect what it can support. Structure makes data easier to validate but does not make it correct.
data.rule: Ask where the data came from, how it was transformed, and which schema and version apply.
data.deep: The same facts can appear in raw observations, normalized records, indexes, and presentation projections, so provenance is needed to avoid counting copies as independent evidence.

dataset.label: dataset
dataset.preview: A dataset is an identified collection of related data records assembled for analysis, testing, training, or reference.
dataset.card: A dataset needs a description of its membership, source, format, collection process, and known limitations. Size alone does not establish representativeness or quality.
dataset.rule: Read the dataset's provenance and sampling boundary before generalizing from it.
dataset.deep: Splits, filtering, deduplication, labels, and later corrections can materially change what a dataset supports even when its name remains the same.

decision.label: decision
decision.preview: A decision is a recorded choice among alternatives that determines a status, route, permission, or next action.
decision.card: A decision should name what was chosen, why, who or what had authority, and what evidence was considered. It can later be reviewed without pretending it was an objective fact.
decision.rule: Read a decision together with its authority, rationale, and consequences.
decision.deep: Separating decisions from observations prevents policy choices and judgment calls from being smuggled into the system as if they were measurements.

declaration.label: declaration
declaration.preview: A declaration is one named item in a proof library: a single theorem, definition or structure, as written in the source.
declaration.card: It is the unit the Lean corpus is counted in. Declarations are not equally interesting: one may be a substantial theorem and the next a mechanical step generated in bulk, and a count that does not separate them will mislead. That is why the corpus is reported both as raw declarations and as the far smaller number of distinct statements they reduce to.
declaration.rule: A declaration count measures size, not content. Ask how many distinct statements it reduces to.
declaration.deep: Counting declarations is the easiest metric to inflate and the least informative to inflate, because generated steps are cheap. The interesting figure is what survives deduplication.

declare.label: declare
declare.preview: To declare something is to state its value, status, dependency, or boundary explicitly in the governing data instead of leaving it to inference.
declare.card: A declaration makes a fact inspectable and checkable by giving it a named field or row. It improves accountability, but it does not make the statement true merely because someone wrote it down; evidence and validation still have to support it.
declare.rule: Treat a declared value as explicit input to a check, not as proof that the value is correct.
declare.deep: Declarations are useful because disagreement becomes visible: a builder can compare a declared source hash, status, scope, or dependency with the state it recomputes and fail when the two diverge.

definition.label: definition
definition.preview: A definition states what a term means in a particular context and which nearby meanings it excludes.
definition.card: A useful definition is self-contained enough for a cold reader and precise enough to distinguish the term from its siblings. It does not merely repeat the word or list examples.
definition.rule: Use the definition to identify the concept, then read its scope and non-example to find the boundary.
definition.deep: Definitions on this site are governed projections: they help readers interpret the public material but defer factual authority to the sources and records they describe.

denominator.label: denominator
denominator.preview: The denominator is the bottom number of a fraction, the one you are dividing by.
denominator.card: If an infinite sum turns out to be rational, it has an exact denominator, and that single number constrains everything about it. Several results here work by showing what the denominator would have to be and then showing no such number can exist, which is why so much of the argument is about denominators rather than about the sum.
denominator.rule: A statement about a possible denominator is a statement about whether the value can be rational at all.
denominator.deep: The denominator is the handle rationality gives you. It is the reason assuming rationality is productive: it converts an infinite object into a finite one you can reason about.

dependency.label: dependency
dependency.preview: A dependency is other software a project needs in order to run, which must be installed before its checks will work.
dependency.card: Undeclared dependencies are the usual reason something works for its author and fails for everyone else: the author's machine already had it. Declaring them is what makes a cold clone meaningful, and a probe that checks them before anything else is what turns a confusing failure into a clear one.
dependency.rule: Check that dependencies are declared before treating a project as runnable.
dependency.deep: The failure this prevents is silent rather than loud. An undeclared dependency does not announce itself; it simply makes the published thing work for exactly one person.

deployment.label: deployment
deployment.preview: A deployment is the act and recorded result of publishing a built artifact to the environment where its intended readers or users can access it.
deployment.card: Deployment moves a verified build into a live location and then checks that the served bytes match the intended output. It does not by itself approve the product, prove the content correct, or establish that every route works in every client.
deployment.rule: Treat deployed as an availability state and look for a separate live-verification receipt before assuming the intended build is being served.
deployment.deep: A reliable deployment binds the source revision, generated output, destination, content hashes, and post-publish probes so a later reader can distinguish successful publication from a command that merely exited without error.

derivation.label: derivation
derivation.preview: A derivation is an ordered sequence of valid transformations or inferences that obtains a result from stated starting material.
derivation.card: Derivations occur in mathematics, logic, data processing, and generated systems. Each step should follow an allowed rule so the result can be traced back to its premises or inputs.
derivation.rule: Check a derivation by examining its starting assumptions, transformation rules, intermediate steps, and final result.
derivation.deep: A derivation explains how a result follows; it does not by itself show that the starting assumptions accurately describe the intended real-world subject.

design.label: design
design.preview: Design is the intentional shaping of something's structure, behaviour, appearance, or use to satisfy stated goals and constraints.
design.card: Design connects purposes to choices. It includes trade-offs among usability, correctness, maintainability, cost, safety, and other requirements rather than appearance alone.
design.rule: Evaluate a design by the goals and constraints it addresses and by evidence from its actual use.
design.deep: A design can be coherent yet based on wrong requirements, so intent, implementation, and observed outcome must remain distinguishable.

deterministic.label: deterministic
deterministic.preview: Deterministic means the same declared inputs and environment produce the same output and decision every time, without hidden randomness or external variation.
deterministic.card: Determinism makes a result easier to reproduce and compare because changes in output can be attributed to changed inputs or code. The claim must name the relevant environment, since clocks, network responses, dependency versions, and unordered data can otherwise reintroduce variation.
deterministic.rule: When a process is called deterministic, check which inputs and environmental conditions are fixed.
deterministic.deep: Determinism is a property of the transformation under a specified boundary, not a promise that the transformation is correct or that every external system it calls will behave consistently.

diagram.label: diagram
diagram.preview: A diagram is a visual representation that uses spatial arrangement, shapes, and connections to explain structure or relationships.
diagram.card: Diagrams compress relationships that may be hard to scan in prose. Their labels and edges are selective, so the source graph or text remains necessary for exact membership and semantics.
diagram.rule: Use a diagram for orientation and follow its legend and source pointers for precision.
diagram.deep: A generated diagram can remain synchronized with structured source, while a hand-drawn diagram needs an explicit maintenance and freshness claim.

diebold_mariano_test.label: Diebold-Mariano test
diebold_mariano_test.preview: The Diebold-Mariano test compares the forecast errors of two competing methods and asks whether the difference between them is larger than chance would produce.
diebold_mariano_test.card: It is the standard first check on a claim that one forecasting method beats another. It compares two named methods on the same data, so it does not license a claim about methods it did not see.
diebold_mariano_test.rule: A significant result compares the two methods tested, on the sample tested. It is not a general ranking.
diebold_mariano_test.deep: Forecast-skill claims in this corpus are put through Diebold-Mariano, Hansen's superior predictive ability test, and a stationary bootstrap, over synthetic market fixtures. Synthetic fixtures mean the check establishes that the statistical machinery runs and refuses as specified, not that any live market was predicted.

digest.label: digest
digest.preview: A digest is a short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, used to check that two copies are byte-for-byte identical.
digest.card: Digests are how this site checks that a published copy really matches its source: the deploy compares the digest of every paper against the public repository before it will publish, and refuses if any differ. A digest proves sameness cheaply and exactly, which is worth more than a promise that nothing changed.
digest.rule: A matching digest proves the bytes are identical. It proves nothing about whether they are right.
digest.deep: This is the precise limit of digest-based evidence, and the reason components carry source bodies rather than only hashes: identical bytes can still be the wrong bytes.

directory.label: directory
directory.preview: A directory is a named container in a filesystem that groups files and other directories under one path.
directory.card: Directories organize location and ownership but do not by themselves state the meaning of their contents. A repository convention or index explains what belongs there.
directory.rule: Use the directory path to locate files and the governing documentation to understand their roles.
directory.deep: Renaming or moving a directory changes paths and can break references even when the contained files are unchanged.

disclosure.label: disclosure
disclosure.preview: Disclosure is the act or result of making relevant information visible to an intended audience.
disclosure.card: A disclosure can reveal limitations, interests, provenance, risks, or previously private facts. Good disclosure identifies what is being revealed, to whom, and for what decision.
disclosure.rule: Read a disclosure as bounded information and do not infer that unmentioned matters were also examined or released.
disclosure.deep: Transparency depends on relevance and clarity, not merely on publishing a large volume of material.

discrete_mathematics.label: discrete mathematics
discrete_mathematics.preview: Discrete mathematics studies structures made of distinct, separately countable objects rather than continuously varying quantities.
discrete_mathematics.card: Its subjects include combinatorics, graph theory, logic, algorithms, and many parts of number theory. Discrete does not mean small: an infinite set can still have discrete structure.
discrete_mathematics.rule: Look for individually distinguishable objects and exact relations rather than continuous change.
discrete_mathematics.deep: Computer science and formal proof frequently use discrete mathematics because symbolic states and program steps can be represented as countable structures.

divergence.label: divergence
divergence.preview: Divergence means that a sequence, series, or limiting process does not approach a finite limit in the stated sense.
divergence.card: Divergence is relative to a specified mode of convergence: values may grow without bound, oscillate, or fail to settle for another reason. The reason matters to later arguments.
divergence.rule: Identify the object and definition of convergence before reading a divergence claim.
divergence.deep: A divergent series can still have meaningful partial sums, transformed expressions, or alternative summation methods, but those are not ordinary convergence.

divisor.label: divisor
divisor.preview: An integer divisor of an integer n is an integer d for which n equals d times another integer.
divisor.card: The notation d ∣ n means that d divides n with no remainder. Divisibility is an exact integer relation, not an approximate numerical one.
divisor.rule: Check the domain and whether zero or negative divisors are included by the convention in use.
divisor.deep: Divisors organize factorisation, primality, congruences, and multiplicative functions such as Euler's totient. Distinguishing positive, negative, proper, and unit divisors is therefore a theorem-level convention, not cosmetic notation.

documentation.label: docs
documentation.preview: Docs are human-readable explanations and instructions that help a reader understand or use the system without replacing the source files, records, or contracts they describe.
documentation.card: Documentation supplies orientation, examples, and routes through the underlying material. Some docs are authored and some are generated, so a reader should check the page's source and freshness before treating a current detail as settled.
documentation.rule: Use docs to understand and navigate, then follow their source references for authority-sensitive claims.
documentation.deep: Documentation is a reading surface rather than one evidence class: a page may faithfully project live data, summarize a stable rule, or simply explain how to run a command, and those roles carry different authority.

doctrine.label: doctrine
doctrine.preview: Doctrine is the curated, searchable layer of principles, concepts, mechanisms, routes, and interpretations that explains why the system is shaped as it is, distinct from the code that implements those ideas.
doctrine.card: Doctrine is not one document but a network of governed artifacts: principles, anti-patterns, concepts, mechanisms, standards, and recorded lessons, each given a name and a place. It captures the operating theory of the system, the rules it holds itself to and the ideas it is built around, so that the reasoning behind a design is written down rather than left implicit. Each piece can be opened on its own and traced back to the source it came from.
doctrine.rule: Treat a doctrine entry as a statement of intent and principle, not as proof that the running code obeys it. It tells you what the system means to do and why; the matching component or check is where that intent is actually carried out.
doctrine.deep: Doctrine entries come in kinds, including axioms the system takes as given, principles it follows, anti-patterns it forbids, and concepts and mechanisms it names; together they form the meaning lattice the rest of the system is read against.

doi.label: DOI
doi.preview: A DOI is a permanent identifier that a publisher or repository mints for a document, so citations to it keep resolving after the document moves.
doi.card: The identifier resolves through a registration agency rather than through whatever web address a document currently sits at, which is the whole point: a publisher can reorganise its site, or a repository can move, and existing citations keep working. Getting one requires depositing the document somewhere that is a member of such an agency and undertakes to keep resolving it.
doi.rule: A DOI records that a document was deposited and will keep resolving. It says nothing about whether the document was reviewed, whether its results are correct, or whether anyone read it.
doi.deep: None of the papers here carries one, because none is deposited anywhere that mints them, and that is stated rather than left for a reader to notice. A citation pins a manuscript by its source commit instead, which is a stronger identity in one respect, since the commit fixes the exact bytes cited, and weaker in another, since it depends on the repository remaining reachable.

download.label: download
download.preview: A download transfers a copy of data or a file from a remote service to a reader's device or local environment.
download.card: Downloading changes where a copy is stored, not where its authority originates. The local copy can become stale or be modified independently after transfer.
download.rule: Check the source, file type, version, integrity, and license before relying on a download.
download.deep: A download provides possession of bytes under available permissions; it does not by itself verify authenticity or safety.

drift.label: drift
drift.preview: Drift is the gap that opens when a generated surface stops matching the source it was generated from, so a page, count, or copy keeps reporting something that is no longer true.
drift.card: Drift is quiet by construction. Nothing errors; a stale page simply carries an old number with the same confidence as a current one, and a reader has no way to tell. This is why so much of the site is a projection with a build that fails when its output no longer matches its source. Drift caught by a build is a broken build; drift caught by a reader is a broken claim.
drift.rule: If two surfaces disagree, suspect drift and find the source authority before believing either.
drift.deep: The dangerous case is a hand-edited copy that is more current than its source, because regenerating destroys the correction and looks like a fix. Keeping authorship in one place is what makes drift recoverable.

drilldown.label: drilldown
drilldown.preview: A drilldown is a route from a summary or aggregate view into more specific underlying detail.
drilldown.card: Plectis keeps the first view deliberately small, then lets the selected object open through progressively richer bands: a glossary definition can open its contextual card and scope, an option row can open its source-backed card, and a paper-module summary can open the module itself. A valid drilldown preserves the object’s stable identity and moves closer to its evidence or owner; it does not merely send the reader to another page mentioning the same words.
drilldown.rule: Use a drilldown when the summary no longer answers the question, and verify that the deeper surface refers to the same identified object.
drilldown.deep: Drilldown is a depth transition, not an authority promotion. The summary remains a projection, while the destination contributes whatever authority its own contract grants. Stable ids and source references are therefore part of the operation: without them, a deeper-looking page may silently change subjects.

dyadic.label: dyadic
dyadic.preview: Dyadic means built from powers of two.
dyadic.card: Several of these series divide their terms by successive powers of two, which is the same as writing the value in binary. That connection is what makes the binary digits of the sum the object of study: a question about whether the value is a fraction becomes a question about whether its digits eventually repeat.
dyadic.rule: Dyadic questions are usually questions about binary digits.
dyadic.deep: Powers of two are the smallest interesting base, which makes these the easiest cases to state and often the only ones anyone can prove anything about.

edge.label: edge
edge.preview: An edge is a recorded connection between two nodes in a graph, usually carrying a direction, type, or label.
edge.card: Edges make relationships traversable and machine-readable. Their meaning comes from the relation type, so an edge can mean depends on, supports, contains, or merely links to.
edge.rule: Read an edge's endpoints and relation label before inferring what it asserts.
edge.deep: Directed edges distinguish source from target, while undirected edges represent symmetric relationships; neither form implies evidence unless the relation says so.

element.label: element
element.preview: An element is one member or structural unit: a member of a mathematical set, an item in a data collection, or a node such as an HTML element.
element.card: Plectis uses the same ordinary word in mathematical and software material. In a theorem, x ∈ S means set membership; in a JSON path, an element is one indexed list item; in a generated page, an HTML element is a browser-interpreted node. These are parallel domain senses, not one locally redefined object.
element.rule: Use the container and notation to resolve the sense: set membership, indexed data item, or HTML node.
element.deep: Each sense has different identity and checks. Mathematical elements obey the surrounding structure, list elements have positions, and HTML elements have tags, attributes, and document-tree relationships.

emit.label: emit
emit.preview: To emit something is to produce and send out an output, event, signal, record, or generated artifact.
emit.card: Emission names the outward result of a process without implying that a recipient consumed or accepted it. The emitted item should retain an identity and source relationship when later stages depend on it.
emit.rule: When a tool emits output, identify its format, destination, source run, and whether the emission is authoritative or projected.
emit.deep: Producing output and successfully delivering or applying it are separate events.

engine.label: engine
engine.preview: An engine is one mechanism for attacking a problem: a family of arguments sharing a common method, which can be closed off as a group.
engine.card: Naming the engines is what lets progress and barriers be stated precisely. Without the names, a barrier is described as closing an approach and nobody can check which approaches that covers, because no list of them exists.
engine.rule: When a barrier closes an engine, ask which other engines remain.
engine.deep: The register exists because a barrier was once thought to close a set of engines that turned out to have another member. The failure was not the mathematics; it was that nothing enumerated the set.

engine_room.label: engine room
engine_room.preview: Engine room is the label for the components that run the system itself rather than serve a reader: the routers, gates, drift checks and queues the machinery uses on its own operation.
engine_room.card: Most components here do something for a user. Engine-room components do something for the system, which is why they read as unusually inward-facing. They are published for the same reason as the rest, that the claim is checkable, but their subject is the system's own behaviour and their fixtures are drawn from its own runs.
engine_room.rule: Read an engine-room component as a statement about the system's internal handling, not about anything it produces for a reader.
engine_room.deep: The engine room is where self-referential failure lives. A gate that checks the system's own output can pass because it stopped checking, and nothing downstream would notice. That is why these components carry negative cases as a rule rather than as an option.

entry.label: entry
entry.preview: An entry is a supported starting route or one selectable item in a governed collection.
entry.card: Plectis uses entry in two related but distinct ways. A collection entry is one stable selectable row, such as a glossary term or component. A system entry is a supported first-contact surface that accepts a task or question and returns a bounded next route, such as the kernel’s task-conditioned entry packet. Both uses promise identity and direction: the reader should know what object or route was entered and where its deeper source lives.
entry.rule: First identify whether entry means a collection row or a first-contact route. In either case, rely on it only when it names the object or task and provides a supported path to deeper source-backed material.
entry.deep: The local distinction is support. Many files can be opened, but only an entry is deliberately designed to orient a cold reader or process without prior knowledge. A good entry spends little context, preserves the selected identity, and hands off to a drilldown rather than trying to contain the whole system.

environment.label: environment
environment.preview: An environment is the surrounding operating system, tools, versions, configuration, permissions, and external services under which a command or program runs.
environment.card: The environment is part of a result even when the source code is unchanged. A check may pass locally and fail elsewhere because a dependency, platform feature, permission, or network service differs, so reproducible work records the relevant environment instead of assuming it.
environment.rule: Compare environments before treating different run results as evidence about the code alone.
environment.deep: Environment capture can range from a version list to a locked container or toolchain; the necessary detail depends on which surrounding conditions can affect the result.

epistemic_control_plane.label: epistemic control plane
epistemic_control_plane.preview: An epistemic control plane is a proposed runtime form of the Workingness Instrument that connects the system's current beliefs and acknowledged unknowns to actions that are allowed, blocked, or routed for review.
epistemic_control_plane.card: It works as a chain: evidence sets the status of a claim, the status of that claim sets which actions are permitted, and any unresolved uncertainty stops a change from being made. It would draw together the recorded checks, judgments, appeals, and projection comparisons into claim rows and matching action boundaries, so that the system only acts where its own beliefs are backed and holds back where they are not. Today it exists as a stated target and an alias; the written-up artifact behind it is the Workingness Instrument paper module and a candidate standard.
epistemic_control_plane.rule: Treat it as a planned bridge from self-observation to safe action, not a shipped runtime: where you meet it, expect a description of how belief is meant to gate action, with the live writer still to be built.
epistemic_control_plane.deep: The core rule it encodes is that changing evidence changes a claim's status, changing status changes the allowed actions, and an open question blocks any mutation until it is settled.

equality.label: equality
equality.preview: An equality is a statement that two expressions denote the same value or object under the stated assumptions.
equality.card: Equality is exact and symmetric: if a = b, either side can replace the other where the expression is defined. Numerical approximations use a different relation.
equality.rule: Check the domain, assumptions, and whether the symbol denotes exact equality or an approximation.
equality.deep: Proofs of equality may proceed by calculation, algebraic rewriting, extensionality, or showing both sides satisfy a unique characterization.

equation.label: equation
equation.preview: An equation is an equality containing one or more unknowns whose allowed values are to be found or constrained.
equation.card: In the Plectis papers, equations are exact mathematical constraints, not formatted approximations. They may define a quantity, express a recurrence, or state the equality from which a proof derives a denominator or integrality condition; the permitted values depend on the declared number system.
equation.rule: Read the variables, domain, hypotheses, and equivalence of each transformation before treating a displayed equation as solved.
equation.deep: A Lean theorem can machine-check an equation and the transformations applied to it, but the surrounding prose still has to identify why that formal equality represents the intended Erdős problem.

equivalence.label: equivalence
equivalence.preview: An equivalence is a proved two-way relationship in which each of two statements implies the other under the same stated hypotheses.
equivalence.card: Equivalent statements may look very different while carrying exactly the same truth conditions. Proving only one direction gives an implication or reduction, not an equivalence.
equivalence.rule: For an equivalence, locate both directions and verify that their hypotheses and domains match.
equivalence.deep: Equivalences are valuable because they let a problem move into a representation with better tools without changing what would count as a solution.

erdos.label: Paul Erdős
erdos.preview: Paul Erdős (1913–1996) was a Hungarian mathematician known for posing and solving problems across number theory, combinatorics, and discrete mathematics.
erdos.card: The numbered Erdős problems discussed here are questions associated with Erdős and indexed by the independently maintained Erdős Problems database. A label such as “Erdős #249” identifies that database entry; it is not a claim that Erdős assigned the number himself.
erdos.rule: Read “Erdős #n” as a database identifier for a mathematical problem associated with Paul Erdős.
erdos.deep: Erdős worked extensively through collaboration and left a large body of questions that continue to organize research; the site covers only the explicitly listed problems and makes no claim about the rest.

erdos_problem.label: Erdős problem
erdos_problem.preview: An Erdős problem is one of the questions Paul Erdős posed or collected, as indexed in the Erdős Problems database maintained by Thomas Bloom.
erdos_problem.card: The eight problems on this site are all recorded there as open. The database supplies the numbering and the current reported status; the exact statement comes from Erdős's own papers, which each problem note cites. Several of the eight ask whether one particular infinite sum is an irrational number.
erdos_problem.rule: Use the number to find the problem; use the problem note for the exact statement, its sources and what has been proved.
erdos_problem.deep: Open status is the database maintainer's present assessment and may omit relevant literature, so each problem note also records the prior work it knows of.

error.label: error
error.preview: An error is a detected condition in which data, reasoning, behaviour, or execution differs from what is valid or expected.
error.card: Errors may be defects in the system, invalid inputs, incorrect assumptions, measurement mistakes, or explicit diagnostic values. An error message is evidence about the detector's view, not automatically the root cause.
error.rule: Read an error with the operation, input, expected condition, observed condition, and source that detected it.
error.deep: Useful diagnosis separates symptom, cause, and impact so repair targets the owning layer rather than the nearest visible message.

establish.label: establish
establish.preview: To establish something is to provide sufficient basis for it to be accepted as present, true, valid, or operative within a stated standard.
establish.card: What establishes a fact depends on the claim: observation may establish presence, a proof may establish a theorem, and a successful gate may establish conformance. The verb should not erase those different evidence standards.
establish.rule: When a result establishes a claim, identify the claim, standard, evidence chain, and boundary beyond which the establishment does not extend.
establish.deep: Establishing one premise or property can support further reasoning without automatically establishing every downstream conclusion.

evaluator.label: evaluator
evaluator.preview: An evaluator is a read-only component that measures something and reports, without changing what it measured.
evaluator.card: Separating measurement from repair matters because a tool that both judges and fixes can quietly redefine the standard it is judging against. An evaluator emits a report and stops, leaving the decision about what to do with it outside itself.
evaluator.rule: An evaluator reports. If a tool also repairs what it measures, ask what its measurement means.
evaluator.deep: The independence is what makes an evaluator's number worth reading. A measurement produced by the thing being measured is not a measurement.

evidence.label: evidence
evidence.preview: Evidence is a source, observation, check result, or record that supports a specific claim within a stated scope and can be inspected independently of that claim.
evidence.card: Evidence is the backing under a statement, not the statement itself. Its strength depends on what produced it, whether the record is current, and whether its scope actually matches the claim being made.
evidence.rule: Ask which exact claim the evidence supports, how it was produced, and where its coverage stops.
evidence.deep: The same artifact can be strong evidence for one narrow assertion and irrelevant to a broader one; a passing fixture run may establish that a validator handles those fixtures while saying nothing about real-world performance.

evidence_band.label: evidence band
evidence_band.preview: An evidence band is the label a statement carries in the long working records saying what kind of support it has: Lean (checked by the proof assistant), Cert (an exact finite computation), Math (an ordinary proof in the sources, not formalised), Cited (established in the published literature) or Open (not proved).
evidence_band.card: The bands are never blurred: a statement with one band is not described in the language of another. A second tag gives the scale at which a parameter-indexed statement holds: at listed values, below an explicit bound, for arbitrarily large parameters, or for all of them.
evidence_band.rule: Read the band before the statement. It tells you what would have to be re-checked and by what means.
evidence_band.deep: Sorting by band and scale keeps the unresolved endpoint visible: the open problems each depend on a statement at a scale the checked results have not reached.

exact.label: exact
exact.preview: Exact describes correspondence or value with no permitted difference under the stated representation and comparison rule.
exact.card: Exactness is stricter than approximation but remains relative to what is compared. Two rendered pages can look the same while their bytes differ, and two numbers can be mathematically equal despite different textual forms.
exact.rule: When exact is claimed, identify the representation, normalization, and equality rule used for comparison.
exact.deep: Exact results can still be irrelevant or stale; exactness addresses difference, not purpose, authority, or freshness.

exact_rational_arithmetic.label: exact rational arithmetic
exact_rational_arithmetic.preview: Exact rational arithmetic works with fractions as pairs of whole numbers rather than as decimal approximations, so rounding error cannot enter.
exact_rational_arithmetic.card: It is slower than floating-point arithmetic and answers a different question. A floating-point computation shows a value is close to something; an exact rational computation shows it is that something, for the case computed.
exact_rational_arithmetic.rule: Exactness removes rounding error from a finite computation. It does not extend that computation to cases it did not run.
exact_rational_arithmetic.deep: One Plectis component recomputes an Erdős certificate in exact rational arithmetic and compares the result against the checked-in value. A pass establishes that the recorded certificate is the one the arithmetic produces, for that certificate.

example.label: example
example.preview: An example is a concrete instance chosen to show how a definition, method, or claim applies.
example.card: Examples make an abstract idea easier to inspect by supplying actual values, objects, or steps. They illustrate a rule but normally do not prove it for every possible case.
example.rule: Use an example to understand the mechanism, not to infer universal coverage.
example.deep: A counterexample has the stronger logical role of disproving a universal claim, whereas an ordinary positive example only demonstrates one instance.

exclude.label: exclude
exclude.preview: To exclude something is to deliberately leave it outside a set, scope, result, permission, or process.
exclude.card: Exclusion depends on a boundary and a rule for membership. It may protect privacy, remove invalid cases, narrow a claim, or identify an omission that weakens coverage.
exclude.rule: When something is excluded, check the criterion, reason, and whether the exclusion is reflected in downstream counts and claims.
exclude.deep: An exclusion can make a result more precise while also limiting who or what the result represents.

executable_cross_section.label: executable cross-section
executable_cross_section.preview: An executable cross-section is a bounded public slice of a larger system whose included components, checks, source, and result records can be run and inspected independently.
executable_cross_section.card: An executable cross-section is the public middle ground between a description and a complete system release. Plectis selects mechanisms whose code, fixtures, validation commands, source links, and result records can stand together and be rerun by a cold reader. That makes the selected behavior inspectable rather than merely narrated. The selection remains a boundary: omitted mechanisms, private inputs, live orchestration, and the behavior of the larger working system do not inherit evidence from the runnable slice.
executable_cross_section.rule: Judge the executable cross-section by the components and records it actually publishes; do not infer that it represents or proves the unpublished remainder.
executable_cross_section.deep: The important distinction is not size but evidential closure. A cross-section is executable only when the included source, inputs, commands, expected negatives, and durable records are sufficient to inspect the selected mechanism without private context. It is still a projection because the act of selecting that closed slice does not establish equivalence with everything outside it.

execution.label: execution
execution.preview: Execution is the act of carrying out instructions, a command, a program, a plan, or a defined procedure.
execution.card: Execution turns a description into an actual run with inputs, environment, effects, and output. It therefore carries operational consequences that merely reading or proposing the instructions does not.
execution.rule: Before execution, verify the target, authority, side effects, and rollback or containment conditions appropriate to the action.
execution.deep: An execution can complete mechanically while failing its intended higher-level purpose, so outcome validation remains separate.

exit_code.label: exit code
exit_code.preview: An exit code is the number a command returns when it finishes: zero means it succeeded, anything else means it failed.
exit_code.card: This is the smallest honest unit of evidence on the site. A check that returns exit 0 passed; one that returns anything else failed. A pass is only worth reading if the check could have failed, because a repository where nothing ever fails is usually a repository whose checks stopped discriminating.
exit_code.rule: Read the exit code, not the surrounding prose. Zero passed; anything else did not.
exit_code.deep: The useful question about a green run is whether the check was capable of going red. These checks have gone red before: one lane was found silently skipped in July and fixed in the release that followed, and that correction is recorded beside the current run.

expand.label: expand
expand.preview: To expand something is to increase its extent, detail, coverage, or explicit content.
expand.card: Expansion can add new material or reveal detail that was already compressed or hidden. The operation should preserve the identity and boundaries of the subject it expands.
expand.rule: When a view expands, distinguish newly authored content from previously available detail that is merely being displayed.
expand.deep: More detail can improve understanding but can also increase noise, so expansion should remain tied to a reader need or coverage goal.

expected.label: expected
expected.preview: Expected describes a result or condition predicted, required, or treated as normal under stated assumptions.
expected.card: Plectis uses expected in two distinct ways: a schema or test can require an exact value, while a model or prior run can merely predict one. Both are compared with an observation, but only the first is a conformance condition; the second can be wrong without making the system invalid.
expected.rule: Identify the source of the expectation—contract, fixture, model, convention, or historical baseline—before classifying a mismatch.
expected.deep: Keeping expected separate from observed lets checks report honest deltas. A fixture mismatch can be a regression, an intended source change, stale generated output, or a bad expectation; the comparison alone does not choose the cause.

explain.label: explain
explain.preview: To explain something is to make its meaning, cause, mechanism, or reasoning understandable by connecting it to relevant facts and relationships.
explain.card: An explanation answers why, how, or what something means rather than merely restating that it exists. Its depth should match the reader's question and distinguish evidence from interpretation.
explain.rule: Judge an explanation by whether it identifies the relevant relationship and remains consistent with the available evidence.
explain.deep: Explanations can be useful at several levels, but a simpler account must not contradict or conceal the deeper mechanism it compresses.

exponent.label: exponent
exponent.preview: An exponent states how many times a base is multiplied by itself, so `b^n` uses base `b` and exponent `n`.
exponent.card: Exponents index the terms in several series on this site. Choosing which exponents are included changes the support, while their least common multiple can control repeating arithmetic patterns.
exponent.rule: Distinguish the exponent that selects a power from the value of the power itself.
exponent.deep: The arithmetic relationship among exponents—divisibility, gaps, and least common multiples—often matters more than their individual size.

export.label: export
export.preview: An export is an artifact or data package deliberately produced from one environment for use in another.
export.card: Exporting selects and transforms allowed material across a boundary, often removing private paths or unsupported fields. The exported copy remains traceable to its source and build.
export.rule: Inspect the export policy, source fingerprint, and omissions before treating the package as complete.
export.deep: An export can preserve content faithfully while changing paths, labels, or format to fit the destination's access and safety constraints.

external.label: external
external.preview: External describes something originating, operating, or existing outside the boundary currently being discussed.
external.card: The relevant boundary may be a repository, organization, process, network, or public site. External does not mean untrusted by definition, but it does mean authority and availability must be checked separately.
external.rule: Whenever material is external, identify the boundary it sits outside and the conditions under which it enters or influences the system.
external.deep: External dependencies can change independently, so provenance, versioning, and failure handling matter even when the source is reputable.

factor.label: factor
factor.preview: A factor is one quantity or expression multiplied with others to form a product.
factor.card: For integers, saying d is a factor of n usually means d divides n. In algebra, factors can be expressions whose product expands to the original expression.
factor.rule: Identify whether factor refers to integer divisibility, algebraic factorisation, or a multiplicative term.
factor.deep: Factorisation exposes multiplicative structure and can make divisibility, roots, cancellation, and proof obligations easier to see.

factorisation.label: factorisation
factorisation.preview: Factorisation is the expression of an integer or algebraic object as a product of simpler factors, especially the unique prime factors of a positive integer.
factorisation.card: Prime factorisation exposes divisibility structure that addition or decimal notation hides. Arithmetic functions such as the totient depend directly on which primes divide a number and with what multiplicities.
factorisation.rule: When a result uses factorisation, check which object is being factored and whether the factors are required to be prime or merely nontrivial.
factorisation.deep: Some certificate algorithms deliberately avoid factoring large integers because repeated modular checks can verify the needed property more cheaply.

failure.label: failure
failure.preview: A failure is an outcome in which a required function, condition, check, or expectation is not satisfied.
failure.card: Failures can arise from defects, invalid inputs, unavailable dependencies, unsafe conditions, or incorrect expectations. Classifying the cause matters because each class has a different repair path.
failure.rule: Read a failure with the operation attempted, expected condition, observed result, and evidence that locates the cause.
failure.deep: A failure result is information about a boundary; it should not be generalized to unrelated operations or causes without evidence.

failure_class_propagation.label: failure class propagation
failure_class_propagation.preview: Failure-class propagation tests whether one local break recurs on sibling surfaces, then repairs only the proven class boundary.
failure_class_propagation.card: When something fails in one place, that failure is taken as evidence about one location and as a question about others: does the same cause sit in sibling files, standards, routes, tests, or generated records. Failure class propagation answers that question by scanning those siblings, stating exactly where the pattern holds and where it stops, and then making a fix that covers the proven extent and no more. A deliberate decision not to widen counts as a valid outcome when it records what was checked and why widening would currently cause harm.
failure_class_propagation.rule: When you see a fix described as failure class propagation, read what siblings were scanned and where the boundary was drawn: it claims to have repaired a bounded class, not every instance everywhere and not just the one case that was first noticed.
failure_class_propagation.deep: It carries a fixed set of parts: the concrete local case, the sibling scan, the class boundary, the counter-force against overgeneralising, the plane that owns the repair, and the validation. A no-op or deferred repair is sound only when it names what was examined and why holding back is the right call for now.

false.label: false
false.preview: False describes a proposition that is not true or a boolean value representing the negative branch of a two-valued condition.
false.card: In logic, falsity concerns the truth of a proposition; in software, false is a value interpreted by a program under a condition. A failed check can provide evidence of falsity but may instead indicate an invalid test or environment.
false.rule: Distinguish the proposition or condition being denied from the mechanism that reported false.
false.deep: Showing a universal statement false requires one valid counterexample, while showing an observed field false only reports its encoded value.

falsifiable.label: falsifiable
falsifiable.preview: A claim is falsifiable when there is a specific observation or run that would show it is wrong.
falsifiable.card: It is a property of how a claim is stated, not of whether it is true. A claim nobody can test is not thereby safe; it is outside the reach of evidence.
falsifiable.rule: Ask what result would refute the claim. If nothing would, the claim is not doing evidential work.
falsifiable.deep: The stated position for this site is that the private frontend is not falsifiable by a reader and should not be trusted, while the public repositories are: the commands are given, the fixtures are included, and a disagreement between a claim and its record is visible.

farey_sequence.label: Farey sequence
farey_sequence.preview: A Farey sequence lists, in increasing order, every fraction in lowest terms whose denominator is at most a chosen bound.
farey_sequence.card: Two neighbours in a Farey sequence cannot be arbitrarily close: their separation is fixed by their denominators. So if a target number is shown to lie strictly between two neighbours, it cannot equal any fraction whose denominator is inside the bound.
farey_sequence.rule: A Farey exclusion rules out denominators up to its bound and says nothing whatever about denominators above it.
farey_sequence.deep: The Erdős #249 work uses a 240-bit Farey window to exclude every reduced denominator through 79,639,646,646,701,375,323,355,774,875,831,053, roughly 7.96 times ten to the thirty-fourth. The problem remains open because no argument covers the denominators beyond that bound.

field.label: field
field.preview: A field is one named slot in a structured record, holding a value with an expected meaning and format.
field.card: Fields let producers and readers refer to facts precisely instead of relying on position or prose. A schema may require a field, restrict its type, or explain when it can be empty.
field.rule: Interpret a field through the schema or contract that defines its name and allowed value.
field.deep: A field's presence proves only that a value was recorded, not that the value is true or current.

file.label: file
file.preview: A file is a named sequence of stored bytes addressed at a path and interpreted according to a format or program.
file.card: Files are containers: one may hold code, prose, structured data, an image, or generated output. Its extension and location help identify the format but do not guarantee content or authority.
file.rule: Use the path, format, version, and owning contract together when referring to a file.
file.deep: A file can be source authority, generated projection, cache, or transient output, and confusing those roles leads to edits in the wrong place.

finding.label: finding
finding.preview: A finding is a conclusion or observed condition produced by an investigation, audit, experiment, or analysis.
finding.card: Findings connect a method and evidence to a stated result. They may be positive, negative, tentative, or limited, and should retain the conditions under which they were derived.
finding.rule: Read a finding with its source process, evidence, confidence, scope, and any unresolved alternative explanation.
finding.deep: A finding is a reported result, not automatically a defect or final truth; later evidence can refine or overturn it.

finite.label: finite
finite.preview: Finite means containing or requiring only a limited number of elements, steps, or operations.
finite.card: A finite object can in principle be exhausted by counting or enumeration, even when it is too large to inspect practically. Finiteness is a structural property, not a claim of small size.
finite.rule: Do not confuse finite with computationally easy or already enumerated.
finite.deep: Many proofs separate finite verification from infinite generalization because checking every member is possible only after a finite bound is justified.

finite_computation.label: finite computation
finite_computation.preview: A finite computation is a terminating calculation over a bounded set of inputs that produces an exact or explicitly approximate result.
finite_computation.card: Finite computations can settle individual cases, verify certificates, and discover patterns. They do not settle an infinite family unless a proof shows that the bounded cases exhaust every possibility.
finite_computation.rule: Identify the computed range and the theorem, if any, that connects it to the general claim.
finite_computation.deep: Formal projects often turn large computations into compact certificates so the trusted checker verifies the result without trusting the generator's implementation.

fit.label: fit
fit.preview: Fit is the degree to which something satisfies the needs, constraints, or shape of a particular purpose or context.
fit.card: Fit is relational: a method can be excellent yet unsuitable for a specific task, budget, audience, or evidence standard. The relevant requirements must therefore be named.
fit.rule: When the site says something fits, identify the purpose and constraints against which the fit was judged.
fit.deep: Fit does not imply universal superiority; it means the option aligns with one stated situation better than relevant alternatives.

fixture.label: fixture
fixture.preview: A fixture is the fixed input a check runs against: a small, committed file standing in for the real data, chosen so the same run produces the same result on any machine.
fixture.card: Every component here ships with its inputs rather than reaching for live data. That is what makes a check repeatable on a stranger's laptop: the fixture is in the repository, so the run does not depend on the private system, a network call, or the state of anyone's machine. It also fixes what the check can establish. A component passing against a fixture has been shown to work on that input, which is a smaller claim than working on production data, and the scope limit says so.
fixture.rule: When a check passes, look at the fixture it ran against. The result holds for that input; it is not a statement about data the fixture does not contain.
fixture.deep: Fixtures are why the public repository can be checked at all without the private system. They are deliberately synthetic: shipping real data would leak the substrate this system does not publish. The trade is explicit rather than hidden - a synthetic input buys reproducibility and costs realism, and the component's scope limit records which of the two you are being sold.

follow.label: follow
follow.preview: To follow is to come after, proceed along, result from, or act according to something already given.
follow.card: The intended sense depends on context: a conclusion follows from premises, a reader follows a route, and a task follows a rule. Each describes a directed relationship rather than simple proximity.
follow.rule: Identify what leads and which relationship makes the later item count as following it.
follow.deep: Sequence alone does not establish dependence; a later event follows in time but may not follow logically or causally.

forecasting.label: forecasting
forecasting.preview: Forecasting here means predicting a future value, such as a market series, and then measuring whether the prediction was better than an obvious alternative.
forecasting.card: The measurement is the harder half. Any method looks good on the run that was chosen for it, so a forecast-skill claim has to survive tests built to catch that: comparing named methods, correcting for how many were tried, and resampling the series in a way that keeps its structure.
forecasting.rule: A forecast-skill claim covers the data it was tested on. It is not a claim about future markets.
forecasting.deep: The components in this area run Diebold-Mariano, Hansen's superior predictive ability test, and a stationary bootstrap over synthetic market fixtures. Synthetic means the statistical machinery is shown to run and refuse as specified, not that any live market was predicted.

formal.label: formal
formal.preview: Formal describes something expressed through explicit rules and symbols precise enough for rule-governed checking.
formal.card: A formal statement removes selected ambiguities by giving its objects and allowed operations exact meaning. Formality can support machine checking, but it does not by itself guarantee that the formal statement captures the intended real-world question.
formal.rule: When something is called formal, identify the language, rules, and checker that give the description its precision.
formal.deep: Formality concerns how a claim is represented and checked; truth, relevance, and correspondence to the intended subject remain separate questions.

formal_mathematics.label: formal mathematics
formal_mathematics.preview: Formal mathematics is mathematics written so a machine can check it: every definition and step expressed in a language a proof assistant verifies, rather than in the usual prose of a paper.
formal_mathematics.card: An ordinary paper is checked by referees reading it. Formal mathematics is checked by software, which is unforgiving about steps a human reader would grant. The translation is substantial work and often reveals that a published argument covers slightly less than it appeared to, which is the main reason to bother.
formal_mathematics.rule: When a result is described as formal, look for the source. The formal statement is the claim; the prose is commentary.
formal_mathematics.deep: The gap between a formal statement and its description is where overstatement survives machine checking untouched, which is why the wording is registered and checked separately.

formal_proof.label: formal proof
formal_proof.preview: A formal proof is a mathematical argument encoded in a precise language so a proof checker can verify every inference from the stated definitions, axioms, and hypotheses.
formal_proof.card: Formalization removes hidden appeals to intuition by requiring each step to type-check against explicit rules. It guarantees that the encoded statement follows inside the formal system, not that the statement was translated from informal mathematics exactly as intended.
formal_proof.rule: Read the formal statement and hypotheses as carefully as the fact that its proof checker accepted it.
formal_proof.deep: Trust is concentrated in the definitions, formal statement, axioms, elaborator boundary, and small proof-checking kernel rather than spread across a long human argument.

formalisation.label: formalisation
formalisation.preview: Formalisation is the work of restating a mathematical definition or proof in a proof assistant's language so the software can check every step.
formalisation.card: On this site, formalised means a Lean proof exists and was checked. Formalising a result often exposes a gap or a hidden hypothesis in the informal argument, and a formal statement can differ from the informal one, which is why the papers say what each Lean statement covers.
formalisation.rule: Formalised tells you the stated proposition was checked. Read the proposition to see what was proved.
formalisation.deep: The project treats the Lean statement, its authored meaning and the public claim about it as three separate things; a dense formal proof cannot make the claim stronger than the statement.

fraction.label: fraction
fraction.preview: A fraction is a number written as one integer numerator divided by a nonzero integer denominator.
fraction.card: The numerator is the top integer and the denominator is the bottom integer. A fraction is reduced when those integers share no common factor greater than one, making the denominator canonical up to sign.
fraction.rule: When denominator properties matter, check that the fraction has first been reduced.
fraction.deep: Exact fraction arithmetic preserves numerator and denominator structure that floating-point approximations discard, which is essential in irrationality and multiplicative-order arguments.

front_end.label: frontend
front_end.preview: The frontend is the part of a system a person looks at and clicks: its screens, as opposed to the machinery underneath.
front_end.card: The frontend here is not published. It appears in the recorded videos so a reader can see what the operator sees, while the components and their checks, which are the part that can be verified, are the part released. The split is stated rather than implied.
front_end.rule: Video of a frontend shows that it exists and how it behaves. It is not a check anyone else can run.
front_end.deep: Demonstration and evidence are different currencies. A recording is persuasive and unfalsifiable; a check is dull and repeatable.

frontier.label: frontier
frontier.preview: A problem's frontier is the exact line between what has been proved about it and the step that remains open.
frontier.card: Each problem page has a section headed Results and remaining work. That section is the frontier: the strongest checked statements, the routes that closed, and the precise obligation still to be met. The frontier moves when a new result is accepted; it never claims the problem is solved.
frontier.rule: Read a frontier as a boundary, not a score: it tells you where the proved part ends and what a contribution would have to prove.
frontier.deep: The Lean repository's frontier relay lets a person hand one problem's frontier to their own coding agent as a bounded task, starting from one exact public revision.

full.label: full
full.preview: Full describes material or coverage presented without the omissions made by a named shorter, filtered, or partial form.
full.card: Full is always relative to a defined whole. A full card may include every card field while still being only one projection of a much larger source.
full.rule: When something is called full, identify the collection or schema whose parts are claimed to be included.
full.deep: Completeness at one layer does not imply completeness at every layer, so a full report can remain bounded by its inputs and measurement method.

function.label: function
function.preview: A mathematical function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input in its domain.
function.card: A function is specified by its domain, codomain, and assignment rule, not only by a formula. Different formulas can define the same function on a stated domain.
function.rule: Read the domain and output type before applying or comparing functions.
function.deep: Functions can take numbers, sets, sequences, or other functions as inputs and can be studied through properties such as injectivity, monotonicity, continuity, or multiplicativity.

gate.label: gate
