gate.preview: A gate is a rule-controlled checkpoint that permits or blocks a later action according to declared evidence or conditions.
gate.card: Gates turn requirements into enforceable boundaries: a release gate may require tests, source checks, and safety scans before publication. A gate should explain both its decision and repair route.
gate.rule: Read which evidence the gate consumes and which action its result controls.
gate.deep: A passing gate licenses only the downstream action named by its contract, not a broader claim that the whole artifact is correct.

generalise_up_propagate.label: generalise-up-propagate
generalise_up_propagate.preview: Generalise-up-propagate is the move of taking a lesson learned in one local piece of work and carrying it upward into a durable, system-wide rule, while stating exactly how far that lesson applies and where it does not.
generalise_up_propagate.card: When work on one part of the system reveals something worth keeping, generalise-up-propagation does two things at once: it preserves the original case as evidence, and it names the broader invariant that case revealed. The general rule it produces carries an applicability boundary and a not-when boundary, so a single instance is never written up as if it held everywhere. It also records which layer of the system owns the new rule, so the lesson lands in a definite home rather than floating loose.
generalise_up_propagate.rule: When you meet a rule that arrived this way, check the boundary it states: it was promoted from one concrete case, and it holds only within the limits recorded alongside it.
generalise_up_propagate.deep: It answers three questions about a local finding: what invariant the case actually revealed, which layer of the system should own that invariant, and how broadly it can be stated without claiming more than the single case supports.

git.label: Git
git.preview: Git is the version-control system most software projects use to record every change to their files as a numbered commit.
git.card: Because every commit has an identifier derived from its contents, a claim can be pinned to an exact state of a repository rather than to whatever the project looks like today.
git.rule: A commit identifier names one snapshot. A branch name does not, because the branch moves.
git.deep: Several checks here run real Git commands against a sample repository rather than reading a description of what Git would have said. The receipts record how many calls were made.

github.label: GitHub
github.preview: GitHub is an online service for hosting Git repositories and presenting their code, history, issues, releases, and web-published artifacts.
github.card: This site links GitHub repositories so readers can inspect the public source and its revision history. GitHub hosts the material but does not author, verify, or endorse its mathematical or software claims.
github.rule: Use GitHub to locate and inspect the repository, then rely on the repository's own evidence and licenses.
github.deep: A GitHub URL can identify a moving branch, an exact commit, a file view, a release, or a hosted page, and those routes provide different levels of version precision.

glossary.label: glossary
glossary.preview: A glossary is an organized collection of terms and definitions for a particular body of material.
glossary.card: A glossary helps readers resolve unfamiliar or locally specialized language without interrupting the main text. Its entries should distinguish related terms and state where each meaning applies.
glossary.rule: When a term is ambiguous, use the glossary's scope and examples rather than assuming its everyday sense.
glossary.deep: A governed glossary also acts as a semantic index: one concept can collect variants while preserving a single preferred meaning and identity.

govern.label: govern
govern.preview: To govern something is to set or enforce the rules, authority, and decision process that constrain how it may operate or change.
govern.card: Governance identifies who can decide, which standards apply, how exceptions are handled, and where outcomes are recorded. It differs from implementation because it controls the conditions under which implementation is accepted.
govern.rule: When material is governed, locate the owning rule, authority surface, and required validation or approval.
govern.deep: Governance can be encoded in tools and schemas as well as prose, but it remains ineffective if the operating path bypasses those controls.

graph.label: graph
graph.preview: A graph is a structure made of nodes and edges used to represent objects and the relationships between them.
graph.card: Graphs support navigation, dependency analysis, and topology checks by making relationships explicit. The relation types and node identities determine what the graph means.
graph.rule: Inspect the node and edge schemas before reading visual proximity as a relationship.
graph.deep: A graph may be directed, typed, weighted, or acyclic, and each property changes which paths and conclusions are valid.

grounding.label: grounding
grounding.preview: Grounding is the connection of a claim, term, or decision to the source, evidence, observation, or rules that give it support and meaning.
grounding.card: Grounding prevents a statement from floating free of the material it summarizes. A grounded answer makes it possible to trace important claims back to evidence or authority appropriate to the question.
grounding.rule: When something is described as grounded, follow the cited route and check that it directly supports the stated claim.
grounding.deep: A source can ground what it actually contains without grounding broader inferences that the reader adds afterward.

hard_coded.label: hard-coded
hard_coded.preview: Hard-coded means a value is written directly into the code rather than computed or read from a source, so it stays fixed until someone edits it by hand.
hard_coded.card: Hard-coded values are the usual origin of drift. A number typed into a page cannot notice that the thing it describes has changed, so it keeps reporting the old figure with full confidence. Most counts on this site are computed from their source for exactly this reason.
hard_coded.rule: Treat a hard-coded figure as true at the moment it was typed and unverified since.
hard_coded.deep: The problem is not the value but the absence of a link back to what it describes, which is what turns a stale number into an undetectable one.

harness.label: harness
harness.preview: A harness is the scaffolding that runs a check: it supplies the inputs, executes the thing under test, and captures what came out.
harness.card: The harness is not the thing being tested; it is what makes testing repeatable. Keeping it separate means the same scenario can be re-run identically, and that a failure can be attributed to the component rather than to how it happened to be invoked.
harness.rule: Distinguish a harness failure from a component failure. They look alike and mean different things.
harness.deep: Scaffolding is worth naming because it is where flakiness usually lives. A check that fails intermittently is more often a harness problem than a real defect.

hologram.label: hologram
hologram.preview: A hologram is a compressed whole-system view whose rows preserve enough identity, purpose, relationships, authority, reading cost, and drilldown commands for a reader to choose the next source without loading everything.
hologram.card: A hologram is a layered summary derived from the source. A top band gives the shortest useful view, and any row can be expanded into the detail beneath it. The same tiered behaviour is sometimes named telescope or Russian doll: read the smallest layer first, then open only the part that matters. It is a way to grasp the shape of the system before reading source or running a search.
hologram.rule: Treat a hologram as a reading surface, not the source of record. Start from the smallest band, expand the one row you need, and follow its evidence commands when a decision needs proof.
hologram.deep: The defining rule is that each row preserves the shape of the larger system at its own compression band, so a single facet, such as naming, dependency, or source span, can expand through declared layers without forcing the whole file open.

html.label: HTML
html.preview: HTML is the markup language browsers use to structure the text, links, controls, metadata, and other content of a web page.
html.card: HTML describes document structure and semantics; CSS controls presentation and JavaScript can add behavior. A generated HTML page is still a projection of its source data and templates.
html.rule: Inspect HTML when exact page structure, links, anchors, or accessible semantics matter.
html.deep: Browsers build a document object model from HTML, which scripts and assistive technologies then traverse rather than reading the raw file as plain text.

hypothesis.label: hypothesis
hypothesis.preview: A hypothesis is a condition a result assumes rather than proves, so the conclusion holds only where the condition does.
hypothesis.card: Hypotheses are where formal work is most often overread. A theorem proved under two assumed analytic inputs is a real theorem, and it is not a statement about the unrestricted problem. The registry separates results by whether their hypotheses are proved, cited from the literature, or simply assumed.
hypothesis.rule: Read the hypotheses before the conclusion. They decide what the result covers.
hypothesis.deep: An assumed hypothesis is not a defect; leaving it unstated is. The distinction between derived and assumed is the whole difference between a proof and a reduction.

implementation.label: implementation
implementation.preview: An implementation is a concrete realization of a design, specification, algorithm, interface, or policy.
implementation.card: Implementation turns intended behaviour into executable code, configured tools, data, or operational procedures. Multiple implementations can satisfy the same specification while differing internally.
implementation.rule: Evaluate an implementation against the requirements it claims to realize and the conditions under which it runs.
implementation.deep: A correct design can be implemented incorrectly, and a working implementation can expose ambiguity or error in the original design.

implication.label: implication
implication.preview: An implication is a one-way statement that whenever its antecedent holds, its conclusion must also hold.
implication.card: An implication transfers truth from a stated condition to a consequence but does not prove that the condition itself holds. Reversing the direction requires a separate proof.
implication.rule: Identify the antecedent, conclusion, hypotheses, and direction before treating an implication as progress.
implication.deep: Conditional reductions are implications whose antecedent is still open, so they relocate a problem's difficulty without settling the conclusion unconditionally.

import.label: import
import.preview: An import brings named material from another file, package, source, or system into the current context.
import.card: Importing makes outside definitions or data available without rewriting them locally. The imported material keeps an origin and may change when its source changes, so provenance and version matter.
import.rule: Treat an import as a dependency and check what was brought in, from where, and at which version.
import.deep: An import can expose names or data while leaving their authority with the source that supplied them.

index.label: index
index.preview: To index something is to build a lookup over it, so an item can be found by what it is rather than by reading through everything.
index.card: An unindexed corpus can only be used by someone willing to read it. Indexing turns it into something answerable: what depends on this, where is this used, what is still open. For a corpus of this size the index is not a convenience, it is the only practical way in.
index.rule: An index tells you where something is. It does not tell you whether it is right.
index.deep: The cost of an index is that it can fall out of step with what it describes, which is why the indexed count and the orphan count are published together.

inequality.label: inequality
inequality.preview: An inequality is a statement that compares two expressions using an order relation such as less than, greater than, or at most.
inequality.card: In the Plectis mathematics, inequalities usually do one of three jobs: bound the tail of an infinite series, constrain a possible denominator or counterexample, or trap a quantity tightly enough to contradict integrality. An exact inequality can therefore advance a problem without computing the underlying value.
inequality.rule: Check the compared quantities, direction, strictness, hypotheses, and whether the bound is uniform over the claimed cases.
inequality.deep: Machine checking verifies the encoded chain of inequalities, but scope still matters: a bound proved only up to a finite cutoff, under a hypothesis, or for one base cannot be read as a universal estimate.

infinite.label: infinite
infinite.preview: Infinite means not finite: no finite count exhausts the elements, steps, or extent under discussion.
infinite.card: An infinite set can still be described precisely, and different infinite sets can have different structures or cardinalities. Finite computation samples or bounds an infinite object but cannot enumerate it completely.
infinite.rule: Distinguish a statement about all infinitely many cases from evidence covering only a finite range.
infinite.deep: Proofs about infinite objects use general arguments, induction, limits, compactness, or structural properties rather than checking each case one by one.

input.label: input
input.preview: An input is data, a parameter, file, event, or condition supplied to a process before it produces an output.
input.card: Inputs determine which case a program, test, or proof is handling. Reproducible results record exact inputs rather than describing them loosely.
input.rule: Check input identity, format, and version before comparing outputs.
input.deep: Some inputs are explicit command arguments while others come from environment variables, network state, defaults, or dependencies, and hidden inputs weaken reproducibility.

integer.label: integer
integer.preview: An integer is a whole number, positive, negative or zero, with no fractional part.
integer.card: Integers do most of the work in these problems. The usual route to proving something is not a fraction runs through showing that some quantity would have to be a whole number and cannot be, so the arguments turn on integrality far more than on size or approximation.
integer.rule: When a proof turns on whether something is an integer, that is usually the whole argument rather than a detail.
integer.deep: Integrality is a rigid condition, which is what makes it useful: there is no room between two consecutive integers, so a quantity trapped strictly between them cannot exist.

irrational.label: irrational
irrational.preview: A number is irrational when it cannot be written as one whole number divided by another.
irrational.card: Most of the problems here ask whether a particular infinite sum is irrational. The question is usually much harder than it sounds: a sum can be computed to any number of digits without that revealing which kind of number it is, because a rational number with an enormous denominator looks exactly like an irrational one for as far as anyone can compute.
irrational.rule: Irrationality is not settled by computing digits. It needs a proof.
irrational.deep: This is why the work is formal rather than numerical. No amount of computation distinguishes the two cases, so the only route is an argument, and the only way to be sure of the argument at this scale is to have it checked.

issue_report.label: issue
issue_report.preview: An issue is a tracked report on a repository: a failed command, a mistake in a statement, a broken link or a question.
issue_report.card: Both repositories use issue forms so a report lands with the command or page that produced it. Reporting a mistake is a contribution and is credited as one.
issue_report.rule: Report the exact command or page and what you saw; the form asks for both.
issue_report.deep: Issues are public, so a correction made in response is visible with its cause.

json_format.label: JSON
json_format.preview: JSON is a plain-text format for structured data, readable by both people and programs without special software.
json_format.card: Most records here are written as JSON so that a result is inspectable in a text editor and processable by a script without choosing between the two. It is a deliberately boring choice: no proprietary format sits between a reader and the evidence.
json_format.rule: A JSON record can be opened directly. If evidence is only available through an interface, ask why.
json_format.deep: Format choice is an access-control decision in disguise. Anything that requires a viewer restricts who can check it.

kernel.label: kernel
kernel.preview: The kernel is the command-line control layer, kernel.py, that answers system questions with small structured packets before anyone opens source files directly.
kernel.card: The kernel sits in front of the deeper source material and hands back compact, bounded answers rather than raw files. Ask it where a subsystem lives, what phase is running, how to route a task, or what the current runtime state is, and it returns a focused view drawn from the underlying records. Its output is a map over deeper source authority, so it points at the real files rather than replacing them.
kernel.rule: Treat the kernel's reply as a view over deeper source, not the source itself: it tells you where to look and what is active, and the files it names are the underlying authority.
kernel.deep: The kernel runs locally and reads the system's own files directly, which lets it inspect current on-disk state and route work interactively inside one repository; this is what distinguishes it from surfaces that coordinate work across separate runtimes.

label.label: label
label.preview: A label is a short human-readable name attached to an object, category, or status so it can be recognized in a surface.
label.card: Labels help readers scan, but they compress detail and may change without changing the underlying identifier. Their meaning should be traceable to a definition or classification rule.
label.rule: Use labels for recognition and stable identifiers for joins, references, and migrations.
label.deep: A label can express identity, category, or state, so the field that carries it must say which role it plays.

laboratory.label: laboratory
laboratory.preview: A laboratory is a bounded, fixture-backed lane for exercising a candidate standard, check, route, validator, or runtime contract before live use, producing evidence and a possible promotion candidate but never authority by itself.
laboratory.card: A laboratory runs a proposed mechanism against a deliberately small, self-contained fixture so the system can see how that mechanism behaves without putting the real files and records at risk. Each run collects records of what happened, names the gaps it found, and can hand back a candidate worth promoting. Its results stand as evidence for that one experiment; they do not by themselves change a standard, a rule, or a release decision.
laboratory.rule: Treat what a laboratory produces as the findings of one bounded trial: useful evidence and a possible candidate for promotion, not a settled standard or a guarantee about the live system.
laboratory.deep: Because a laboratory works on an isolated fixture rather than the live body of files and records, anything it shows is provisional until it passes the system's standards and release gates. Some older parts of the system call this lane a microcosm probe, which points to the same thing.

lambert_series.label: Lambert series
lambert_series.preview: A Lambert series is a particular way of building an infinite sum in which each term is divided by one less than a power of the base.
lambert_series.card: Two of the problems here are about Lambert series, one at integer bases and one at rational bases. The form matters because the small adjustment of subtracting one from each power changes the arithmetic completely and is what makes the questions hard rather than routine.
lambert_series.rule: Note the base a Lambert-series result is proved at. Results at base two rarely extend to other bases.
lambert_series.deep: The base is where most of the open ground is. Several results settle base two and leave every other base untouched, which is a much narrower statement than the phrasing usually suggests.

large_language_model.label: large language model
large_language_model.preview: A large language model is the kind of statistical text model behind assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.
large_language_model.card: Its output depends on chance, so the same request can produce different answers, and a fluent answer carries no guarantee that the underlying action happened.
large_language_model.rule: A model's report of what it did is not evidence that it did it. The evidence is the record the action left.
large_language_model.deep: The stated design response is to push repeatable rules out of the model and into parts of the system that do not vary: hooks, guards, and checks that read a claim against the record.

latex.label: LaTeX
latex.preview: LaTeX is a document-preparation system in which authors write structured source text that a typesetting engine turns into formatted documents such as PDFs.
latex.card: Mathematical papers use LaTeX because it represents equations, references, and document structure precisely in source form. Compilation checks syntax and cross-references, not the truth of the paper.
latex.rule: Use the LaTeX source to inspect the authored text and the generated PDF to inspect its published rendering.
latex.deep: LaTeX separates semantic document commands from final layout, allowing the same source to be rebuilt consistently with a pinned toolchain.

lattice.label: lattice
lattice.preview: A lattice is the network connecting the system's artifacts, routes, standards, skills, principles, runtime surfaces, and records, with every edge labelled by a relationship such as authority, implementation, or navigation.
lattice.card: The system is not one flat list of rules but a graph of related parts spread across different kinds: a standard, a skill, a paper module, a vocabulary entry, a navigation route, and a runtime surface can all be joined by an edge that states how they relate. The lattice is that whole-system relationship graph. Because the edges are typed, a lesson learned in one place can move to the part of the system that can safely reuse it while its origin and authority stay intact.
lattice.rule: When something is described as living in the lattice, read it as a position in a connected map rather than an isolated note: it has edges to the standards, routes, and units it relates to, and those edges tell you where else to look.
lattice.deep: The typed edges are what stop the system collapsing into flat doctrine: they keep authority, implementation, navigation, compression, and runtime as distinct but linked layers, so a claim carries its provenance as it travels rather than being copied loose.

lattice_transposition.label: lattice transposition
lattice_transposition.preview: Lattice transposition is the move of extracting the reusable rule from a local lesson and placing it in the governing skill, standard, paper module, vocabulary, axiom, or principle so other artifact kinds can inherit it.
lattice_transposition.card: When a fix or insight surfaces in a single file or task, it often encodes a rule that should not stay tied to that one spot. Lattice transposition is the disciplined version of moving it: it keeps the original case on record, names the portable rule, states where the rule applies and where it does not, and deposits it in the narrowest mature plane that can carry it. A friction met while promoting one principle can refine the standard for writing principles; a routing failure can refine a skill and its documentation. The move is only valid if it preserves the source case and respects the authority of the plane it lands in.
lattice_transposition.rule: When you see a rule presented as transposed, check that it cites the concrete case it came from and states its applicability and limits. It is a generalisation that is meant to stay accountable to its source, not a free-floating maxim.
lattice_transposition.deep: It is the cross-plane form of up-propagation: up-propagation says a lesson moves upward into durable material, while transposition adds that the lesson changes coordinates, from one artifact kind to the underlying invariant that governs several kinds. It is vocabulary the system's agents author, and it remains tied to cited source surfaces and to the promotion rules of the plane it enters.

launch.label: launch
launch.preview: To launch something is to start it operating or make it newly available to its intended audience.
launch.card: Launching may start a process, open an application, or publish a product or service. The word should not blur technical startup with public release when those have different gates.
launch.rule: Identify what begins, who can reach it, and which readiness conditions were satisfied at launch.
launch.deep: A launch is a transition into use, not proof that the launched thing will remain reliable or meet every goal.

launch_scope_decision.label: launch-scope decision
launch_scope_decision.preview: A launch-scope decision is a judgment about whether something is ready to ship, host, or share publicly, an authority that components on this site explicitly do not possess.
launch_scope_decision.card: A component can establish that a check passed. It cannot establish that the result is sufficient to launch, and the distinction is enforced rather than left to taste: a component whose wording claims launch readiness, hosting authority, or public-sharing authority is rejected by the release gate with a named finding code. Readiness stays a human decision made with evidence in hand.
launch_scope_decision.rule: Treat component evidence as input to a separate operator or release-owner decision. No passing component grants readiness to host, ship, publish, or share.
launch_scope_decision.deep: The gate exists because the overclaim is so natural. A run that passes reads as permission, and prose drifts toward it without anyone intending to lie. Naming the refusal and giving it a finding code turns a matter of tone into something a build can fail on.

lean.label: Lean
lean.preview: Lean is a proof assistant: software that checks a mathematical proof step by step and refuses it if any step does not follow.
lean.card: A proof written in Lean is checked by machine rather than by a reader's judgement. That removes a specific class of error, the plausible step that turns out not to hold, and it is why a Lean-checked result carries more weight than a written argument of the same length. It does not remove every error: Lean confirms the proof establishes the statement written in the source, and whether that statement is the interesting one is a human question.
lean.rule: For a Lean result, read the formal statement rather than the summary. Lean checked the statement, not the description of it.
lean.deep: Machine checking moves the risk rather than deleting it. What remains is whether the formal statement means what the prose says it means, which is exactly the proof boundary.

lean_kernel.label: Lean kernel
lean_kernel.preview: The Lean kernel is the small fixed core of the Lean proof assistant that decides whether a completed proof is accepted.
lean_kernel.card: Everything else in Lean, including tactics, automation, and the Mathlib library, only produces a candidate proof. The kernel is what checks it, and it is deliberately small so that trusting Lean means trusting that one component.
lean_kernel.rule: Kernel acceptance means the written formal statement was proved. It does not mean the English sentence printed beside that statement says the same thing.
lean_kernel.deep: The alignment between a formal statement and its public wording is an authored judgement, checked separately. Beyond the kernel, this corpus also runs Comparator, an independent checker, over nineteen propositions declared apart from their proofs.

lean_standard_axioms.label: Lean's standard axioms
lean_standard_axioms.preview: propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice are the three axioms Lean assumes beyond its core logic: propositional extensionality, the soundness of quotient types, and the axiom of choice.
lean_standard_axioms.card: Essentially all of Mathlib rests on these three, so a proof that uses only them is standing on ordinary mathematical foundations rather than on anything the author added.
lean_standard_axioms.rule: A count of added axioms means axioms beyond these three. A non-zero count means the proof assumed something extra, which has to be read and judged.
lean_standard_axioms.deep: The corpus reports 0 added axioms and 1 admitted proof step, the latter in ExternalVerification/Challenge.lean. An admitted step is a different thing from an added axiom: it is a gap left open inside a proof rather than an assumption introduced for it.

least_common_multiple.label: least common multiple
least_common_multiple.preview: The least common multiple of a set of whole numbers is the smallest number all of them divide into exactly.
least_common_multiple.card: It appears here as the quantity governing when a repeating pattern comes back into alignment. Several results turn on the least common multiple of a set of exponents, because that number determines the period at which the structure of a sum repeats.
least_common_multiple.rule: Where a least common multiple appears, it is usually setting the period of something.
least_common_multiple.deep: Least common multiples grow quickly, which is what makes the periods involved large enough to be hard to search directly.

lebesgue_measure.label: Lebesgue measure
lebesgue_measure.preview: Lebesgue measure is the standard way of assigning a length to a set of numbers, extended to sets far more broken up than an interval.
lebesgue_measure.card: Measure and topology disagree on what counts as small. A set can contain no interval at all and still have positive measure, and a dense set can have measure zero. The two answer different questions about the same set.
lebesgue_measure.rule: Measure says how much of the line a set fills. It does not say whether the set contains any particular number.
lebesgue_measure.deep: The set of subsums of the sum of one over two to the n minus one is compact, nowhere dense, and of Lebesgue measure exactly one, which is Lean-checked. Being nowhere dense and of positive measure at once is the substance of that statement. It leaves open whether one half is one of those subsums over an infinite support, which is a separate question about membership.

lemma.label: lemma
lemma.preview: A lemma is a proved supporting statement introduced mainly for use in proving a later theorem or organizing an argument.
lemma.card: Lemma describes the statement's role, not its difficulty or truth status. In a formal library a lemma is checked in exactly the same way as a theorem and may be mathematically substantial.
lemma.rule: Read a lemma's exact statement and dependencies rather than assuming it is minor because of the label.
lemma.deep: Breaking a proof into lemmas exposes reusable structure, gives the proof checker smaller obligations, and makes later results' dependency chains inspectable.

lemniscate.label: lemniscate
lemniscate.preview: A polynomial lemniscate is the set of points in the plane where a polynomial has one fixed size, so it is a level curve of the polynomial's absolute value.
lemniscate.card: For a small threshold the curve is a set of separate loops around the roots; as the threshold grows the loops merge. Where and how they merge is what Erdős #1041 asks about.
lemniscate.rule: A lemniscate is fixed by the polynomial and the chosen level, so a statement about one level is not a statement about the family.
lemniscate.deep: Erdős #1041 asks about short connections inside polynomial lemniscates. The Lean work formalises a no-connection criterion, the exact translation ray-collision locus, finite-line avoidance, and a root-retention bound. The global topology and length gluing remain open.

library.label: library
library.preview: A software library is a reusable collection of code and interfaces intended to be called by other programs or modules.
library.card: Libraries supply shared functionality so each project does not reimplement it. Using a library introduces a dependency on its version, behavior, license, and compatibility.
library.rule: Record the exact library version and interface assumptions when a result depends on it.
library.deep: A library can be source code, a compiled package, or a formal collection of definitions and theorems, but in each case consumers rely on a maintained external contract.

license.label: license
license.preview: A license is a permission granted under stated terms to use, copy, modify, distribute, or otherwise act on protected material.
license.card: A license defines allowed uses and conditions but does not transfer every right or guarantee the material's quality. Different files or dependencies can have different licenses.
license.rule: Before reusing material, check the applicable license, its scope, attribution duties, and compatibility with the intended use.
license.deep: Public availability is not the same as permission to reuse; access and licensing are separate questions.

limit.label: limit
limit.preview: A limit is a boundary or restriction; in Plectis, the surrounding phrase distinguishes a scope limit, mathematical limit, or service rate limit.
limit.card: Unqualified limit is a routing word, not one local technical object. In evidence pages it marks where a claim stops; in mathematics it is a value approached by a sequence or function; in runtime prose a rate limit caps requests over time. Plectis uses scope limit and mathematical limit when precision matters.
limit.rule: Read the noun phrase around limit before following the definition; never transfer conclusions between scope, analytic, and rate limits.
limit.deep: The senses share the ordinary idea of a boundary but have different authorities and checks: scope contracts govern claims, proofs govern mathematical limits, and provider or service policies govern rate limits.

line.label: line
line.preview: A line is a sequence of text or source characters separated from neighbouring sequences by a line boundary or displayed as one row.
line.card: Lines support editing, diagnostics, and citation, but visual wrapping can make one stored line appear as several displayed lines. Meaning often spans several lines.
line.rule: Use line references with a specific file or document version so the location remains interpretable.
line.deep: Line position is a convenient locator, not a stable identity when earlier edits can shift later lines.

lineage.label: lineage
lineage.preview: Lineage is the recorded chain of origins and transformations through which an artifact or claim came to exist.
lineage.card: Lineage connects a current result to its source material, intermediate versions, builders, and prior names. It lets a reader distinguish inherited material from newly authored or transformed material.
lineage.rule: Follow lineage when you need to know where something came from and which transformations may have changed it.
lineage.deep: Lineage establishes ancestry, not correctness; a faithfully traced claim can still be wrong at its source.

link.label: link
link.preview: A link is an actionable reference that takes a reader from the current surface to another page, file, anchor, or external resource.
link.card: A link supplies a route, while its text and relationship explain why the destination matters. It does not by itself establish support, equivalence, or authority.
link.rule: Read the destination and relationship before treating a link as evidence.
link.deep: Internal links are validated against generated routes and anchors; external links also depend on the continued availability and meaning of another site.

list.label: list
list.preview: A list is an ordered or unordered collection of separate items presented under a shared purpose or rule.
list.card: Lists support enumeration and scanning but may omit relationships beyond membership and order. Completeness depends on the list's stated source and inclusion boundary.
list.rule: Read a list by identifying what qualifies as an item, whether order matters, and whether the list claims completeness.
list.deep: A list can be a projection over richer records, so each item may have deeper fields not visible in the compact display.

live.label: live
live.preview: Live describes a currently operating or directly accessible state rather than a static copy, simulation, or historical snapshot.
live.card: Live material can change while it is being observed, and actions against it may affect the real system. That makes freshness, authority, and mutation safety more important than for a detached copy.
live.rule: Treat live access as current but mutable, and verify what actions the interface is authorized to perform.
live.deep: A live reading is temporally closer to current truth, but it can still be partial, inconsistent during change, or misinterpreted.

living_system_posture.label: living system posture
living_system_posture.preview: Living system posture is the stance that every page, result, doctrine row, raw quote, or runtime claim is dated evidence from one system state rather than a timeless fact, so present truth must be checked against the live source and its freshness.
living_system_posture.card: The system changes continuously, so a claim that held when it was written can later be out of date while the record of it stays on file. Living system posture keeps both halves separate: the past claim is preserved as a record of what was true then, and current authority comes from the live files and the surface that tracks how fresh each thing is. Reading something under this posture means asking what was true when it was written, what is true now, what changed, and which check proves it.
living_system_posture.rule: Treat any record on this site as carrying a date and a state of the system, not as a permanent truth: it tells you what held when it was made, and a current claim is confirmed against the live source and its freshness check.
living_system_posture.deep: Different layers go stale in different ways: a generated summary can lag its source, a recorded result can describe wiring that has since moved, and an early piece of doctrine can predate the rule that now governs it. The posture makes the gap between then and now something you can locate and check rather than something hidden.

llms_txt.label: llms.txt
llms_txt.preview: llms.txt is a plain-text file at the root of a site that tells an AI assistant where the site's readable content is.
llms_txt.card: It is the counterpart of robots.txt for assistants: rather than restricting crawling, it points at the files worth reading and says what each one is for.
llms_txt.rule: It is a routing file. It carries no claim that an assistant reading it has run anything.
llms_txt.deep: It is offered here alongside the AI packet and the reviewer brief as a direct route for readers whose buttons fail or who have JavaScript off.

load.label: load
load.preview: To load something is to bring data, code, configuration, or a resource into a program or environment so it can be used.
load.card: Loading may read from disk, network, memory, or a package system and can fail because the source is absent, invalid, unauthorized, or incompatible. Loaded state may persist only for the current run.
load.rule: When material is loaded, identify its source, version, validation, and lifetime in the receiving environment.
load.deep: Loading provides availability to a consumer but does not change the source's authority or guarantee safe interpretation.

local.label: local
local.preview: Local describes something situated within the current machine, repository, scope, or immediate context rather than a broader or remote one.
local.card: The relevant boundary must be named: local to a function differs from local to a repository or computer. Local access is often direct, but it does not automatically grant authority over the material.
local.rule: When local is used, identify the containing boundary and whether outside dependencies still influence the result.
local.deep: A local result can be correct within its boundary while failing to generalize or match deployed conditions.

locus.label: locus
locus.preview: A locus is a specific place where a feature, rule, effect, or piece of evidence resides or becomes observable.
locus.card: In software and documentation, a locus may be a file, function, field, route, or generated section. Naming it makes responsibility and inspection more precise than referring to the whole repository.
locus.rule: Use a locus to point to the smallest stable place that owns or demonstrates the relevant behaviour.
locus.deep: An effect can have several loci, such as one source definition, one builder transformation, and one public projection.

machine_checked.label: machine-checked
machine_checked.preview: Machine-checked means a result has been verified by software rather than accepted on a reader's judgement.
machine_checked.card: It is the strongest evidence class on this site, and also the narrowest. A machine-checked theorem is settled for exactly the statement checked, which is often a smaller claim than the surrounding description suggests. Reading the statement rather than the headline is the whole discipline.
machine_checked.rule: Machine-checked applies to the formal statement. Check what that statement actually says.
machine_checked.deep: The label is worth distrusting when it appears near prose rather than near a source reference, because that is where the range quietly widens.

machine_readable.label: machine-readable
machine_readable.preview: Machine-readable means structured so a program can use it directly, rather than written as prose a program would have to interpret.
machine_readable.card: A page of prose describing a proof corpus can be read by a person and only guessed at by a program. The same content as structured data can be queried: which results depend on this one, which are still conditional, what has already been ruled out. That is the difference between a corpus you must read to use and one you can ask.
machine_readable.rule: Machine-readable is about form, not truth. Structured data can be structured and wrong.
machine_readable.deep: Publishing the structure rather than only the prose is what lets someone else's tool check a claim without reimplementing the reading.

maintainer.label: maintainer
maintainer.preview: The maintainer is the person responsible for a repository: deciding what is merged, released and stated publicly.
maintainer.card: Both public repositories have one maintainer, Will Cook, who reviews returned contributions, records credit and is responsible for the released claims. Contributors do not need the maintainer's tools to do the work; they need the maintainer to accept the return.
maintainer.rule: Direct corrections and returns to the maintainer through the repository's issue forms and pull requests.
maintainer.deep: Because one person maintains both repositories, the site says plainly that no independent party has yet reviewed the whole.

manifest.label: manifest
manifest.preview: A manifest is a structured inventory that lists the artifacts in a release or build together with the metadata needed to identify and check them.
manifest.card: A manifest answers what was included and often records paths, hashes, roles, sizes, or source revisions. It is an inventory, not the content or proof of correctness of every listed item.
manifest.rule: Use the manifest to establish membership and identity, then inspect the listed artifact for substance.
manifest.deep: Manifests make omissions and unexpected additions mechanically detectable because the declared collection can be compared with disk or build output.

map.label: map
map.preview: A map here is a generated view over a body of material, built from that material rather than written alongside it, showing what is in it and how the parts connect.
map.card: Several things on this site are called maps: the architecture map over the components, the semantic map over the proof corpus, the site map for machine readers. They share a form rather than a subject. Each is regenerated from what it describes, so it cannot quietly disagree with it, and each is meant to be entered at any point rather than read from the start.
map.rule: A map is regenerated from its subject. If it disagrees with the subject, the map is stale.
map.deep: The distinction from documentation is that documentation is written and maps are derived. Written documentation ages silently; a derived map either regenerates or shows as stale, which is why the maps carry the coverage and orphan counts that let you check them.

match.label: match
match.preview: A match is a correspondence that satisfies stated comparison criteria.
match.card: Matching may compare text, identifiers, structures, values, or expected outcomes. The result is only as meaningful as the criteria and tolerance used to decide correspondence.
match.rule: When two things match, check which features were compared and whether exact or approximate agreement was required.
match.deep: Objects can match on one property while differing on others, so a match does not imply identity unless the criteria require complete equality.

mathematical_limit.label: mathematical limit
mathematical_limit.preview: A mathematical limit is the value a sequence or function gets arbitrarily close to as its index or input approaches a stated point or infinity.
mathematical_limit.card: In the Plectis mathematics, limits turn infinite processes into exact statements. Saying a_n tends to L means that every requested tolerance is eventually met; it does not require any term to equal L, and it is separate from calling a claim boundary a limit.
mathematical_limit.rule: Identify the varying object, target value, direction of approach, and quantified notion of closeness.
mathematical_limit.deep: For the infinite series discussed in the papers, convergence establishes that partial sums have a limit, while irrationality asks what kind of number that limit is. A long numerical prefix can suggest the value but cannot replace the quantified proof.

mathematics.label: mathematics
mathematics.preview: Mathematics is the study of abstract structures, quantities, patterns, and logical relationships through definitions, conjectures, proofs, and computation.
mathematics.card: This site focuses on number-theoretic problems and distinguishes informal exposition, computational evidence, and machine-checked formal proof. Those are complementary ways of doing and communicating mathematics.
mathematics.rule: Match each mathematical claim to the kind of argument or evidence that supports it.
mathematics.deep: Mathematical certainty applies to conclusions proved from explicit assumptions within a formal or accepted logical framework, not automatically to interpretations, significance, or empirical claims.

mathlib.label: Mathlib
mathlib.preview: Mathlib is the community-maintained mathematical library for Lean, providing reusable definitions, theorems, tactics, and notation.
mathlib.card: The formal mathematics in this project can depend on Mathlib instead of rebuilding standard foundations. Exact proof reproduction therefore pins a compatible Lean and Mathlib revision.
mathlib.rule: Treat imported Mathlib theorems as checked dependencies and record the revision used by the build.
mathlib.deep: Mathlib's breadth makes formalization faster, but an imported result still has an exact statement whose hypotheses and types must match the local proof.

mean.label: mean
mean.preview: To mean something is to signify, express, entail, or be interpreted as that thing within a language or context.
mean.card: Meaning connects a sign, statement, or action with what a reader should understand from it. The same form can mean different things under different definitions or contexts; arithmetic mean is a separate mathematical use.
mean.rule: Resolve what something means from its governing definition and context rather than from appearance alone.
mean.deep: Meaning may be conventional, formally specified, or inferred from use, and those sources can disagree unless the system names which one governs.

measurement.label: measurement
measurement.preview: A measurement is a value obtained by applying a defined procedure or instrument to an observed object or process.
measurement.card: Measurements need units, method, conditions, uncertainty, and provenance to be interpreted. Repeating a measurement can test stability without proving a universal law.
measurement.rule: Read what was measured, how, when, with which units, and under which conditions.
measurement.deep: Computed metrics and physical measurements share a result shape but differ in error sources: one depends on code and input data, the other also depends on instruments and observation conditions.

mechanism.label: mechanism
mechanism.preview: A mechanism is an account of how something in the system happens: how an object moves, transforms, routes, validates, or changes state, stated as the actual flow of inputs, steps, and outputs rather than as a label.
mechanism.card: A mechanism names the working path behind a piece of doctrine or behaviour: what goes in, what is done to it, what comes out, what authority governs it, and how it can fail. It ties an idea to running code, a standard, or a runtime surface, so a claim about how the system behaves can be traced to the steps that actually carry it out.
mechanism.rule: When a mechanism is described, follow it down to the inputs, steps, and outputs it names, and check that those steps are grounded in real code or standards rather than asserted in the abstract.
mechanism.deep: A mechanism is meant to bind meaning to flow: inputs, transformations, outputs, authority, validation, failure modes, and the relationships between the parts. A description that names a behaviour without those moving parts is a slogan, not a mechanism.

menu.label: menu
menu.preview: A menu is a presented set of choices from which a reader or operator can select an action or destination.
menu.card: Menus compress an available option space into labels and groupings. Their quality depends on whether the choices are understandable, reachable, and appropriate to the current context.
menu.rule: Use a menu as a choice surface and verify that its labels lead to the destinations or actions they promise.
menu.deep: A menu can hide options through grouping or filtering, so it should not be assumed to enumerate every possible action unless declared complete.

mersenne_number.label: Mersenne number
mersenne_number.preview: A Mersenne number is one less than a power of two: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, and so on.
mersenne_number.card: Erdős #257 asks about sums of reciprocals of these numbers, taken over a chosen set of exponents. At a general whole-number base b the same construction uses b to the n minus one instead.
mersenne_number.rule: Base two is the critical case for these questions, not a representative one, so a result at base two does not automatically extend to other bases.
mersenne_number.deep: The reduced denominator of a finite subsum over Mersenne numbers has multiplicative order exactly the least common multiple of the support, which is Lean-checked. That is a statement about finite supports and does not settle the infinite case.

metabolism.label: metabolism
metabolism.preview: Metabolism is the governed upkeep loop that refreshes derived artifacts from their authoritative sources and records the checks.
metabolism.card: Where ordinary navigation reads what is already there, metabolism is the layer that produces and refreshes it. It watches the authoritative source material, queues bounded pieces of work, populates or rebuilds derived surfaces such as generated summaries and indexes, checks the results, and records what it did. It is durable upkeep, not a one-off answer: enforcing standards, refreshing generated views, and repairing scaffolding all run here. It is bounded by design and halts at the point where a human or a higher authority must decide.
metabolism.rule: When something on this site is described as metabolized, take it as a surface that the upkeep loop generated and last refreshed, not source material edited by hand.
metabolism.deep: There are two kinds: deterministic metabolism handles fixed, well-defined refresh once the rules exist, while the judgement-bearing kind handles unsettled cases such as naming a new concept or resolving a contradiction before any automatic refresh can take over.

metadata_only.label: metadata-only
metadata_only.preview: Metadata-only describes a record that carries the shape and verdict of a run but none of the content it read: counts, classes, digests and outcomes, without the bodies behind them.
metadata_only.card: This is what lets a run over private inputs still produce something publishable. The record says how many rows were classified and how, or that a body matched its declared digest, without reproducing the row or the body. It is a deliberate reduction, and it is checkable in its own right: the build refuses a record that has let content leak into a field meant to hold only shape.
metadata_only.rule: Read a metadata-only record as evidence about a run, never as the data the run saw.
metadata_only.deep: The guarantee is enforced rather than promised. Result-record fields are checked for body leakage on every build, and a record carrying content where it should carry shape raises a specific failure code instead of passing quietly.

method.label: method
method.preview: A method is an ordered way of carrying out an analysis, computation, proof, or construction.
method.card: A method explains how a result was reached so another reader can inspect or repeat it. The method can be valid even when a particular implementation or input is flawed.
method.rule: Separate the method from the evidence that one execution of it succeeded.
method.deep: Methods range from informal reasoning strategies to exact algorithms; their reproducibility depends on how fully their inputs, steps, and assumptions are stated.

missing.label: missing
missing.preview: Missing describes something required, expected, or referenced that is not present or cannot be found in the relevant place.
missing.card: Missingness depends on an expectation and a search boundary. A value can be absent by design, unavailable because of access, or lost through a defect, and those cases need different responses.
missing.rule: When something is reported missing, check what should exist, where the search looked, and whether absence was permitted.
missing.deep: Failure to observe an item is evidence of absence only when the observation method and coverage are strong enough.

model.label: model
model.preview: A model is a deliberately simplified representation or computational system used to describe, predict, classify, or generate outcomes about something else.
model.card: On this site, “model” may mean an AI model, a mathematical representation, or a structured data model; the nearby qualifier determines which. Every model omits detail and has a domain where its outputs are meaningful.
model.rule: Identify what the model represents, how it was produced, and where its assumptions stop.
model.deep: Model outputs are observations about the model's behavior, not direct facts about the represented world unless validation connects the two.

module.label: module
module.preview: A module is a bounded unit of code or exposition grouped around one responsibility and designed to be referenced as a whole.
module.card: In software, a module collects related definitions or behavior; in this site's paper-module layer, it collects a subsystem's readable explanation. The surrounding label tells which meaning applies.
module.rule: Identify the module kind before assuming that it is executable code or a paper module.
module.deep: Modularity creates boundaries for ownership, testing, reuse, and navigation, but those boundaries are organizational rather than proof that the unit is independent.

morse_saddle.label: Morse saddle
morse_saddle.preview: A saddle is a point where a surface rises in one direction and falls in another, like the middle of a mountain pass.
morse_saddle.card: Non-degeneracy is what pins the number of directions leaving the point. An argument that assumes the wrong number of local branches at a saddle can be locally invalid while looking right globally.
morse_saddle.rule: Morse is a hypothesis about curvature at the point, not a description of the whole surface.
morse_saddle.deep: The Erdős #1041 note reports that a recent manuscript's load-bearing Proposition 12 uses an invalid three-ended local block at an interior Morse saddle. This was diagnosed here independently and matches Tao's public account of the same defect. The proposition is not refuted and may admit a repair.

move.label: move
move.preview: A move is one deliberate change of position, state, ownership, or strategy.
move.card: The word can name a file relocation, an operational action, or a reasoning step. In each case it should identify what changes, from where, to where, and under whose authority.
move.rule: Read a proposed move by checking its target, direction, consequences, and reversibility.
move.deep: A move can preserve content while changing its location or role, but references and ownership may still need updating.

multiple.label: multiple
multiple.preview: Multiple can mean more than one item, or in arithmetic a number obtained by multiplying another number by an integer; Plectis uses both senses.
multiple.card: In system prose, multiple usually means several, as in multiple providers or files. In the mathematical papers, m is a multiple of d exactly when m = d × k for some integer k, equivalently when d divides m. The mathematical sense must be supplied by a product or divisibility context.
multiple.rule: Resolve the sense from the noun phrase: several objects in ordinary prose, or an exact integer product in a divisibility statement.
multiple.deep: The mathematical sense coordinates common denominators, periods, and least-common-multiple constraints. It includes zero and can include negative values under the theorem's convention; none of that structure is implied by the ordinary adjective.

multiplicative_order.label: multiplicative order
multiplicative_order.preview: The multiplicative order of an integer `b` modulo `Q` is the smallest positive exponent `k` for which `b^k` leaves remainder one when divided by `Q`.
multiplicative_order.card: The order exists when `b` and `Q` are coprime and measures the period of repeated multiplication by `b` modulo `Q`. It can connect a reduced denominator to the least common multiple of a set of exponents.
multiplicative_order.rule: Check the modulus, base, coprimality condition, and minimality of the claimed exponent.
multiplicative_order.deep: Verifying `b^k ≡ 1 mod Q` only shows that the order divides `k`; proving exact order also requires excluding every smaller positive divisor candidate.

name.label: name
name.preview: A name is the human-readable word or phrase used to refer to a person, object, concept, or release.
name.card: Names make things recognizable, but they can be ambiguous, translated, or changed. Stable identifiers and compatibility routes preserve identity when names move.
name.rule: Use the name for communication and the stable identifier when exact identity matters.
name.deep: A rename changes the public handle without necessarily changing the underlying object, which is why migrations record old and new names explicitly.

narrow.label: narrow
narrow.preview: To narrow something is to reduce its scope, possibilities, range, or level of detail under consideration.
narrow.card: Narrowing helps make questions answerable and actions safer by excluding irrelevant or unauthorized territory. It should preserve the relationship between the smaller question and the larger one it came from.
narrow.rule: When scope is narrowed, record the exclusions so the resulting claim is not later read as broader than it is.
narrow.deep: A narrow result can be strong within its boundary while leaving the general case entirely open.

natural_number.label: natural number
natural_number.preview: A natural number is a whole number used for counting, with the convention about whether zero is included stated by the surrounding formalization.
natural_number.card: Different texts use ℕ for either {0,1,2,…} or {1,2,3,…}; Lean includes zero in its natural-number type. Positive natural numbers exclude zero.
natural_number.rule: Check the zero convention before transferring a statement between sources.
natural_number.deep: Natural numbers support induction, recursion, divisibility, and finite counting, and formal systems encode them as a specific type rather than an informal collection.

navigation.label: navigation
navigation.preview: Navigation is the system’s browse-and-drilldown layer for moving from a question to the smallest source-backed answer surface.
navigation.card: Rather than opening the whole codebase to find one thing, navigation presents the system as a series of choices that can be opened in stages: a top-level map, then groups, then individual rows, then the source or evidence behind a row. Each step shows what exists and what it contains before the full text is loaded, so a path through the material can be chosen deliberately. It is the layer that makes the system inspectable in order, from overview down to a single record.
navigation.rule: Treat a navigation surface as a map of what is available, not the thing itself: follow it down to the underlying record before relying on what a row says.
navigation.deep: Navigation works by compression, turning a large body of files into visible rows that can be expanded at widening levels of detail, so the system can present its own structure instead of each reader rebuilding the map from scratch.

negative.label: negative
negative.preview: Negative describes a result, condition, value, or case that denies, fails, opposes, or falls below a chosen reference point.
negative.card: Its meaning depends on context: a negative test expects rejection, a negative finding reports absence, and a negative number lies below zero. The surrounding noun supplies the relevant sense.
negative.rule: Do not treat negative as automatically bad; identify the test, sign convention, or proposition it negates.
negative.deep: Negative evidence can be highly useful when it rules out an unsafe input, disproves a conjecture, or narrows a search.

negative_case.label: negative case
negative_case.preview: A negative case is an input a check must reject, shipped beside passing inputs so a detector that stops discriminating fails visibly instead of quietly accepting everything.
negative_case.card: A check that only ever sees valid input cannot tell you it is working. Break it and it still passes. The negative case closes that hole: it is a deliberately bad input with a recorded expectation that the check refuses it. If a component's negative case starts passing, the component is broken even though nothing has thrown an error. This is the difference between a check that runs and a check that discriminates.
negative_case.rule: Read a component's negative cases to see what it can actually detect. A check with no negative case has not shown it can fail.
negative_case.deep: Negative cases are the cheapest defence against the failure mode this system is most exposed to: machinery that reports success because it has stopped looking. They are why a passing result is treated as evidence rather than as a green light - the run has demonstrated both that it accepts what it should and refuses what it should not.

newton_flow.label: Newton flow
newton_flow.preview: The Newton flow is the continuous version of Newton's method: instead of jumping in steps toward a root of a polynomial, a point drifts smoothly in the direction Newton's method would push it.
newton_flow.card: Along that flow the value of the polynomial decays in a controlled way, which turns a question about curves in the plane into a question about how those trajectories can meet.
newton_flow.rule: A statement about the flow constrains the trajectories, not the polynomial's roots directly.
newton_flow.deep: For Erdős #1041, Lean checks that the polynomial value decays as exp of minus t along the flow and therefore stays on one oriented ray, and formalises the resulting no-connection criterion. The global topology and the length gluing remain open.

node.label: node
node.preview: A node is one uniquely identified object represented as a point in a graph.
node.card: Nodes carry identity and attributes, while edges record their relationships. A node may stand for a page, theorem, component, term, or another artifact kind.
node.rule: Read the node type and stable identifier before following its edges.
node.deep: The same real object should not become several accidental nodes merely because it appears on several pages; projections preserve a join back to one identity.

normal_form.label: normal form
normal_form.preview: A normal form is a standard way of rewriting an object so that two objects are equal exactly when their rewritten versions match.
normal_form.card: Putting a problem into a normal form does not solve it. It moves the difficulty into a shape where the remaining obligation can be stated exactly, which is often what makes a machine check possible at all.
normal_form.rule: A normal form is a reformulation, so it carries the same difficulty as the statement it rewrites unless a separate result says otherwise.
normal_form.deep: Erdős #68 has an exact factorial-successor normal form in Lean, and Erdős #257 an exact carry-pivot normal form. Both are exact reformulations, and both problems remain open.

note.label: note
note.preview: A note is a short record or explanation attached to a larger body of work.
note.card: Notes preserve context, qualifications, reminders, or observations that do not belong in the main flow. Their authority depends on who wrote them and what evidence they cite.
note.rule: Read a note as supplementary context unless the governing surface explicitly gives it stronger authority.
note.deep: Brevity does not make a note informal or unimportant, but it often means the note omits the fuller argument or evidence.

nowhere_dense.label: nowhere dense
nowhere_dense.preview: A set is nowhere dense when it contains no interval, and neither does the set you get by adding all its limit points.
nowhere_dense.card: It is the topological sense of thin: however far you zoom in, you always find a gap. The Cantor set is the standard example.
nowhere_dense.rule: Nowhere dense is a statement about gaps, not about size in measure. A set can be nowhere dense and still fill most of an interval in Lebesgue measure.
nowhere_dense.deep: The achievement set studied for Erdős #257 is compact, nowhere dense, and of Lebesgue measure one at the same time. The pairing is the point: no interval sits inside it, and yet it is not negligible.

number.label: number
number.preview: A number is an abstract mathematical object used to count, measure, order, or represent quantities.
number.card: Different number systems include natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, real numbers, and complex numbers, each with different operations and properties. A theorem's domain states which kind is intended.
number.rule: Identify the number system before applying divisibility, order, or approximation rules.
number.deep: The same written numeral can denote elements embedded across several number systems, but formal proofs keep their types explicit.

number_theory.label: number theory
number_theory.preview: Number theory is the area of mathematics that studies integers and related structures, including divisibility, primes, congruences, and arithmetic functions.
number_theory.card: The Erdős problems on this site are largely number-theoretic, often involving sequences, reciprocal sums, denominators, and multiplicative behavior. Number theory can use tools from analysis, algebra, combinatorics, and computation.
number_theory.rule: Identify which integer or arithmetic structure the problem is asking about.
number_theory.deep: Elementary statements in number theory can require deep proofs because simple integer operations encode strong global constraints.

numerator.label: numerator
numerator.preview: The numerator is the top part of a fraction: in P/Q, it is P, the quantity being divided by Q.
numerator.card: Plectis uses numerators when an exact finite sum is reduced to P/Q. P and Q must be tracked as a pair: cancelling a common factor changes both, and only the reduced denominator Q is later used for the order and divisibility certificates.
numerator.rule: When a paper or component writes P/Q, check whether the fraction is reduced and do not transfer a claim about Q to P.
numerator.deep: In the finite denominator-certificate work, exact rational summation produces P/Q before the denominator is reconstructed independently from least-common-multiple and factorisation data. The numerator records the accumulated finite sum; it is not the certificate target, and its value depends on the same cancellation that determines the final denominator.

obs_studio.label: OBS Studio
obs_studio.preview: OBS Studio is the free screen-recording and streaming program most people use to record a screencast.
obs_studio.card: It is named here only as a point of comparison: the recording console used for these videos does a similar job but sits inside the system being recorded, so it can index what was on screen rather than only capturing it.
obs_studio.rule: The comparison is to the recording function alone, not to a claim about features.
obs_studio.deep: The Demo Take Console records, transcribes, indexes frames against words, and compiles cuts. That indexing is what a general-purpose recorder does not do.

observation.label: observation
observation.preview: An observation is information recorded by inspecting an event, artifact, measurement, or behavior.
observation.card: Observations report what was seen under particular conditions and can become evidence for a claim. Interpretation and generalization require a separate argument.
observation.rule: Record the observer or instrument, conditions, time, and exact thing observed.
observation.deep: In software work an observation may come from logs or output; in research it may come from an experiment or dataset; neither becomes a universal fact automatically.

observe.label: observe
observe.preview: An observe is a read-only pass that gathers structured evidence from files, probes, and responses into a bounded record before any decision or change is made.
observe.card: Observe is the evidence-gathering half of the observe/apply pairing the system runs. An observe pass learns, maps, compares, or probes a target and writes down what it found: the questions it asked, the files it examined, the responses it got back, a synthesis, and any validation signals. It can run locally or across a bridge of helpers, but it never mutates code or doctrine. Its job is to keep exploration separate from action so a decision rests on collected facts rather than a first guess.
observe.rule: Read an observe pass as a record of what was examined and found, not as a completed change. The work it describes has been looked into, not yet carried out.
observe.deep: Keeping the observe step explicit means the evidence behind a later change is inspectable on its own, and the system does not treat its first plan as if the work were already done.

omission_receipt.label: omission receipt
omission_receipt.preview: An omission receipt is the note on a compressed row that states what was left out, why that omission is allowed at the current depth, and which command reopens the full source.
omission_receipt.card: Pages and browse rows on this site are compressed views of a much larger body of source material. An omission receipt is the part of such a row that keeps the compression honest: it names what was dropped, such as the underlying source bodies, deeper relationships, or fuller command output, gives the reason that omission is acceptable for a quick-scan row, and points to the drilldown that recovers the complete material. It lets a row be useful for choosing what to open without quietly pretending to be the whole story.
omission_receipt.rule: Treat the omission receipt on a row as the row's own statement of its limits: it tells you what is not shown and how to reach the full source, so follow that pointer when you need the complete picture rather than assuming the short row is everything.
omission_receipt.deep: Its function is to stop a compact view from claiming false completeness: the row stays cheap to read, yet the receipt records exactly what was excluded, why that exclusion is acceptable at this level of detail, and which command restores the full source behind it.

open_obligation.label: open obligation
open_obligation.preview: An open obligation is the exact statement that would still have to be proved for a result to reach its target.
open_obligation.card: Problem pages list open obligations after the checked results. Each is written so that a proof of it, combined with the results already checked, would settle the named question. The list specifies the remaining work; it does not rank or predict it.
open_obligation.rule: Treat an open obligation as a precise target. Proving one is a contribution; restating one is not.
open_obligation.deep: Obligations are kept separate from conjectures and from failed approaches, so a reader can tell what is needed from what was guessed and what was tried.

open_problem.label: open problem
open_problem.preview: An open problem is a precisely stated question for which no proof or counterexample accepted by the relevant mathematical community is currently known.
open_problem.card: A problem can remain open despite extensive computations, conditional reductions, solved special cases, and formalized supporting theory. Those results narrow or reorganize the question but do not settle its universal statement.
open_problem.rule: When a problem is marked open, distinguish the original question from the partial and conditional results reported around it.
open_problem.deep: Open status is time-sensitive and source-sensitive, so a responsible statement names the problem, date or source of the status, and any claimed resolution that would need independent review.

operation.label: operation
operation.preview: An operation is a defined transformation, calculation, or state change applied to specified objects or inputs.
operation.card: Operations range from mathematical addition to file writes and API calls. Their meaning comes from the domain, operands, preconditions, and expected effect.
operation.rule: Identify the operation's inputs, permitted target, and result contract before executing or reasoning from it.
operation.deep: An operation can be pure, producing a value without changing external state, or stateful, changing files, services, or records.

operator_proxy.label: operator proxy
operator_proxy.preview: An operator proxy is an outside worker acting on the operator's behalf for one bounded task from a prepared context-and-instruction packet, carrying the operator's intent without acquiring the operator's authority.
operator_proxy.card: When the system hands a task to a separate worker, such as a chat model or coding agent, it sends a packet that holds the purpose, the relevant doctrine, worked examples, the output shape, and the constraints. The worker runs as an operator proxy: it can do real work because the packet makes the intent executable, but its remit is fixed to that one task. Choosing what context to send, validating the result, and deciding whether the output enters the system stay with the owning side, not the proxy.
operator_proxy.rule: Treat an operator proxy's output as work done to order, not as a decision made by the operator. It is bounded to the task it was given, and it becomes part of the system only after the owning side validates and admits it.
operator_proxy.deep: The role separates how capable a worker is from how much authority it holds: a highly capable proxy can outperform a less capable owner on a well-prepared packet, yet it still cannot see context it was not given, change the system's rules, or speak as the operator.

operator_voice.label: operator voice
operator_voice.preview: Operator voice is the preserved first-person record of what the operator said directly, kept separate from every later agent-authored summary or interpretation as the original human input behind the system.
operator_voice.card: Operator voice is the unmediated expression of the person who runs the system: raw seed paragraphs, spoken notes, and direct instructions, recorded as they were given. It holds authority over every later artifact, so paper modules, standards, and agent-written summaries may compress or route it but can never replace or contradict it. The raw record is kept append-only for this reason: it is the layer everything else answers to.
operator_voice.rule: When something is marked as operator voice, treat it as the original human source, above any summary or agent rephrasing of it. If a later page conflicts with it, the operator voice is the one that holds.
operator_voice.deep: It is distinct from two nearby things: a Bridge proxy acting for the operator under a prepared packet, and an agent-authored projection that compresses operator voice into doctrine. Both of those are downstream; only operator voice is the original.

option_surface.label: option surface
option_surface.preview: An option surface is a browse layer of stable, kind-grouped, selectable artifact rows used to choose and inspect a specific item before opening the authoritative source it points to.
option_surface.card: An option surface sits between the top-level Kind Atlas and the underlying source material. For a chosen kind of artifact, such as components, paper modules, or doctrine cards, it enumerates the available rows cheaply, lets one be selected by its stable id, and shows a compact card for that row that states what is and is not included and how current it is. Only after a row is chosen does it hand off to the authoritative standard, registry, skill, or paper module behind it.
option_surface.rule: Treat an option surface as a catalogue for finding and selecting one row, not as the final authority on that row. The card it shows is a summary with its own currentness and omission notes; the binding detail is in the source it links to.
