option_surface.deep: It works in bands: a cheap listing band shows many rows at a glance, and a card band expands a single selected id into more detail, including a record of any id that was asked for but not found. This keeps browsing inexpensive while keeping the path back to source explicit.

orbit.label: orbit
orbit.preview: An orbit is the sequence of values produced by applying the same step over and over from a starting point.
orbit.card: Orbits turn a question about a number into a question about long-run behaviour: does the sequence stay bounded, return, drift, or vanish. That is often easier to state exactly, and no easier to prove.
orbit.rule: A finite stretch of an orbit is a computation. Statements about the whole orbit need a separate argument.
orbit.deep: Erdős #243 becomes rigidity of a centred integer error orbit once denominators are cleared, and the remaining Erdős #257 targets reduce to explicit alternatives about infinite orbits. In both cases the reformulation is exact and the problem is open.

order.label: order
order.preview: Order is the arrangement of items or actions according to position, precedence, dependency, or a comparison rule.
order.card: Order can be alphabetical, chronological, logical, numerical, or procedural. The chosen rule determines what earlier and later mean and whether the order affects validity.
order.rule: When order matters, identify the ordering rule and which steps or items depend on their position.
order.deep: Some collections are displayed in an order for convenience even though their underlying meaning is unchanged by permutation.

orientation.label: orientation
orientation.preview: Orientation is the material meant to be read first: a short account of what this is and how to navigate it, as distinct from the evidence itself.
orientation.card: Orientation is deliberately separated from evidence, because the two carry different weight. An orientation guide is the author describing the work, which is useful and is not proof of anything. Keeping the boundary visible stops a good explanation from being mistaken for a good result.
orientation.rule: Read orientation to find your way. Read records to check claims.
orientation.deep: The separation is easy to lose, because clear description is persuasive in the same register as evidence.

orphan.label: orphan
orphan.preview: An orphan is an item an index has failed to place: something present in the source but connected to nothing in the map built over it.
orphan.card: The orphan count is how you tell an index apart from a partial index. A map with orphans is one that quietly stops covering part of its subject, and any question asked of it will return an answer that looks complete. Publishing the count is what makes coverage checkable rather than assumed.
orphan.rule: Check the orphan count before trusting a map's coverage. Zero is the only reassuring number.
orphan.deep: The failure mode is silence: an orphaned declaration does not raise an error, it simply never appears in an answer, so the gap is invisible from the outside.

output.label: output
output.preview: An output is the data, artifact, message, or state produced by a process after it consumes inputs.
output.card: Outputs should be interpreted through the producing command, source version, and contract. Generated output is usually rebuilt from source rather than edited directly.
output.rule: Trace an output back to its inputs and producer before treating it as authoritative.
output.deep: A process can emit several outputs with different roles, such as a human page, a machine packet, and a validation receipt derived from the same source.

overview.label: overview
overview.preview: An overview is a compressed account of a subject's main parts and relationships intended to orient a reader before detail.
overview.card: An overview trades completeness for navigational value. It should reveal the shape of the subject, important boundaries, and where to continue without pretending to contain all evidence.
overview.rule: Use an overview to choose a route, then open the owning detail before relying on a precise claim.
overview.deep: Compression can omit exceptions and implementation detail, so an overview is a projection rather than exhaustive authority.

package.label: package
package.preview: A package is a collection prepared to travel as one unit.
package.card: A software package carries code, metadata, dependencies, and a version for package tooling. A submission package instead gathers the files and records needed for review or delivery. Neither meaning is automatically the same as an AI packet or evidence bundle, which have their own reader and provenance contracts.
package.rule: Use install, import, dependency, or version context for the software sense; use submit, review, or delivery context for the assembled-artifact sense.
package.deep: Plectis also preserves some package identifiers for compatibility and lineage. Such an identifier can keep an old route or dependency resolvable without making that package name a current public category or product identity.

packet.label: packet
packet.preview: A packet is a single bundled file prepared for an AI assistant to read, carrying the site's content and structure in one download rather than as pages to browse.
packet.card: An assistant reading a website page by page gets an incomplete and arbitrary slice of it. A packet removes that problem by shipping the whole public surface at once, in a form built for machine reading. Different sizes exist for the same reason: some tools refuse large files.
packet.rule: A packet tells an assistant what the site says. It does not let the assistant run anything.
packet.deep: The distinction between reading and running survives the packet. A packet improves the quality of a summary, and a summary is still not evidence.

page.label: page
page.preview: A page is one rendered reading surface at a stable site route, presenting selected prose, data, and links from underlying source material.
page.card: Pages are designed for orientation and reading, not as independent authority. A generated page may accurately project source data, but the page still needs a route back to the file, record, or contract that owns the underlying claim.
page.rule: Read a page as a presentation of source material and use its links to inspect the owning record when accuracy matters.
page.deep: A page can combine authored prose with generated facts and relationships, so its trust boundary is field-specific rather than uniform across the whole document.

palomar.label: Palomar
palomar.preview: Palomar is an external registry for machine-checked mathematical results.
palomar.card: The project prepares result families for Palomar and keeps its own ranking of them in the Lean repository's showcase file. Submission, a passed automated check and public registration are three different states, and the site names which one applies wherever it mentions a record. A Palomar record does not certify the rest of the corpus, establish novelty or replace peer review.
palomar.rule: Read a Palomar reference as a pointer to a pinned, checked formal statement, then check which state the record has reached.
palomar.deep: Palomar's automated checks and review have stated limits. The project's own claim records remain the authority for what each result claims, and Comparator remains the check that a stated proposition matches its Lean proof.

paper.label: paper
paper.preview: A paper is a rendered PDF write-up that gives a human-readable account of a project, question, method, result, and evidence boundary, linked to its supporting source where available.
paper.card: The Plectis paper shelf contains reader-facing rendered PDFs: short problem notes, longer working records, mathematical expositions, and systems write-ups. Calling one a paper identifies that presentation form, not peer review, journal publication, novelty, or proof authority. A paper module is different: it is an internal ai_workflow document that maps a subsystem, its owners, and its routes. For mathematical claims, the paper explains the argument while the Lean declarations and claim registry own what was checked and what remains open.
paper.rule: Use a paper to understand the argument and its significance, then follow its claim and source references for verification.
paper.deep: A paper integrates source records into a coherent human exposition and is versioned with the source used to render it. Its value is explanation and synthesis. Its limits come from the cited evidence: formal claims remain subordinate to Lean and the claim registry, measurements remain subordinate to their records, and the label paper alone grants no academic status.

paper_module.label: paper module
paper_module.preview: A paper module is a stable explanation packet mapping one subsystem's purpose, structure, invariants, source locations, and current state without replacing the code or records it describes.
paper_module.card: Each paper module covers a single subsystem and records its intent, its shape and boundaries, the rules that must hold, the source files it points down to, its current state, what it still owes, and how it is kept fresh. It points downward to source and upward to the principles, components, and standards the area connects to, so an area can be understood without reopening every file. It is an explanation of running machinery, not the machinery, and not the final authority over it.
paper_module.rule: Treat a paper module as an orientation for one area, then check the source it points to for any detail you will rely on. It describes a subsystem at a point in time and can lag the code if it has not been refreshed.
paper_module.deep: A paper module is one ontology row per subsystem: it names the area and links it to source loci below and to principles, concepts, mechanisms, skills, standards, and navigation surfaces above.

part.label: part
part.preview: A part is a constituent portion of a larger whole that can be identified by its role, boundary, or composition.
part.card: Parts may be physical, logical, textual, or procedural. Understanding a part requires both its internal properties and the relationships through which it contributes to the whole.
part.rule: Read a part by asking what whole contains it and what role distinguishes it from neighbouring parts.
part.deep: A part can be independently inspectable without being independently useful or authoritative. Membership alone does not give a part the scope, authority, or behaviour of the containing whole.

partial_sum.label: partial sum
partial_sum.preview: A partial sum is the finite sum of the first selected terms of an infinite series.
partial_sum.card: Partial sums are the finite objects used to define and approximate a series. Convergence means that these sums approach one fixed value as the cutoff moves farther out.
partial_sum.rule: Do not confuse a computed partial sum with the exact value of the infinite series without a bound on the remaining tail.
partial_sum.deep: A rigorous approximation pairs the partial sum with an error estimate controlling every term not yet included.

pass.label: pass
pass.preview: A pass is one bounded traversal or execution of a process, often producing a result that can pass or fail its checks.
pass.card: A pass may be an editing pass, validation pass, audit pass, or test pass. The noun names one run through a defined procedure; the verb says that its stated acceptance conditions were met.
pass.rule: Check which procedure ran and which conditions its passing result actually covers.
pass.deep: Passing is local to the gate that was evaluated, so one green pass does not establish unrelated qualities or future correctness.

passion.label: passion
passion.preview: Passion is the judgment trait that keeps the operator's live aim and stake present while the work remains bounded by standards, evidence, and source authority, preserving why the work matters as well as what it must complete.
passion.card: Passion is one of the named traits the system uses to describe disciplined human judgment, alongside care and common sense. It is the trait that resists flattening a request into sterile task completion: it carries the person's theory, urgency, and meaning into the action so the action stays intelligible. It is bounded, not free rein. Whatever it motivates must still be backed by a source and constrained by the standards, so the live purpose is preserved without becoming unchecked enthusiasm.
passion.rule: When you see passion named, read it as the stake and intent behind a piece of work, held alongside the evidence rather than in place of it. It signals why something matters; it does not on its own license a claim.
passion.deep: In this system passion sits inside a wider surface of judgment traits: passion supplies the live purpose, while care and common sense keep that purpose grounded in artifacts that can be located, checked, and maintained. Passion without standards is noise, and standards without passion miss the point the work exists to serve.

path.label: path
path.preview: A path is an ordered location identifier that tells a program or reader where a file, directory, or web route sits within a larger hierarchy.
path.card: Paths answer where something is, not what it means or whether it is authoritative. Repository paths use directory separators to locate files; URL paths locate public routes; compatibility paths may continue to resolve after a human-facing name changes.
path.rule: Use a path to locate an object, then inspect the object's role and source before drawing conclusions from it.
path.deep: Because paths can be renamed or redirected, durable references often pair the path with a stable identifier, role, source fingerprint, or compatibility route.

path_handle.label: path handle
path_handle.preview: A path handle is a stable short identifier that resolves to a current file path, its role, and its verification command.
path_handle.card: A path handle separates the identity of a reference from the place a thing is stored. Instead of repeating a long or unstable filesystem path everywhere, the system keeps one governed entry that records where the target lives now, what job it plays, how to display it, how fresh it is, which older references still point to it, and the command that expands it back to the full path. Because the handle stays stable while the underlying location can move, it lets the system keep packets compact and references intact without renaming files on disk.
path_handle.rule: When you meet a path handle, treat it as a stable pointer rather than the location itself: it names where the target lives now and carries the command to expand it, while old references it lists still resolve to the same target.
path_handle.deep: A path handle carries the target path, a role, a display label, a source fingerprint or freshness posture, compatibility redirects, an expansion command, and a migration state, so a reference can stay constant even as the storage container behind it changes.

pattern.label: pattern
pattern.preview: A pattern is a recurring or recognizable arrangement in data, behaviour, structure, or reasoning.
pattern.card: Patterns compress multiple observations into a shared form that can support recognition, prediction, or reuse. Their value depends on whether the similarity is real and relevant rather than superficial.
pattern.rule: When applying a pattern, compare the new case's important conditions with the cases from which the pattern was learned.
pattern.deep: A pattern suggests a route or hypothesis but does not guarantee that every instance will behave identically.

pdf.label: PDF
pdf.preview: PDF is a document file format designed to preserve a page's visual layout across devices and software.
pdf.card: The site publishes papers as PDFs for stable human reading and links their source separately. A PDF preserves presentation but is less suitable than source or structured data for exact reuse and machine inspection.
pdf.rule: Use the PDF for the published reading copy and follow its source links for editable text and proof authority.
pdf.deep: A PDF can embed text, fonts, images, links, and metadata, but its appearance does not reveal whether the underlying claims were checked.

peer.label: peer
peer.preview: A peer is another capable coding-agent instance working on the system that can inherit durable lessons recorded by earlier agents, without implying shared memory or authority beyond those records.
peer.card: The system is built to be operated by capable AI coding agents, and a peer is one such agent considered in relation to the others. When an earlier agent records a piece of judgment it learned, a later peer can pick that lesson up and use it. The transfer is agent to agent: it carries practical know-how between siblings of comparable capability, and it sits below the human operator's own words and below the system's settled doctrine until it has been reviewed and adopted.
peer.rule: When something is marked as coming from a peer, treat it as one capable agent's preserved judgment offered to another, not as the operator's instruction or as confirmed doctrine.
peer.deep: A peer is an authority boundary as much as a kind of actor: it marks the level at which one agent may help a future agent by passing on judgment, a level that remains beneath the human voice and beneath active doctrine until that material is curated and promoted.

peer_review.label: peer review
peer_review.preview: Peer review is evaluation of scholarly work by other qualified researchers before or after publication.
peer_review.card: Peer review can identify errors, unclear arguments, and unsupported claims, but it is not a guarantee of correctness. The papers on this site state separately whether they have been peer-reviewed.
peer_review.rule: Treat peer-review status as one quality signal and inspect the underlying proof and evidence independently.
peer_review.deep: Different venues use different review processes, levels of anonymity, and standards, so the label should name the relevant publication context when it matters.

peer_propagate.label: peer-propagate
peer_propagate.preview: A peer-propagate is a source-linked, reusable lesson in operating judgment that one capable agent records for future peer agents to inherit.
peer_propagate.card: When an agent working in this system learns something genuinely useful but not yet settled enough to become a formal rule, it writes that lesson down as a peer-propagate record so a later agent can find and apply it. Each record cites where the lesson came from, where it applies, where it does not, and how confident it is. It is held as candidate knowledge passed between agents, kept distinct from the operator's own words, from private memory, and from the system's active rules.
peer_propagate.rule: Treat a peer-propagate record as one agent's tested advice to the next, not as a settled rule: check what it says it applies to and where it says it does not before leaning on it.
peer_propagate.deep: It sits deliberately below the formal lanes, a skill, standard, paper module, or established principle, and stays marked as a candidate so that useful working knowledge survives between agents without being mistaken for the operator's voice or for confirmed doctrine.

perfect_set.label: perfect set
perfect_set.preview: A set is perfect when it is closed and has no isolated points, so every point in it is approached arbitrarily closely by other points of the set.
perfect_set.card: Perfectness rules out the picture in which the set is a scatter of separate points. It is one of the exact structural facts established about the achievement sets in Erdős #257, alongside their coding, topology, and measure.
perfect_set.rule: Perfect is a topological property of the set. It does not tell you which numbers belong to it.
perfect_set.deep: The restricted achievement sets for Erdős #257 receive exact coding, topology, perfectness, and measure statements, each with its finite or infinite hypothesis attached. The hypotheses matter: results proved for finite support do not carry to infinite support.

periodic.label: periodic
periodic.preview: A sequence is periodic when a fixed block repeats forever, and eventually periodic when such repetition begins after a finite initial segment.
periodic.card: The period is the smallest positive shift that preserves the repeating tail. Positional digit expansions of rational numbers are eventually periodic, which makes forbidden repetition a route to proving irrationality.
periodic.rule: Check whether periodicity begins immediately or only eventually and whether the claimed period is minimal.
periodic.deep: Finite data can be consistent with a long period or a repetition beginning beyond the observed range, so no finite prefix alone rules out eventual periodicity.

phase.label: phase
phase.preview: A phase is a scoped work packet inside a family of related work: a bounded unit of execution that holds one objective, the active wave of work, the references it draws on, and the state needed to pause and resume it later.
phase.card: A phase is how the system breaks a broad area of work into a single resumable unit. Each phase narrows a wide family objective into a concrete sequence of waves, revisions, ledgers, and a closeout record, and it preserves the current objective, the execution mode, the active wave, and the legal next steps so the work can be picked up exactly where it was left.
phase.rule: When you meet a phase, read it as the live container for one stretch of work: it tells you what is currently being done, how far it has got, and what may happen next, rather than describing the system as a whole.
phase.deep: A phase is temporary by design. It exists to carry a piece of work from its starting objective through its waves and revisions to a recorded closeout, after which it can be archived.

pip.label: pip
pip.preview: pip is Python's package installer, the command that fetches a project's dependencies and puts them where Python can find them.
pip.card: Square brackets after a package name select an optional group of extra dependencies, so pip install with a test extra pulls in the packages the test suite needs and a plain install does not.
pip.rule: An optional extra is not installed by default, so a lane that needs one will silently have nothing to run without it.
pip.deep: The quickstart route no longer asks for an install on first contact. The August 2026 rerun receipt is dated for that reason: two of its four commands needed an install the repository no longer requires.

planted_error.label: planted error
planted_error.preview: A planted error is a fault introduced on purpose to check that a detector notices it.
planted_error.card: A check that has never caught anything has not been shown to work. Planting an error and confirming it is rejected is the difference between a gate that runs and a gate that discriminates. This site records one such case: a deliberately false claim was introduced after a real failure had been repaired, and the repaired gate refused it.
planted_error.rule: Ask what a detector has actually caught. An untested detector is an assumption.
planted_error.deep: The honest version of this reports both halves: the real failure that got through first, and the planted case that the repair then caught. Reporting only the second would make a repair look like foresight.

planted_forgery.label: planted forgery
planted_forgery.preview: A planted forgery is a deliberately false claim placed in a test input so that a check can be observed refusing it.
planted_forgery.card: Watching a check pass on correct input shows only that it does not object. Watching it reject a known-false input by name shows it can tell the difference, which is the harder half.
planted_forgery.rule: A run that plants a forgery and does not report a refusal has failed, even when it reports a pass.
planted_forgery.deep: The completion-faithfulness audit runs against notes carrying three planted forgeries: a fake commit claim, a fake test claim, and a fake work-record claim. The external verification job uses the same idea, running a second fixture with one statement altered and counting as passed only when the checker rejects it by name.

policy.label: policy
policy.preview: A policy is a stated rule for choosing, permitting, restricting, or handling actions and information in recurring situations.
policy.card: Policies guide decisions where raw facts alone do not determine what should happen. Enforceable policies name their scope, authority, conditions, and consequences.
policy.rule: Separate the policy choice from the evidence used to evaluate its conditions.
policy.deep: A policy can be expressed in prose, structured data, or executable checks, but those projections should remain synchronized with one governing source.

positive_integer.label: positive integer
positive_integer.preview: A positive integer is an integer greater than zero.
positive_integer.card: The positive integers are 1, 2, 3, and so on, excluding zero and all negative integers. Formal statements often use positivity to permit division, ordering, or finite counting arguments.
positive_integer.rule: Check whether the domain is positive integers, nonnegative integers, or all integers.
positive_integer.deep: A positivity hypothesis can be essential even when it looks routine, because removing it may introduce zero denominators or sign changes.

present.label: present
present.preview: Present describes something that exists or is available in the relevant place or time, or the act of displaying it to an audience.
present.card: The adjective is the opposite of missing within a search boundary; the verb concerns presentation. Context should identify whether presence in state or communication to a reader is meant.
present.rule: When presence matters, check where, when, and under which observation method the item was found.
present.deep: Presence establishes existence within the observed boundary but not correctness, relevance, or freshness.

preserve.label: preserve
preserve.preview: To preserve something is to keep its relevant content, meaning, condition, identity, or availability through change or over time.
preserve.card: Preservation requires naming which properties must remain and which transformations are allowed. A format conversion may preserve meaning while changing bytes, layout, or metadata.
preserve.rule: When a process claims preservation, identify the invariant and the comparison that verifies it before and after the change.
preserve.deep: Preserving one property can sacrifice another, so content, structure, provenance, and presentation should not be silently conflated.

prime.label: prime
prime.preview: A prime is a whole number greater than one divisible only by itself and one.
prime.card: Primes appear in several of these problems as the rule generating the terms of a series, either directly or through the gaps between consecutive primes. That makes the series inherit every difficulty of the primes themselves, which is a large part of why the questions are hard.
prime.rule: A series built from primes is at least as hard as what is known about primes.
prime.deep: Results about such series are often conditional on facts about prime distribution that are themselves deep, which is why several claims here rest on stated analytic hypotheses rather than standing alone.

prime_gap.label: prime gap
prime_gap.preview: A prime gap is the difference between two consecutive prime numbers.
prime_gap.card: Prime gaps vary irregularly: most are small compared with the primes themselves, but arbitrarily large gaps occur. A series built from them inherits hard questions about how primes are distributed.
prime_gap.rule: Check whether a statement concerns every gap, average behaviour, infinitely many gaps, or a bounded finite range.
prime_gap.deep: Writing consecutive primes as a starting prime plus accumulated gaps can transform a prime-generated series into an equivalent gap-generated series with different proof handles.

principle.label: principle
principle.preview: A principle is a durable operating law that constrains how agents and the system behave, stored as a numbered rule with a written rationale.
principle.card: A principle states a rule that holds across many cases rather than a fix for one situation, such as "status fails closed" or "derive before you assert". Each principle carries not just the rule but the design instinct behind it: the underlying tradeoff and the reasoning a later decision should reuse when a new case differs from the one that first prompted it. Principles are more stable than a single observation and more general than a mechanism, and each is grounded in recorded evidence and a curation history.
principle.rule: Read a principle as a standing commitment the system holds itself to, and look at the rule it states and the reason given for it, not just its label.
principle.deep: A principle is one layer in a doctrine hierarchy: above a local note or a one-off observation, below nothing it cannot still be traced back to, and always anchored to the evidence and curation that promoted it.

prior.label: prior
prior.preview: Prior describes something that existed, occurred, or was believed before the current item or update.
prior.card: A prior can be earlier work, an earlier state, or an initial belief used in reasoning. The relevant ordering may be temporal, logical, or procedural.
prior.rule: When prior is used, identify what it precedes and whether the comparison is about time, dependency, or belief.
prior.deep: Earlier material can inform current work without remaining current or authoritative after later corrections. Chronology and authority remain separate: later evidence may supersede an earlier claim while preserving its provenance.

prior_art.label: prior art
prior_art.preview: Prior art is earlier published work that already contains what is being claimed.
prior_art.card: Finding it retires a priority claim without saying anything against the work. The result stands; it is simply not first, and saying so is the honest move rather than a concession.
prior_art.rule: Failing to find prior art is not evidence that none exists. Novelty needs a positive clearance, not an absent search result.
prior_art.deep: Two cases are recorded here. Steve Fan published the two-prime reduction for Erdős #269 first, on 26 June 2026, so no priority is claimed for it. Two implications in the Erdős #243 work coincide with prior lemmas of Koizumi in canonical coordinates, and no priority is claimed over them.

private.label: private
private.preview: Private means intentionally unavailable to the general public and accessible only under stated permissions or within a restricted environment.
private.card: Private describes an access boundary, not secrecy, wrongdoing, or superior authority. Public projections may summarize allowed facts without exposing the private source material behind them.
private.rule: Do not infer the contents of private material from the existence of a public projection.
private.deep: A private boundary can protect personal data, unfinished work, credentials, operational state, or simply material outside the release scope, and those reasons carry different handling rules.

probe.label: probe
probe.preview: A probe is a small check that establishes one narrow fact about an environment, run before the work that depends on it rather than after something has already failed.
probe.card: A probe is not a test of the system; it is a question about the ground the system is standing on. Is this a fresh clone, are the declared dependencies actually present, does this command exist. Probes are cheap and specific on purpose, so a failure names one missing precondition instead of producing a long trace nobody can localise.
probe.rule: Read what single fact a probe establishes. It is not a statement about whether the system works.
probe.deep: The value is in the ordering. A precondition checked first fails with a usable message; the same precondition discovered halfway through a run fails with a symptom.

problem.label: problem
problem.preview: A problem is a precisely stated question or task whose answer, construction, or proof is not supplied by the statement itself.
problem.card: In mathematics, a problem specifies the objects, assumptions, and conclusion to be established or refuted. “Open” means no accepted solution is currently known, not that the statement is vague or that no partial results exist.
problem.rule: Read the exact statement, hypotheses, and requested conclusion before judging whether a result solves the problem.
problem.deep: A problem can accumulate equivalent formulations, partial theorems, computational evidence, and failed approaches while remaining open until the full requested claim is settled.

problem_note.label: problem note
problem_note.preview: A problem note is a short standalone paper on a single open mathematical problem, stating what has been formally proved, what remains open, and where the boundary between them lies.
problem_note.card: The notes exist because a formal proof and a readable account of it are different artefacts, and the gap between them is where overstatement lives. Each note is written for a mathematician reading cold, records the exact range proved rather than the impression it creates, and names the adjacent stronger statement that is still open.
problem_note.rule: Read a problem note for the boundary, not the headline. The interesting content is what it declines to claim.
problem_note.deep: Keeping the note honest is itself checked: the relationship between a note's public wording and the formal statement behind it is registered, so a later edit that erases a distinction fails rather than passing quietly.

process.label: process
process.preview: A process is an ordered set of activities or a running program that changes inputs or state over time toward an outcome.
process.card: In workflow prose, a process means the sequence of steps; in operating-system prose, it means one executing program instance. The surrounding context should distinguish them.
process.rule: Identify the process kind, start conditions, state, and completion rule.
process.deep: Processes can be deterministic or interactive, local or networked, and short-lived or persistent, which changes how their results can be reproduced and monitored.

product.label: product
product.preview: In Plectis, product usually means a user-facing software offering or capability; in mathematical passages, a product is the result of multiplication.
product.card: The site actively uses both senses. Product performance, product quality, and product authority concern a software offering and what may be claimed about it. Prime products, running-LCM products, and product formulae concern factors multiplied together. One sense supplies no evidence about the other.
product.rule: Read the surrounding noun: performance, launch, quality, or authority indicates the software sense; factors, primes, LCM, or a formula indicates multiplication.
product.deep: This is a real vocabulary collision in Plectis, not a local redefinition of either ordinary meaning. The popup therefore keeps both senses visible so mathematical language cannot silently overwrite product-governance prose.

profile_gap.label: profile gap
profile_gap.preview: A profile gap is a recorded admission that an artifact kind exists but lacks the supported summary and card rows needed for honest row-by-row browsing, so navigation shows the gap instead of pretending the option surface is complete.
profile_gap.card: The system arranges its artifacts into kinds and lets each kind be enumerated as stable rows that can be selected and drilled into. A profile gap marks a kind that has a registry, source files, or generated index entries but no fully supported rows yet, so it is visible at the top level without being claimed as fully navigable. It is a deliberate marker of navigation debt: a way of saying the support is incomplete rather than papering over the difference between data that exists and a surface that can honestly list it.
profile_gap.rule: Treat a profile gap as an honest "not yet browsable here" sign, not a defect: the kind is real and visible, but its row-level listing has not been finished, so do not expect to enumerate or open every member of it.
profile_gap.deep: It exists to stop a kind's mere presence (a registry entry, a legacy command, a generated index, or raw data bands) from being mistaken for full navigability until the navigation layer can actually enumerate and open its members by stable identifier.

program.label: program
program.preview: Program can mean executable computer instructions or an organized initiative such as a bug-bounty program; Plectis uses both senses.
program.card: Most component pages use program for code that a machine runs. Policy and disclosure pages can instead use program for an organized activity with participants, rules, and a purpose. The initiative does not execute merely because it shares the word.
program.rule: Commands, inputs, source code, and runtime indicate the executable sense; participation, eligibility, disclosure, or administration indicate the initiative sense.
program.deep: Plectis needs the distinction because a component may be a computer program while the vulnerability-disclosure page explicitly says the project is not a bug-bounty program. Conflating them turns a scope disclaimer into a claim about executable software.

projection.label: projection
projection.preview: A projection is a derived view generated from one or more source artifacts to make selected facts easier to read, query, or navigate without becoming their authority.
projection.card: A projection selects, reorganizes, or compresses source material into a useful surface such as a page, index, card, or report. Because it can become stale, a trustworthy projection records its inputs, builder, source fingerprint, and refresh path.
projection.rule: Use a projection for access and orientation, then follow its source pointer when the underlying fact or authority matters.
projection.deep: Projection quality has two independent dimensions: fidelity to the source and usefulness to the reader; a perfectly accurate dump may be unusable, while a beautiful summary may be dangerously incomplete.

projection_drift.label: projection drift
projection_drift.preview: Projection drift is what happens when a copy stops matching the source it was made from.
projection_drift.card: Every page on this site is generated from the repositories behind it, so a stale copy would say something the source no longer supports without anything visibly breaking. Drift is dangerous precisely because it is quiet.
projection_drift.rule: When a copy and its source disagree, the source is the authority. A copy that agrees with its source proves nothing about whether the source is right.
projection_drift.deep: One group of components exists to recompute a copied projection against its source and fail when the two differ, which is also the rule the videos state: if the map and the source disagree, the source wins.

proof.label: proof
proof.preview: A proof is a logically valid argument showing that a mathematical statement follows from stated definitions, assumptions, and previously established results.
proof.card: A human proof communicates the reasoning to qualified readers; a formal proof encodes enough detail for a proof checker. Both establish only their exact conclusion under their exact assumptions.
proof.rule: Read the theorem statement and dependencies before treating a proof as settling a broader claim.
proof.deep: Proof validity is different from exposition quality, novelty, significance, or whether the theorem solves the motivating open problem.

proof_assistant.label: proof assistant
proof_assistant.preview: A proof assistant is a program that verifies mathematical proofs mechanically, requiring every step to be justified in a form it can check.
proof_assistant.card: Writing mathematics for a proof assistant is slower than writing it for a reader, because nothing can be left to the reader. That cost buys a specific guarantee: if it compiles, the argument holds. The tool is honest about scope in a way prose rarely is, since a proof that only covers a finite range simply will not check for the general one.
proof_assistant.rule: Treat a machine-checked result as settled for what it states, and no further.
proof_assistant.deep: Proof assistants make gaps visible rather than making authors careful. An argument with a hole does not compile, so the hole is found at writing time instead of at review time.

proof_boundary.label: proof boundary
proof_boundary.preview: A proof boundary is the line between what a formal proof establishes and what the prose around it claims: the point where machine-checked certainty stops and ordinary description begins.
proof_boundary.card: A proof assistant checks that a proof establishes the formal statement written in the source. It does not check that a README or a paper describes that statement faithfully. The proof boundary is where those two diverge, and it is the gap where a correct proof can sit underneath an overstated summary without anything failing.
proof_boundary.rule: For any formal result, find the formal statement and read it. The prose is a description of the proof, not part of it.
proof_boundary.deep: This site records one real instance: an edit that erased a finite-versus-open distinction passed, because the relationship between wording and formal statement had not been registered. Registering it made a later deliberately false version fail. That is one failure and one repair, not complete claim discovery.

proof_checker.label: proof checker
proof_checker.preview: A proof checker is the small trusted program that accepts a formal proof only when every encoded inference follows from the system's rules and stated assumptions.
proof_checker.card: The checker does not invent the proof or judge whether the formal statement captures the intended mathematics; it verifies the derivation it receives. Keeping this trusted core small makes the result less dependent on large generators, tactics, or user interfaces.
proof_checker.rule: Separate what the checker verified from what translators, generators, and theorem authors supplied to it.
proof_checker.deep: In Lean, elaboration and automation may be complex, but accepted declarations are replayed through a compact kernel whose rules define the final formal trust boundary.

proposition.label: proposition
proposition.preview: A proposition is a declarative mathematical statement that has a definite truth value once its terms and assumptions are fixed.
proposition.card: A proposition can be a theorem, lemma, conjecture, or intermediate claim depending on whether and how it has been proved. Its wording, not its label, determines what must be established.
proposition.rule: Separate the proposition's exact statement from its proof status.
proposition.deep: Formal systems represent propositions as types whose inhabitants are proofs, making hypotheses and logical structure explicit.

prove.label: prove
prove.preview: To prove a claim is to establish it from accepted premises by an argument that satisfies the relevant standard of proof.
prove.card: In mathematics, a proof connects premises to a conclusion through valid reasoning; in software documentation, a check may prove only a narrower operational fact. The governing standard determines what counts.
prove.rule: Ask what premises, method, and proof boundary support any statement that something was proved.
prove.deep: Proof is stronger than evidence that merely raises confidence, but it remains conditional on the formalization, premises, and checker used.

provenance.label: provenance
provenance.preview: Provenance is the record of where something came from: which source a copied file was taken from, and whether it still matches.
provenance.card: Copies drift from their sources silently. Provenance is what makes that detectable rather than discovered later, by recording the origin alongside the copy and checking the two still agree. It is the reason a published body can be trusted to be the real implementation rather than an old snapshot of it.
provenance.rule: For any copied artefact, ask where it came from and whether that link is still checked.
provenance.deep: Provenance is more durable than correctness. A wrong thing with recorded provenance can be traced and repaired; a right thing without it cannot be maintained.

public.label: public
public.preview: Public means intentionally available for anyone to inspect without private repository, account, or operator access.
public.card: Public describes access, not endorsement, completeness, peer review, or permission to infer private material. The public site and repositories expose a deliberately bounded source slice whose omissions and claim limits remain part of what is being published.
public.rule: Read public as an access classification and check separate fields for review status, evidence strength, license, and completeness.
public.deep: A public projection may be generated from private work only when its exported content passes the public boundary; the existence of a public artifact never implies that the private whole is equivalent or available.

published.label: published
published.preview: Published here means released openly to a public code repository, not accepted by a journal or peer-reviewed.
published.card: The distinction is easy to lose and worth keeping. Everything here is public in the sense that anyone can read, download and run it, and none of it has been through peer review. Those are different kinds of standing: the first is about access, the second is about scrutiny, and only the first has happened.
published.rule: Published means available. It does not mean reviewed, accepted, or endorsed by anyone.
published.deep: The gap is why the claim registry records what is proved separately from what is asserted. Open publication removes the gatekeeper and with it the external check, so the burden of stating limits accurately moves onto the author.

pull_request.label: pull request
pull_request.preview: A pull request is a proposed change to a repository, submitted so the maintainer can review it and merge it.
pull_request.card: Contributions to the Lean repository arrive as pull requests or as issues. The contribution guide says what a return should contain and which local checks to run before opening one.
pull_request.rule: Open a pull request when you have a concrete change; open an issue when you have a report or a question.
pull_request.deep: A merged pull request becomes part of the versioned record, so its author is visible in the history as well as in the credit record.

purpose.label: purpose
purpose.preview: Purpose is the intended use, function, or reason for which something exists or an action is taken.
purpose.card: Purpose helps evaluate fit because the same artifact can be useful for one decision and misleading for another. Stated purpose does not guarantee actual performance.
purpose.rule: Read an artifact or action by comparing its declared purpose with its design, evidence, and observed effect.
purpose.deep: A clear purpose narrows evaluation criteria but does not excuse harms or failures outside the designer's attention when they remain foreseeable.

pytest.label: pytest
pytest.preview: pytest is the standard tool for running automated tests in Python projects.
pytest.card: It reports an exit status: zero when every test passed, non-zero otherwise. A check that runs pytest and then ignores that status has learned nothing, which is a failure mode this system explicitly looks for.
pytest.rule: Running a test suite is not the same as checking its result. Look for the exit status.
pytest.deep: The completion-faithfulness audit runs one real pytest process and checks its exit status explicitly. That lane needs the test extra installed; a plain install leaves it nothing to run.

question.label: question
question.preview: A question is a request for a particular piece of information, explanation, decision, construction, or proof.
question.card: A well-formed question makes the expected answer shape and relevant scope clear. The same topic can support several different questions with different evidence requirements.
question.rule: Identify exactly what is being asked before selecting sources or claiming an answer.
question.deep: Question routing matters because a source suitable for orientation may be insufficient for proof validity, current status, or operational permission.

quickstart.label: quickstart
quickstart.preview: The quickstart is the shortest path from nothing to a first result: clone, install, run one check, read the file it wrote.
quickstart.card: It exists so that the first thing a reader does is produce evidence rather than read more prose. Everything else on the site is easier to evaluate once you have run something and seen what it writes.
quickstart.rule: Run the quickstart before evaluating any claim here. It takes minutes and changes what you are able to check.
quickstart.deep: The shape is deliberate: the reader ends holding a file they produced, which is a different epistemic position from having read a description of one.

radix.label: radix
radix.preview: A radix is the base of a positional numeral system, so a radix-two expansion is binary and a radix-ten expansion is ordinary decimal.
radix.card: Choosing a radix fixes which digits are available and therefore what carrying looks like. Several arguments in this corpus turn on exactly which digit values can occur.
radix.rule: A digit-level result is stated relative to one radix and does not transfer to another without proof.
radix.deep: The Erdős #269 work gives an exact running-lcm product, logarithmic cells, shell bounds, and a four-value radix at the primes 2, 3 and 5, together with a rank-two nonseparability witness. The remaining criterion is conditional and the problem stays open from three primes onward.

rational.label: rational
rational.preview: A number is rational when it can be written as one whole number divided by another.
rational.card: Rationality is the property most of these problems are trying to rule out. It is a strong constraint: if an infinite sum is rational, its value has an exact denominator, and that denominator forces detectable structure. Much of the formal work here consists of showing that the required structure cannot occur.
rational.rule: Assuming rationality and deriving a contradiction is the standard route to proving irrationality.
rational.deep: The reason rationality is attacked rather than irrationality proved directly is that rationality gives you something finite to work with, and irrationality gives you nothing to hold.

raw_seed.label: raw seed
raw_seed.preview: A raw seed is the append-only, unedited record of the operator's own words and thinking, serving as the source layer from which later summaries, doctrine, and routes are derived.
raw_seed.card: The raw seed holds the operator's voice in its first form: the intent, the recurring phrases, the changes of mind, and the provenance of an idea, written down before any tidying. Indexes, shards, principles, and paper modules elsewhere in the system are summaries drawn from it; the raw seed is the thing they summarise, and it is never overwritten or compressed away. When a higher layer needs to be checked against what was actually meant, the raw seed is the bottom authority it answers to.
raw_seed.rule: Treat the raw seed as the original wording and the summaries above it as maps of that wording. When the two seem to disagree, the raw seed is the record of what was actually meant.
raw_seed.deep: Because it is append-only, the raw seed preserves the full history of an idea, including reversals and recurring motifs, so a later summary can be traced back to the exact source it came from.

read.label: read
read.preview: To read is to interpret written, symbolic, or structured material in order to recover meaning or data from it.
read.card: People read prose and interfaces, while programs read files and data structures according to parsing rules. In both cases, successful access does not guarantee correct interpretation.
read.rule: When the site says something reads a source, distinguish byte access, parsing, and semantic understanding.
read.deep: Reading is observational unless the reader also performs a separate action that changes the material or records state.

reader.label: reader
reader.preview: A reader is the person or software consumer trying to understand, navigate, or use a published artifact.
reader.card: Reader needs depend on prior context: a cold reader starts without the repository's house vocabulary, while an expert may need exact source and proof routes. Public pages try to serve both through layered definitions and drilldowns.
reader.rule: Choose the shallowest explanation that makes the next step clear, while preserving a route to deeper evidence.
reader.deep: A software reader can consume structured packets and pointers that would be awkward for a person, but it still needs definitions, authority boundaries, and unambiguous identifiers.

reader_packet.label: reader packet
reader_packet.preview: A reader packet is a generated, portable guide that gathers routes, short summaries, source references, and scope limits so a person or AI assistant can inspect a public source slice without mistaking the guide for that source.
reader_packet.card: A reader packet is the compact starting document handed to someone, or to an automated assistant, who is opening the public slice for the first time. It carries the routes worth following, brief descriptions of components and glossary rows, links back to the underlying source files, and an explicit note of what it does and does not cover. It is reproducible and built from the source, so its job is to point at where to inspect rather than to stand in for the records it summarises.
reader_packet.rule: Follow a reader packet through to the source records it links rather than treating its summaries as the final word. It tells you where to look and where its own boundaries are.
reader_packet.deep: A reader packet is built to cut cold-start confusion without turning its own summary text into authority: it is compact and source-linked precisely so that its claims can be checked against the records it routes to.

real.label: real
real.preview: Real describes something that exists or occurs in the referenced world or system rather than being merely hypothetical, simulated, or fabricated.
real.card: The word is contrastive and therefore needs a comparison: real data versus synthetic data, live effects versus rehearsal, or an actual source versus an invented example. In mathematics, real number is a separate defined term.
real.rule: Read real by identifying what alternative is being ruled out in that sentence.
real.deep: Reality is not the same as correctness; real observations and production data can still be noisy, misleading, or incorrectly interpreted.

real_number.label: real number
real_number.preview: A real number is a point on the continuous number line, including every rational and irrational number.
real_number.card: Plectis first treats the value of a convergent series as a real number and then asks the narrower arithmetic question: is that real value rational or irrational? A decimal approximation locates the value but does not settle that exact classification.
real_number.rule: Separate existence as a real limit from the stronger claim that the limit is rational, irrational, algebraic, or transcendental.
real_number.deep: Finite certificate computations may live in exact rational arithmetic while the completed infinite series lives in the reals. Moving between those levels requires an explicit limit argument and, in formal work, explicit type coercions; a rational partial sum does not make the real limit rational.

reason.label: reason
reason.preview: A reason is a fact, consideration, rule, or inference offered to explain or justify a belief, decision, event, or action.
reason.card: Reasons can be causal, evidential, logical, or practical. A useful record distinguishes what caused an outcome from what justifies believing or choosing it.
reason.rule: Evaluate a reason by its relevance, truth, connection to the conclusion, and consistency with governing constraints.
reason.deep: Having a reason does not make it sufficient; competing reasons, missing evidence, or a broken inference can still defeat the conclusion.

receipt.label: receipt
receipt.preview: A receipt is the durable output that proves an action happened: the file or record a step writes, kept so the claim can be checked later rather than taken on trust.
receipt.card: Actions here are expected to leave something behind. A commit reports a hash, a deploy reports the bytes it verified live, a check writes its result record. The pattern is deliberate, because the failure it guards against is the confident report of work that did not occur. A receipt turns that from a matter of trust into something you can look up.
receipt.rule: When a step is reported as done, ask what it wrote. No receipt, no completion.
receipt.deep: The discipline extends to failure. A refused action produces a receipt too, naming what stopped it, which is what stops a blocked step from being quietly reported as finished.

reciprocal.label: reciprocal
reciprocal.preview: The reciprocal of a number is one divided by it.
reciprocal.card: Most of the series here are sums of reciprocals, which is why the terms shrink and the sums settle on a value at all. Taking reciprocals also inverts the difficulty: a fast-growing sequence gives a fast-shrinking sum, and the arithmetic of the sum depends delicately on how the original sequence grew.
reciprocal.rule: In a reciprocal sum, how fast the underlying sequence grows controls almost everything.
reciprocal.deep: The delicacy is the point: sequences that grow at similar rates can give sums of entirely different character, so growth conditions have to be stated exactly.

recompute.label: recompute
recompute.preview: To recompute something is to calculate or derive it again from its inputs rather than reuse a previous result.
recompute.card: Recomputation can verify reproducibility, refresh a stale projection, or incorporate changed inputs. It should use a defined procedure so differences can be attributed to inputs, environment, or implementation.
recompute.rule: When a result is recomputed, compare the inputs, method, environment, and output with the earlier run.
recompute.deep: Recomputation is not automatically independent evidence when it uses the same sources and potentially the same defect.

recurrence.label: recurrence
recurrence.preview: A recurrence is a rule defining each term of a sequence from the ones before it, rather than by a direct formula.
recurrence.card: Recurrences appear here on both sides of the work. Some problems ask whether a sequence must eventually satisfy a particular recurrence; elsewhere, assuming a sum is rational forces a recurrence in its long division, which then gives something concrete to contradict.
recurrence.rule: A forced recurrence is usually a proof strategy rather than a result: it is the structure the contradiction will come from.
recurrence.deep: The reason recurrences are useful in irrationality arguments is that they propagate: establish one at a single index and it constrains every later one.

reduction.label: reduction
reduction.preview: A reduction turns one problem into another, so that solving the second would solve the first.
reduction.card: A reduction is not progress on its own. If the new statement is no easier than the original, the problem has been restated rather than advanced. Several results in this corpus are exact reformulations and are labelled as such rather than presented as progress.
reduction.rule: Count results, not restatements. Statements each proved equivalent to a problem are one result about that problem, not many.
reduction.deep: The claim registry records 39 of its 103 claims as conditional reductions, and separately records that neither Erdős #249 nor Erdős #257 is settled. The Lean repository also lifts the hypotheses of its conditional theorems into standalone propositions and proves 17 of the 23 substantial ones equal in strength to the open problem they were meant to approach.

referee.label: referee
referee.preview: A referee is the expert a journal asks to assess a submitted paper, usually anonymously, before deciding whether to publish it.
referee.card: Refereeing is what gives a published mathematical result its standing. A correct proof and a refereed proof are different states: the second has had someone independent try to break it.
referee.rule: Machine checking and refereeing answer different questions. A proof assistant checks the formal statement; a referee judges whether the paper says something true, correctly attributed, and worth publishing.
referee.deep: No referee, editor, or venue has assessed any of the papers on this site. Every one is author-released, so no result in them carries the standing such an assessment would confer.

reference.label: reference
reference.preview: A reference is a pointer that identifies another source, record, definition, or location relevant to the current statement.
reference.card: References make claims traceable by naming where supporting or explanatory material can be found. A reference may provide context without itself being evidence for the claim.
reference.rule: Follow the reference and inspect the role assigned to its destination.
reference.deep: Exact references include stable identifiers, paths, anchors, versions, or citations so later readers can resolve the same object rather than a nearby substitute.

reformulation.label: reformulation
reformulation.preview: A reformulation restates a problem or theorem in a different representation while preserving a proved relationship to the original statement.
reformulation.card: A reformulation can expose new structure—digits instead of sums, recurrences instead of rationality, or gaps instead of primes—without solving anything by itself. Its value depends on whether the new form is equivalent, merely implied, or only heuristically related.
reformulation.rule: Check the exact relation between the original and reformulated statements before treating them as interchangeable.
reformulation.deep: Productive reformulations preserve the target while moving the difficulty into objects with stronger tools, clearer barriers, or finite certificates.

refuse.label: refuse
refuse.preview: To refuse is to deliberately decline an action, request, input, or inference because permission or required conditions are absent.
refuse.card: Refusal is a controlled outcome, not simply a crash or omission. A useful refusal states the boundary it protects and, when safe, the condition or route that could allow progress.
refuse.rule: Read a refusal by identifying who or what declined, which rule applied, and whether the refusal changed any state.
refuse.deep: Refusal can be evidence that a safety or authority boundary worked as designed.

registry.label: registry
registry.preview: A registry is a governed collection of uniquely identified records for one kind of object.
registry.card: A registry defines membership, identifiers, and required fields for a class of artifacts. Generated indexes and pages should project from it rather than maintain competing lists.
registry.rule: Use the registry to answer which records exist and which identifier names each one.
registry.deep: Registries make additions, removals, and duplicates mechanically visible, but the truth of each record's substantive claims still depends on its own evidence.

regression.label: regression
regression.preview: A regression is the return of a previously fixed failure or the loss of behaviour that an earlier version demonstrably supported.
regression.card: A regression test preserves a concrete past expectation so later changes fail visibly if they break it again. The baseline must be real and dated; calling any new failure a regression is inaccurate when the earlier behaviour was never established.
regression.rule: To call something a regression, identify the prior passing evidence and the change after which it failed.
regression.deep: Regression protection turns a bug fix into durable system memory by keeping the smallest reproducing case and its expected outcome in the validation path.

reject.label: reject
reject.preview: To reject something is to refuse its acceptance, admission, use, or continuation because stated conditions are not satisfied.
reject.card: Rejection should name the gate and the reason an input or claim failed it. A deterministic rejection is useful evidence when the same conditions reliably produce the same outcome.
reject.rule: When an item is rejected, inspect the rule, failing condition, and whether correction or appeal is possible.
reject.deep: Rejection establishes non-acceptance under one process, not that the item is worthless or false in every context.

release.label: release
release.preview: A release is an intentionally published, versioned set of artifacts made available to a defined audience.
release.card: A release turns working material into a distribution with stated contents, source revision, licenses, and claim boundaries. Publication does not imply production readiness or peer review.
release.rule: Read the release manifest and limits before treating the published set as complete.
release.deep: A release may include generated pages, source repositories, papers, checks, and compatibility routes that must agree on identity and version.

reliability.label: reliability
reliability.preview: Reliability is the degree to which something continues to perform its stated function under specified conditions.
reliability.card: A reliable process behaves consistently across repeated use, expected variation, and relevant failures. Reliability claims therefore need a function, environment, time span, and evidence base.
reliability.rule: Treat reliability as conditional and ask what workload, conditions, and failure rate were actually measured.
reliability.deep: Correctness concerns whether an outcome is right, while reliability concerns how dependably the process produces its intended outcome.

rename_migration_receipt.label: rename migration receipt
rename_migration_receipt.preview: A rename migration receipt is the durable proof that a storage-path rename passed its gate, recording the evidence, obligations, rollback plan, or—when blocked—the unmet precondition that prevented the change.
rename_migration_receipt.card: When a file or directory in the source is renamed, the receipt is the artifact that makes that rename auditable and reversible. It records the scope of the change, the evidence that the rename gate was satisfied, the post-rename tasks, and closure notes. Receipts move through fixed states, planned, blocked, in progress, completed, and reverted, so the history of a rename is legible from a single object rather than reconstructed from the file system. A completed receipt is evidence the migration happened safely; a blocked receipt is the honest record that it is not yet safe to proceed.
rename_migration_receipt.rule: Check a rename migration receipt's state and its named gate evidence before treating a rename as settled. A blocked receipt means the change was deliberately not made, and it names the precondition that is still missing.
rename_migration_receipt.deep: Each receipt forces the reference-impact map, stable-identifier plan, alias and redirect plan, projection-rebuild plan, verification plan, and rollback plan to be written down before the file system is touched, and the actual outcome to be recorded afterwards.

replay.label: replay
replay.preview: A replay is a check that re-runs a recorded scenario end to end and asserts the outcome, rather than testing a function in isolation.
replay.card: Unit-level checks tell you a part behaves; a replay tells you a situation resolves the way it is supposed to. The scenario is committed as fixtures, including the cases that must fail, so the whole path can be re-run by anyone and compared against a recorded expectation. It is the closest this repository gets to showing a behaviour rather than asserting one.
replay.rule: Read what scenario a replay covers. It establishes that recorded path, not the behaviour of the system around it.
replay.deep: Replays are where negative cases earn their place: a scenario that only ever replays its happy path proves very little, because a component that has stopped discriminating still completes it. The recorded refusals are what make the pass informative.

report.label: report
report.preview: A report is a written account of what happened, as distinct from the record the account was drawn from.
report.card: Reports are useful and are not evidence. The distinction runs through everything here: a component's summary is a report, its result record is not; an agent's account of a session is a report, its transcript is not. Keeping both means the account can be checked against the thing it describes instead of standing in for it.
report.rule: Treat a report as a claim about a record. Ask to see the record.
report.deep: Reports are rarely dishonest and reliably lossy, in a direction that flatters the reporter. That is enough to make the underlying record worth keeping even when nobody suspects anything.

repository.label: repository
repository.preview: A repository is a project's files together with their complete change history, hosted so anyone can copy the whole thing.
repository.card: Two repositories are published here: one holding the runnable components, one holding the formal mathematics. Everything claimed on this site should be traceable to a file in one of them. The history matters as much as the files, because it shows when something was written rather than only that it exists now.
repository.rule: If a claim cannot be traced to a repository file, treat it as description.
repository.deep: History is what makes a claim of priority checkable. A file can be written at any time; a commit is dated.

reproducible.label: reproducible
reproducible.preview: Reproducible means another reader can use the declared source, inputs, environment, and command to obtain the same materially relevant result.
reproducible.card: Reproducibility turns a reported outcome into something independently checkable. It requires enough information to rebuild or rerun the work, plus a criterion for what must match—exact bytes, the same verdict, or values within a stated tolerance.
reproducible.rule: A reproducibility claim should name the inputs, versions, command, expected output, and acceptable comparison rule.
reproducible.deep: Exact byte reproduction is stronger than semantic reproduction, but not every valid workflow can be byte-identical across platforms; the claim must state which level it promises.

require.label: require
require.preview: To require something is to make it a necessary condition for a stated action, result, rule, or dependency.
require.card: Requirements can be logical, technical, procedural, or user-imposed. The source of the requirement determines who can change it and what evidence shows it has been met.
require.rule: When one thing requires another, identify the dependency and the consequence of absence.
require.deep: A requirement expresses necessity within a scope, not preference or universal law. In a workflow, satisfying one requirement can unlock the next step without validating the final result.

required.label: required
required.preview: Required describes something that must be present, performed, or satisfied for a stated rule, goal, or process to hold.
required.card: Requirements can come from a specification, dependency, policy, safety boundary, or user request. They should be distinguishable from recommendations and optional enhancements.
required.rule: When something is required, locate the authority or dependency that makes it mandatory and the check that verifies satisfaction.
required.deep: A requirement is scoped: being mandatory for one release or proof does not make it universally mandatory.

research.label: research
research.preview: Research is a systematic attempt to answer a question or produce new understanding through evidence, reasoning, or experiment.
research.card: Research differs from casual lookup by having an explicit question, a method for gathering or testing information, and a record of what supports the result. Its conclusions may remain provisional.
research.rule: Read a research claim together with its question, method, sources, uncertainties, and reproducibility conditions.
research.deep: Research can narrow uncertainty without closing a question, and a negative result can still add knowledge by ruling out a route.

research_shift.label: research shift
research_shift.preview: A research shift is a bounded piece of work a person gives their coding agent: start from one exact public revision of the Lean repository, attempt a continuation on one problem, and return a checkable result.
research_shift.card: The Lean repository's frontier relay guide defines the shift: inspect the pinned revision, choose a frontier, work, and prepare a return the maintainer can check locally, with contributor credit attached. It needs no account and no access to the private system that produced the corpus.
research_shift.rule: Judge a shift by the checkable return it produces, not by how long the agent ran.
research_shift.deep: A return can be a theorem, a narrower reduction, a closed route, a source correction or a better next question; each is a contribution if it survives review.

result.label: result
result.preview: A result is the outcome produced by a proof, computation, test, experiment, or decision process.
result.card: A result says what happened or was established under particular inputs and conditions. Its significance depends on the producing method, evidence, and scope.
result.rule: Read the result together with how it was produced and what it is allowed to claim.
result.deep: The same underlying outcome may be summarized in prose and stored in a structured result record; the record carries the inspectable provenance while the summary aids reading.

result_record.label: result record
result_record.preview: A result record is the durable file a check writes with what it tested, what it found, and the boundary of that finding, as distinct from an ephemeral message shown while the run executes.
result_record.card: Running a component does not just print something and exit - it writes a result record you can open, keep, and compare against a later run. This is what makes a claim on this site checkable rather than quotable: the record is the evidence, and prose describing it is not. A result record carries its own scope limit, so it states the boundary of what it establishes instead of leaving that to the reader.
result_record.rule: Prefer the result record to any summary of it. If a claim has no record behind it, treat it as description, not evidence.
result_record.deep: Result records are metadata-only by design: they carry the shape and verdict of a run, not the private bodies it read. That is what lets a run over non-public inputs still produce a publishable artefact. It is also why a record can be honest about a failure - an exit-1 record is as publishable as a passing one, and the repository ships both.

return.label: return
return.preview: To return is to go back, hand control back, or produce a result to the caller or originating context.
return.card: In programming, a function returns a value or control; in workflows, work returns to an owner or earlier state. The word should identify both destination and carried result.
return.rule: When an operation returns something, check whether it returned data, status, control, or a durable artifact.
return.deep: A returned value records the operation's immediate output but may not capture side effects that occurred before control came back.

review.label: review
review.preview: A review is an examination of a result, proof, text or contribution by someone other than its author, ending in a recorded judgement.
review.card: Several kinds appear on this site and are kept apart: the author's own review of agent output before release; machine checks such as Lean and Comparator; Palomar's review of a prepared unit; and independent peer review, which has not yet taken place for this work.
review.rule: Ask who reviewed what, and what the review could see.
review.deep: A review can change where future effort goes without changing the truth status of any statement; the project records the two effects separately.

rigidity.label: rigidity
rigidity.preview: A rigidity result says that an object satisfying a few loose conditions is forced to be one specific thing.
rigidity.card: Rigidity is what makes a classification possible: instead of describing many candidates you show there was only ever one. The work is usually in ruling out the near-misses.
rigidity.rule: A rigidity theorem is only as strong as its hypotheses, so read which conditions are assumed before reading what is forced.
rigidity.deep: Erdős #243 is stated here as rigidity of a centred integer error orbit. Lean excludes eventually negative constant magnitude and positive-drift periodic magnitude, and proves that normalised vanishing plus an eventually bounded negative part forces the error to vanish. The negative-part bound remains the missing hypothesis.

root.label: root
root.preview: A root is the designated starting or topmost point of a hierarchy, tree, directory structure, or derivation.
root.card: In a filesystem, the root anchors relative paths; in a graph or explanation, it can be the node from which subordinate material is organized. A structure may have one logical root even when it has several entry routes.
root.rule: Interpret root through the hierarchy it anchors and do not assume it is the authority for every descendant.
root.deep: Roots support orientation and path resolution, while authority and ownership may remain distributed below them.

roster.label: roster
roster.preview: A roster is an organized list of the members, participants, or items recognized as belonging to a group.
roster.card: A roster records membership at a stated time and may attach roles, status, or identifiers. It supports enumeration but does not necessarily explain the relationships among its members.
roster.rule: Treat a roster as a membership snapshot and check its owner, inclusion rule, and freshness.
roster.deep: A roster can be complete for its governed group while excluding related people or artifacts outside that group's boundary.

routing.label: routing
routing.preview: Routing is the path-selection step that maps a query, task, file path, or state to the smallest useful answer surface or owning work lane before source is opened.
routing.card: The system holds far more surfaces, such as documents, components, paper modules, standards, and source records, than anyone can open directly. Routing turns a situation into a ranked, source-linked set of options, each with a reason and a cost, so the right starting point can be chosen first. It selects the path; it does not make the chosen summary authoritative, and the underlying source still has to be opened to confirm what it claims.
