routing.rule: When a page or tool routes you somewhere, treat that as a suggested starting point with its stated reason, not a final answer; the surface it points to is where the real content lives.
routing.deep: Routing emphasises selection, choosing which option surface to enter, whereas navigation emphasises traversing the surface once it has been selected.

row.label: row
row.preview: A row is one horizontally or logically grouped record in a table, list, ledger, or structured collection.
row.card: Rows let repeated objects share a schema while retaining separate identities and values. In JSON a row may be represented as an object even when no visual table is shown.
row.rule: Read a row through the schema that defines its fields and the collection that gives it meaning.
row.deep: A row is an organizational unit, not an authority level; its claims are only as strong as its source and validation.

row_job.label: row job
row_job.preview: A row job is one predeclared, bounded change against a named row, finding, or artifact slice, recording the target, operation, allowed scope, expected delta, required check, and final receipt before any worker runs it.
row_job.card: Rather than handing a broad instruction like "repair every finding" or "use the providers" straight to an automated worker, the system first breaks that pressure into row jobs. Each row job pins down exactly one target and one operation, states the authority ceiling it must stay within, the validation it has to satisfy, and the gate it must clear before its result is promoted. It is a description of one bounded task, settled in advance, not the act of running it.
row_job.rule: Read a row job as the full specification of one small, scoped change: what it touches, what it is permitted to do, and the check it must pass. It governs that one task and grants no wider authority over the system.
row_job.deep: Row jobs are what let the work scale safely across cheap automated workers and external providers: because each job already names its target, limits, and validation, a worker receives a bounded task instead of an open-ended question about the whole body of files.

rowability.label: rowability
rowability.preview: Rowability means an artifact kind can be browsed as stable, source-linked rows instead of found by guessed keywords.
rowability.card: Rowability is the test of whether a category of objects in the system, such as its components or its paper modules, is ready to be navigated as a list. A rowable kind has a place in the system's index of kinds, gives every item a stable id, exposes short summary and detail views without expensive work, marks each item's source and freshness, and states honestly anything it has left out, so the items can be reached by browsing and selecting rather than by guessing search terms. A registry or a source file simply existing is not enough: the kind becomes rowable only once it can be listed, selected, and traced back to source in this way.
rowability.rule: When a kind on this site is described as rowable, you can browse and select its rows directly rather than searching for them; follow any row back to its named source before treating the short summary as the full truth.
rowability.deep: Rowability separates the cheap, listable summary of an item from the source it stands for: a compressed row may omit detail, but it must say so and point back to authority, so a row is never mistaken for the complete object.

run.label: run
run.preview: A run is one execution of a program, command, test, experiment, or governed process.
run.card: Each run has inputs, an environment, a start, an outcome, and often recorded output. Repeated runs may differ when time, external state, randomness, or dependencies differ.
run.rule: Read a run result with its exact command or procedure, inputs, environment, and exit status.
run.deep: A result from one run is historical evidence; reproducibility determines whether the same conditions can produce an equivalent result again.

runnable.label: runnable
runnable.preview: Runnable means a component ships everything needed to execute it locally: the code, its inputs, and a command, so a reader can produce the result rather than read about it.
runnable.card: It is the difference between a repository you can inspect and one you can exercise. Runnable requires that the fixtures are committed, the dependencies are declared, and the command is written down, which is a stricter condition than the code being public. A cold clone is how the claim gets tested.
runnable.rule: Check whether something is runnable before treating its result as reproducible. Published is not the same as runnable.
runnable.deep: The constraint shapes what can be published at all: a component whose real inputs are private is only runnable against synthetic fixtures, and its scope limit has to say so rather than implying the wider case.

runtime.label: runtime
runtime.preview: A runtime is the code and execution context active while a program or workflow is actually running, as distinct from its source files and static descriptions.
runtime.card: Runtime behaviour includes the processes, state transitions, tool calls, permissions, and external interactions that occur during execution. A page or source inspection can describe that behaviour but cannot prove it happened without a run record.
runtime.rule: Treat runtime claims as claims about observed execution and look for a trace, result record, or live probe.
runtime.deep: The same source can exhibit different runtime behaviour under different inputs, environments, permissions, or concurrent activity, which is why runtime evidence is tied to one recorded execution.

safety.label: safety
safety.preview: Safety is the condition in which identified harms are prevented, limited, or kept within an accepted risk boundary.
safety.card: Safety is always relative to hazards, people, assets, and operating conditions. A system can be safe for one use and unsafe for another, so the word needs a stated threat or failure model.
safety.rule: When the site calls an action safe, look for the hazards considered and the conditions that keep risk bounded.
safety.deep: Safety is not the absence of all uncertainty; it is a justified relationship between known risks, controls, and permitted action.

sandbox.label: sandbox
sandbox.preview: A sandbox is an execution boundary that restricts which files, processes, networks, devices, or permissions a program can access while it runs.
sandbox.card: Sandboxing limits the damage a faulty or untrusted process can cause and makes tests more controlled. Its protection is only as strong as the boundary actually enforced, so a sandbox claim must state the resources and escape routes it covers.
sandbox.rule: Read sandboxed together with the allowed and denied capabilities, not as a blanket safety guarantee.
sandbox.deep: A sandbox can isolate filesystem paths, network access, system calls, credentials, or process lifetimes independently; leaving one axis unrestricted may be intentional or may defeat the threat model.

scan.label: scan
scan.preview: A scan is a systematic pass over a defined collection to detect, count, classify, or extract selected features.
scan.card: Scans can be exhaustive within their input boundary or sample only part of it. Their findings depend on the matching rules and on whether all relevant material was reachable.
scan.rule: Read a scan result with its target set, detector, exclusions, and completion status.
scan.deep: A clean scan means no detector match was found in the examined material, not that every possible defect is absent.

schema.label: schema
schema.preview: A schema is a machine-readable contract describing which fields a structured record may or must contain, their types, and the constraints between them.
schema.card: Schemas make malformed or incomplete data fail explicitly instead of being interpreted differently by each consumer. They validate shape, not meaning: a perfectly schema-valid claim can still be false or unsupported.
schema.rule: Use a schema to check record structure and a separate validator or evidence rule to check the record's content.
schema.deep: A schema can encode required fields, enumerated statuses, identifier formats, nested objects, and cross-field constraints, giving producers and consumers a shared contract that can evolve by version.

science.label: science
science.preview: Science is the systematic study of phenomena through observation, explanation, prediction, and tests that can challenge the explanation.
science.card: Scientific work makes methods and evidence inspectable so others can evaluate or repeat them. Different sciences use different instruments and standards, but claims remain answerable to evidence.
science.rule: Read a scientific claim with its method, measurement conditions, uncertainty, and possible falsifiers.
science.deep: Scientific confidence is calibrated rather than absolute and can change when stronger evidence or explanations appear.

scope.label: scope
scope.preview: Scope is the declared set of objects, cases, operations, time, and conditions to which a statement, check, permission, or piece of work applies.
scope.card: Scope says what is inside a result before its limit says where the result stops. A precise scope names the relevant inputs, source version, environment, operations, and exclusions so a local finding cannot be mistaken for a universal one.
scope.rule: Before using a result, compare its declared scope with the case you want to apply it to.
scope.deep: Scope is multidimensional: two results may mention the same component while differing in tested inputs, runtime, date, authority, or permitted action, and those differences decide whether the evidence transfers.

search.label: search
search.preview: Search is the process of finding relevant records or text by matching a query against an indexed or inspectable collection.
search.card: Search helps locate candidates; it does not decide which result is authoritative or sufficient. Index coverage and ranking determine what can be found first.
search.rule: Use search to discover likely destinations, then verify the selected record and source.
search.deep: A generated search index can include labels, aliases, definitions, and route metadata while deliberately excluding private or excessively large content.

secret.label: secret
secret.preview: A secret is information whose disclosure is restricted because possession could grant access, enable misuse, or violate privacy or policy.
secret.card: Secrets include credentials, private keys, tokens, and other sensitive values. They require controlled storage, minimal exposure, rotation after compromise, and exclusion from public artifacts and logs.
secret.rule: Treat a suspected secret as sensitive until its owner and handling policy establish otherwise.
secret.deep: Secrecy protects the value from unauthorized readers but does not prove that systems using it are otherwise secure.

section.label: section
section.preview: A section is a named or visually separated division of a larger document, page, process, or body of material.
section.card: Sections group content around one local concern and provide anchors for navigation. Their meaning depends on the larger object they divide and the heading or rule that identifies their scope.
section.rule: Use section boundaries for local reading and citation, while retaining the qualifications supplied by the containing document.
section.deep: A section can be complete for its local purpose without being a standalone account of the whole subject.

semantic_naming.label: semantic naming
semantic_naming.preview: Semantic naming makes an identifier reveal an artifact’s role, authority, lifecycle state, and route to detail.
semantic_naming.card: Under semantic naming, a name is a compact record rather than an arbitrary tag. From the name alone you can infer the artifact's kind, its job, the authority plane it acts on, and how far you can trust it, before opening the source. Each name compresses these facts in a fixed order, so the smallest reading gives the role and a longer reading gives the detail. A name has several layers, including a stable identifier, a storage path, a display label, and aliases, and these can change independently.
semantic_naming.rule: Read a name as a claim about what the artifact is and what it may do, and trust the stable identifier over the display label or alias when they differ.
semantic_naming.deep: Renaming the underlying storage path is treated as a governed migration because other artifacts point at it, whereas a display label or alias can be adjusted more freely; the layers are deliberately separate so a name can be corrected without breaking the things that reference it.

sequence.label: sequence
sequence.preview: A sequence is an ordered list of terms indexed by positions, usually the positive integers, so each position has a specified value.
sequence.card: Order is part of a sequence: the same values arranged differently form a different sequence. A sequence may be defined by a direct formula, a recurrence, a selection rule, or observed data.
sequence.rule: Identify the indexing set and rule that generates the terms before using a property of the sequence.
sequence.deep: Infinite sequences are known through finite definitions and proofs about all indices, not by listing every term, which is why recurrences and quantified bounds matter.

series.label: series
series.preview: In Plectis, series can mean an infinite mathematical sum or an ordered stream of data values; the two uses are distinct.
series.card: The Erdős papers use series for infinite sums defined through limits of partial sums. Software and forecasting components use series for ordered observations such as yields, prices, or losses. A data series need not be summed or convergent, and an infinite mathematical series is not merely a dataset.
series.rule: Terms, partial sums, convergence, or irrationality indicate the mathematical sense; timestamps, labels, deltas, forecasts, or observations indicate the data sense.
series.deep: For mathematical series, the central question is what limit the partial sums approach and what arithmetic type that limit has. For data series, the central questions are ordering, missing observations, alignment, and change across records. Plectis uses both, so context must select the definition before any inference follows.

set.label: set
set.preview: A set is a collection determined by which distinct elements belong to it, without treating order or repetition as part of its identity.
set.card: In Plectis mathematics, sets usually select indices, exponents, factors, or premises. This matters because several results quantify over every finite or infinite choice of support, not over one listed sequence. The verb “set,” meaning assign a value, is a separate ordinary use.
set.rule: For the mathematical noun, identify the membership condition and whether the set is finite or infinite; do not read the assignment verb as this glossary concept.
set.deep: Finite denominator certificates use a finite exponent set F so an exact rational sum can be computed and checked. The open support questions quantify over infinite sets, where proving one convenient choice says nothing about all choices. Order and duplicate entries remain irrelevant unless the source defines a sequence instead.

shape.label: shape
shape.preview: Shape is the recognizable form, arrangement, or structural pattern of something, abstracted from some of its detail.
shape.card: On this site, shape often describes the fields of a record, the structure of a proof goal, or the organization of a system. It helps route work by revealing which known pattern an object resembles.
shape.rule: When shape is used structurally, identify which features are retained and which details are intentionally ignored.
shape.deep: Matching shape can suggest a method or category but does not establish equality of content or behaviour.

share.label: share
share.preview: To share is to make material, access, responsibility, or information available to more than one person, system, or context.
share.card: Sharing can involve copying, granting access, publishing, or jointly using a resource. Each form has different effects on privacy, authority, versioning, and control.
share.rule: Before sharing, check the audience, permissions, sensitivity, license, and whether the recipient will receive a copy or live access.
share.deep: Shared availability does not erase ownership, confidentiality duties, or the source relationship of the material.

shared_path.label: shared path
shared_path.preview: The shared path is the sequence most components on this site follow: state a claim, run a check against fixtures, write a result record, and record the scope limit of what that establishes.
shared_path.card: Components differ in subject but not in shape. Knowing the shared path means a reader who has understood one component has largely understood how to read the next: find the claim, find the check, open the record, read the limit. The uniformity is the point, because it makes the parts comparable rather than each one a fresh puzzle.
shared_path.rule: Once you have followed the shared path through one component, use the same four steps on any other.
shared_path.deep: The shape is also what makes the components auditable in bulk. A component that departs from it is visible as a departure rather than as a variation in style.

show.label: show
show.preview: To show something is to make it visible, present evidence of it, or demonstrate that it is the case.
show.card: The verb ranges from interface display to logical demonstration. A page can show a number without proving it, while an argument can show a conclusion by establishing it.
show.rule: Determine whether show means display, example, evidence, or proof in the sentence at hand.
show.deep: Visibility establishes that information was presented, not that the information is complete, current, or correct.

site.label: site
site.preview: A site is a collection of related web pages and resources published under a shared identity and navigation structure.
site.card: A site includes more than its landing page: documents, assets, routes, metadata, and links collectively shape what readers can reach. Its public projection may represent only part of the underlying source system.
site.rule: When evaluating a site, distinguish its visible pages from the private or source material used to generate them.
site.deep: A site is a delivery surface, not automatically the authority for every claim it displays.

skill.label: skill
skill.preview: A skill is a discoverable, reusable procedure that packages its invocation triggers, execution steps, constraints, and metadata so an agent does not have to reconstruct the workflow each time.
skill.card: Where a component is a unit of running machinery, a skill is a unit of action: a written-down operating procedure that tells an agent which task shape it matches and the steps to follow. Each skill carries a trigger that says when it applies, an ordered workflow, the limits it must stay inside, and discovery metadata so it can be located in the system's registry. The registry entry routes an agent to the right skill; the skill file then carries the actual procedure, with links out to the standards and modules that grant it authority.
skill.rule: Treat a skill as a procedure with a stated scope: it applies to the task shape named in its trigger and runs within the constraints it declares, not as general permission to act.
skill.deep: A skill is progressive disclosure for action: a short registry row surfaces it during navigation, and the full procedure is opened only once an agent has matched the task to it, keeping the working step list out of the way until it is needed.

skip.label: skip
skip.preview: To skip something is to deliberately omit or pass over a step, item, or route.
skip.card: Skipping can be valid when a step is optional or already satisfied, but dangerous when the omitted step carries a required check or dependency. The reason should be explicit.
skip.rule: When a step is skipped, verify that the governing process permits the omission and records its consequence.
skip.deep: A skip changes the executed path, so downstream claims must not imply that the omitted work ran.

slice.label: slice
slice.preview: A slice is a bounded cut through a larger system: the specific files, paths, or records a piece of work covers, named so that what is inside and outside the cut is explicit.
slice.card: This system is published in slices rather than all at once. A slice names its own edges, which is what lets a component be genuinely runnable while the system it came from stays private. The word carries the same meaning in the working sense: an agent claims a slice of paths, commits that slice, and leaves the rest alone. In both uses the point is the same, that the boundary is stated rather than assumed.
slice.rule: When something is described as a slice, look for what it excludes. The exclusion is the informative half.
slice.deep: A slice is the unit that makes partial publication honest. Publishing a whole system is a decision nobody can review; publishing a named cut, with its edges recorded, is one a reader can check by looking at what was left out.

smoke_check.label: smoke check
smoke_check.preview: A smoke check is a fast, shallow check that the basics work at all, run before anything more detailed is attempted.
smoke_check.card: It answers one question cheaply: is this thing standing up. A smoke check that fails makes deeper testing pointless, and one that passes establishes very little beyond that the obvious is not broken. Both facts are useful in the right order.
smoke_check.rule: A passing smoke check means nothing is obviously broken. It is not evidence the thing works.
smoke_check.deep: The value is entirely in sequence. Run late it is redundant; run first it saves a long investigation of a system that was never up.

software.label: software
software.preview: Software is the collection of code, data, configuration, and executable behavior that directs computing systems to perform tasks.
software.card: Software includes more than source code: dependencies, builds, runtime environment, and operational state all affect what it does. Public source may expose only a bounded slice of a larger software system.
software.rule: State which artifact, version, and runtime behavior a software claim covers.
software.deep: A software system can be inspected at source, build, test, and runtime layers, and evidence at one layer does not automatically settle the others.

solution.label: solution
solution.preview: A solution is an answer or construction that satisfies every condition of a stated problem.
solution.card: For an equation, a solution is a value that makes it true; for an open problem, a solution is a proof or counterexample that settles the full question. Partial progress can narrow the possibilities without being a solution.
solution.rule: Compare the proposed solution with every requirement in the original problem statement.
solution.deep: A correct solution can use a reformulation or unexpected method, but it must preserve the problem's domain and conclusion and withstand independent checking.

source.label: source
source.preview: A source is the originating artifact, observation, or publication from which a statement, record, or projection draws its content or support.
source.card: Sources provide provenance, but their roles differ: one may own a fact, another may supply evidence, and another may offer background. The surrounding source label should say which role applies.
source.rule: Identify the source's role and version before relying on it.
source.deep: A generated page can have several sources, such as a registry for membership, a paper for exposition, and a result record for current evidence, without any one of them owning every displayed field.

source_body.label: source body
source_body.preview: A source body is the actual code of a function or module carried into a public bundle, as opposed to a description, signature, or hash of it.
source_body.card: A file hash proves bytes match; it says nothing about whether the logic is right. Carrying the source body means the published artefact contains the real implementation, so a reader can run it and assert its output rather than trusting a digest. Where the underlying data is private, the body is carried but the records around it stay metadata-only.
source_body.rule: Check whether the public bundle contains the executable implementation or only a description or digest. A source body makes the logic inspectable and runnable; only a named execution receipt shows how it behaved on particular inputs.
source_body.deep: Digest equality proves identity with a declared source, not semantic correctness. Carrying the body closes the inspectability gap because a reader can examine and execute the implementation, while fixtures and result records separately establish observed behavior. Source availability, identity, and execution evidence are three distinct claims.

source_file.label: source file
source_file.preview: A source file is the human-written file a program is actually built from, as opposed to anything generated, compiled or copied from it.
source_file.card: Pointing at a source file is more specific than pointing at a project. It names the exact place a behaviour is implemented, so a reader can go and check whether the description matches the code rather than taking the description on trust. Each component here names its source file directly.
source_file.rule: Follow the source-file link. It is the shortest route from a claim to the thing that implements it.
source_file.deep: The reason to name the file rather than the repository is that the repository is searchable but not answerable. A specific path either supports the claim or visibly does not.

source_slice.label: source slice
source_slice.preview: A source slice is the deliberately selected, bounded set of source files published to back the hosted pages and reader packets, excluding the remainder of the working tree.
source_slice.card: The published repository does not contain the whole working tree. The source slice is the portion that has been exported into the public repository, so the source-linked components, packets, and routes on this site can be opened and checked against real code. The cut is deliberate and stated, so what is available to inspect is clear and nothing unpublished is implied to be present.
source_slice.rule: Treat the source slice as the part you can actually open and verify. It backs the public objects on the site, but it is not the whole codebase, so unpublished routes, ledgers, and operator context will not be found within it.
source_slice.deep: The boundary of the slice is explicit by design: publishing source-linked material does not claim that the public repository is the entire workspace, only that this defined subset is open to inspection.

span.label: linear span
span.preview: The span of a collection is everything you can build from it by scaling its members and adding them together.
span.card: Saying that a family spans a space of a given dimension fixes exactly how much independent information the family carries, which is a sharper statement than saying the family is large.
span.rule: A span is determined by the collection, so adding a member that was already reachable does not change it.
span.deep: The dyadic sections of Euler's totient span a space of dimension exactly two to the e plus one at every level e at least one. Because that holds at every level, the full span is infinite-dimensional.

sparse_checkout.label: sparse checkout
sparse_checkout.preview: A sparse checkout downloads only the parts of a repository you name, so a large repository can be used without fetching everything.
sparse_checkout.card: The Lean repository offers three: the reader files (papers and guides), a quick proof build, and the full Lean source. The README gives the exact commands, and the reproducibility guide says what each one lets you check.
sparse_checkout.rule: Pick the checkout that matches what you want to do; you can widen it later.
sparse_checkout.deep: A sparse checkout is a snapshot at one revision. It does not update itself and it does not contribute anything by itself.

specification.label: specification
specification.preview: A specification is an explicit description of required behaviour, structure, interface, or constraints against which an implementation can be judged.
specification.card: A specification states what must hold without necessarily prescribing every internal method used to make it hold. Good specifications define inputs, outputs, invariants, edge cases, and permitted variation at the needed level.
specification.rule: Use the specification as the comparison surface for implementation and validation, while checking that it reflects the intended purpose.
specification.deep: Completeness and correctness of a specification are separate from conformance to it; an implementation can satisfy a flawed specification.

squarefree.label: squarefree
squarefree.preview: A whole number is squarefree when no prime divides it more than once, so it has no repeated prime factor.
squarefree.card: Ten equals two times five and is squarefree. Twelve equals two times two times three and is not, because two appears twice.
squarefree.rule: A squarefree condition restricts which indices may appear in a support, so a theorem proved for squarefree support does not cover arbitrary support.
squarefree.deep: For Erdős #257, irrationality at squarefree support over power-of-two bases is a cited prior result rather than a contribution of this corpus, and the papers say so.

standard.label: standard
standard.preview: A standard is a machine-readable contract fixing an artifact kind's required fields, authority, validation, and maintenance rules in a form that both people and agents can inspect and check.
standard.card: Each kind of governed artifact in the system, such as a component record, a paper module, or a doctrine card, has a standard that states its grammar: the fields that matter, the authority posture that applies, and the checks a change must pass. Because a standard is itself a structured file rather than prose advice, it can be validated automatically, and an artifact can be confirmed to conform to it. It encodes not just form but intent, lifecycle, and how the artifact is found, so the shape of a thing does not have to be inferred by reading examples.
standard.rule: When something is governed by a standard, the standard is the authority on its shape and rules: it states which fields and checks the artifact is held to, rather than leaving them to be inferred from a single instance.
standard.deep: A standard works as executable grammar for one plane of the system: it carries the artifact kind's form, authority, validation, and maintenance rules together, so the contract and the things it governs stay aligned over time.

state.label: state
state.preview: State is the collection of values and conditions that describe a system or object at a particular time or stage.
state.card: State can live in memory, files, databases, interfaces, or physical conditions. A state transition changes at least one relevant value according to an action, event, or rule.
state.rule: Read a state claim with its time, source, scope, and freshness because mutable state may change immediately afterward.
state.deep: State differs from history: it says how things are at one point, while a history records how they arrived there.

statement.label: statement
statement.preview: A statement is a sentence or formal expression that asserts a particular claim capable of being evaluated in context.
statement.card: Mathematical statements specify objects, assumptions, and conclusions; system statements may report facts, policies, or status. Their authority and proof status come from surrounding records.
statement.rule: Read the exact wording, quantifiers, assumptions, and source before paraphrasing a statement.
statement.deep: Small changes in scope words such as every, some, finite, or positive can produce a logically different statement even when the topic looks unchanged.

statement_node.label: statement node
statement_node.preview: A statement node is one mathematically distinct statement in the map over a proof corpus, which several declarations may share if they establish the same thing in different form.
statement_node.card: This is the unit that makes a large corpus comprehensible. Raw declarations count restatements, generated instances and technical variants separately; statement nodes collapse them to the distinct things actually being asserted. The gap between the two numbers is the honest measure of how much of a corpus is machinery.
statement_node.rule: Read the statement-node count, not the declaration count, when asking how much a corpus says.
statement_node.deep: Collapsing is an authored judgement, not an automatic one: deciding two declarations say the same thing in different dress is exactly the step a machine cannot take unaided.

stationary_bootstrap.label: stationary bootstrap
stationary_bootstrap.preview: The stationary bootstrap resamples a time series in randomly sized blocks, so the resampled series keeps the short-range dependence the original had.
stationary_bootstrap.card: Resampling one observation at a time destroys the ordering, and financial series are not independent from one observation to the next. Blocks preserve enough of the local structure for the resampled series to be a fair stand-in.
stationary_bootstrap.rule: The method preserves short-range dependence. It does not preserve long-range structure or regime changes.
stationary_bootstrap.deep: It is used here to give the forecast-comparison tests a distribution to work against, over synthetic market fixtures rather than live data.

status.label: status
status.preview: A status is a declared label describing an artifact's current position in a defined lifecycle or decision scheme.
status.card: Statuses such as active, open, retired, passing, or blocked have meanings set by their owning schema. They are snapshots and may change when new evidence or actions arrive.
status.rule: Read the status definition, timestamp, and authority before treating it as current.
status.deep: A status should be derived from or bound to the events and checks that justify it, rather than edited as an unsupported adjective.

step.label: step
step.preview: A step is one bounded action, transformation, or inference within an ordered process or argument.
step.card: Steps make a larger procedure inspectable by separating it into transitions with inputs and outputs. Some steps can run independently, while others depend on an earlier result.
step.rule: Read each step with its preconditions, action, output, and relationship to neighbouring steps.
step.deep: The validity of a whole chain depends not only on each step but also on whether the output of one satisfies the next step's assumptions.

stochastic.label: stochastic
stochastic.preview: Stochastic means governed by chance, so the same input can produce different outputs on different runs.
stochastic.card: It is the property that makes a language model unreliable as a witness to its own behaviour. A mechanical check is not stochastic: given the same input it reaches the same verdict.
stochastic.rule: A stochastic step can be useful and still be unusable as evidence.
stochastic.deep: The argument made here is to externalise repeatable lessons into parts of the system that are not stochastic, so that what has been learned survives independently of any one model run.

stop.label: stop
stop.preview: To stop is to cease an activity, execution, process, or progression at a particular condition or point.
stop.card: Stopping can be successful completion, deliberate cancellation, safety intervention, failure, or exhaustion of resources. The reason and resulting state determine which interpretation is correct.
stop.rule: When a process stops, check its exit condition, partial effects, and whether required closeout still remains.
stop.deep: A stop condition makes termination predictable by naming when further work would be unnecessary, unsafe, or outside scope.

strength.label: strength
strength.preview: Strength is the degree of force, support, capability, or resistance something has relative to a stated demand or comparison.
strength.card: In evidence and claims, strength concerns how much a result supports and how broadly it can be relied on. In systems, it may concern guarantees, protections, or performance under stress.
strength.rule: Read strength comparatively and ask which dimension, baseline, and operating conditions are being assessed.
strength.deep: A stronger claim usually requires stronger evidence because it excludes more possible countercases or applies across a wider boundary.

stub.label: stub
stub.preview: A stub is a placeholder with the shape of the real thing but not its contents.
stub.card: A stub lets a public release keep the interface of a private component without shipping what the component actually holds. It is honest only when it is labelled, because an unlabelled stub reads as working code.
stub.rule: A stub is not evidence that the thing it stands in for works. It shows only the shape.
stub.deep: The public release contains source-linked components, public-safe stubs, and synthetic fixtures. The stubs mark where the private data stops.

subsum.label: subsum
subsum.preview: A subsum of a series is the total you get by keeping some of its terms and discarding the rest.
subsum.card: Collecting every subsum of a fixed series gives one set of numbers, called its achievement set. Its shape decides which values the series can reach, so questions about whether a target such as one half is reachable become questions about that set.
subsum.rule: A subsum over a finite selection and a subsum over an infinite selection are different objects, and a result about one does not transfer to the other.
subsum.deep: For Erdős #257 the targets one half and one twenty-first have no finite-support representation, and both reduce to explicit alternatives about infinite orbits. Neither has been decided.

sum.label: sum
sum.preview: A sum is a quantity formed by addition; Plectis distinguishes finite exact sums from infinite sums defined by limits.
sum.card: Finite sums in Plectis can be calculated exactly and reduced to rational form for certificate checks. Infinite sums are series: computation reaches only a partial sum, while the paper’s question concerns the limiting value and its arithmetic type.
sum.rule: Identify the index set and whether the sum is finite, truncated, or infinite before transferring any computed or proved property.
sum.deep: The finite denominator-certificate components deliberately turn selected reciprocal terms into an exact rational P/Q. The Erdős papers ask about completed infinite sums, where convergence, tail control, and justified rearrangement become additional obligations. A certificate for the finite sum is evidence about that bounded object, not automatically the infinite limit.

superior_predictive_ability.label: superior predictive ability
superior_predictive_ability.preview: Hansen's superior predictive ability test asks whether any method in a whole set genuinely beats a benchmark, correcting for the fact that searching many methods will throw up a winner by luck alone.
superior_predictive_ability.card: It exists because comparing one favourite method against a benchmark, after quietly trying fifty, is how spurious forecasting results are produced. The correction is for the size of the search, not for the quality of any one method.
superior_predictive_ability.rule: The test controls for multiple comparisons. It does not establish that the winning method will keep winning.
superior_predictive_ability.deep: Forecast-skill claims here run this test alongside Diebold-Mariano and a stationary bootstrap, over synthetic fixtures. Passing on a fixture shows the check runs and refuses as specified for that fixture.

support.label: support
support.preview: On Plectis, support can mean evidence backing a claim or, in the Erdős mathematics, the set of indices whose terms are included in a sum.
support.card: Evidential support is a scoped relation between a claim and inspectable sources, checks, or records. Mathematical support is a membership set selecting nonzero or included terms. The site uses both heavily, and neither sense should be inferred from the other.
support.rule: Claims, evidence, sources, or authority indicate evidential support; indices, exponents, terms, finite sets, or infinite sets indicate mathematical support.
support.deep: Evidential support answers why a reader may rely on a bounded claim and must preserve provenance and scope. Series support answers which reciprocal terms participate and can itself be the object quantified over by an open problem. Sharing the noun does not turn evidence relations into mathematical membership or vice versa.

sylvester_sequence.label: Sylvester's sequence
sylvester_sequence.preview: Sylvester's sequence is 2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, and onward, where each term is the product of all earlier terms plus one.
sylvester_sequence.card: Its reciprocals sum to exactly one, and it is the greedy way of writing one as a sum of distinct unit fractions. That makes it the extreme case against which nearby sequences are measured.
sylvester_sequence.rule: The recurrence is a condition a sequence may eventually satisfy; saying it begins at some index is weaker than saying it holds from the start.
sylvester_sequence.deep: Erdős #243 asks about the rigidity of sequences near this one. The Lean work proves that normalised vanishing together with an eventually bounded negative part forces the error to vanish and the recurrence to begin. The negative-part bound itself is not proved, and that is where the problem stays open.

symbol.label: symbol
symbol.preview: A symbol is a mark, name, or token used by a language or notation to stand for an object, operation, relation, or instruction.
symbol.card: Symbols gain meaning from a surrounding notation, declaration, or language. The same glyph can denote different things in different mathematical or programming contexts.
symbol.rule: Interpret a symbol through its declaration and scope rather than its visual form alone.
symbol.deep: Formal systems can check symbol use precisely once names, types, and binding rules are fixed. Namespaces and binding rules decide whether identical spellings refer to the same object or to distinct objects.

synth_seed.label: synth seed
synth_seed.preview: A synth seed is the current phase brief: its goal, success conditions, relevant files, and next execution wave distilled from durable intent.
synth_seed.card: A synth seed sits between the system's broad, lasting statement of intent and the moment-to-moment execution of one phase. It carries the goal, the reason the work is happening now, the success criteria, the relevant files, the wave, and the supporting context needed to act without rereading everything upstream. It is deliberately disposable: it is the authoritative model for the phase it describes and is meant to be replaced as the work moves on, not preserved as the system's permanent voice.
synth_seed.rule: Treat a synth seed as the live brief for the phase it names, accurate as of that phase and no wider. It states what one slice of work is trying to do, not the system's lasting intent.
synth_seed.deep: It is produced by distilling the lasting statement of intent down to a task-shaped form, so it is concrete and bounded by design rather than comprehensive.

synthetic.label: synthetic
synthetic.preview: Synthetic means data made up for the purpose of a check, rather than taken from real use.
synthetic.card: Everything runnable here runs on synthetic inputs. That is what allows the components to be published at all, and it is a real limit rather than a formality: a component shown to work on constructed data has not been shown to work on the messier real thing. The scope limit on each result says so rather than leaving it implied.
synthetic.rule: A passing check on synthetic data establishes the constructed case, not the real one.
synthetic.deep: The trade is reproducibility for realism, taken deliberately and in one direction. It is stated because the alternative is a reader assuming the stronger claim for free.

system.label: system
system.preview: A system is a set of connected parts whose relationships let them perform or maintain something together.
system.card: The word points to the parts and their organisation at once. A repository, its tools, its records, and the rules connecting them can therefore be discussed as one system without pretending they are one file or program.
system.rule: When the site says system, look for the named parts, the boundary around them, and the behaviour their connections produce.
system.deep: A system can have properties that no single part has, and a change to one part can travel through its connections to affect the rest.

target.label: target
target.preview: A target is the specific object, destination, outcome, or condition toward which an action, route, check, or claim is directed.
target.card: Targets make operations bounded: a command changes a path, a link reaches a page, and a test evaluates behaviour. Identity and scope matter because acting on the wrong target can make an otherwise valid operation harmful.
target.rule: Resolve a target exactly before mutation and verify that the result concerns the same target afterward.
target.deep: A goal describes a desired condition, while a target identifies the concrete object or value toward which the operation is aimed.

term.label: term
term.preview: A term is a word or phrase given a particular meaning within a subject, document, or system.
term.card: The same word can be an ordinary word in one sentence and a governed term in another. Glossary entries make the intended meaning, aliases, scope, and exclusions explicit.
term.rule: Use the local definition when a word has a specialized meaning and ordinary usage otherwise.
term.deep: Term identity belongs to the concept rather than a single spelling, so aliases and renamed labels can resolve to one governed entry.

terminal.label: terminal
terminal.preview: The terminal is the text interface where you type commands directly to your computer rather than clicking through a screen.
terminal.card: Every route here that produces evidence runs in a terminal. The commands are written out in full so they can be copied rather than reconstructed, and they are ordinary commands with no wrapper of this project's own.
terminal.rule: If a step cannot be expressed as a command you can copy, it has not been made reproducible.
terminal.deep: Writing the exact command down is a small discipline with a large effect: it converts a described procedure into one someone else can execute identically.

test.label: test
test.preview: A test is a defined procedure that supplies cases to a system and compares observed behavior with expected conditions.
test.card: Tests provide evidence about the cases and environment they exercise. Passing tests do not prove correctness for all possible inputs, while failing tests identify a mismatch that still needs diagnosis.
test.rule: Read the tested cases, oracle, environment, and result before generalizing.
test.deep: Tests can target units, integrations, regressions, properties, performance, or end-to-end behavior, and each kind supports a different claim.

text.label: text
text.preview: Text is written language represented as characters rather than as an image, sound, or executable operation.
text.card: Text can carry prose, code, labels, or structured data, depending on the rules used to interpret it. Its visible words and its machine representation are related but not identical.
text.rule: Read text according to its declared format and do not infer executable authority from words alone.
text.deep: The same characters can mean different things in prose, JSON, source code, or a command, because each context assigns different syntax and effects.

theorem.label: theorem
theorem.preview: A theorem is a mathematical statement together with a proof of it.
theorem.card: In a formal corpus each theorem is a named item the proof checker has verified. The count is a measure of size rather than of significance: theorems range from a substantial result to a mechanical step generated in bulk, and most of a large corpus is the latter.
theorem.rule: A theorem is settled for exactly what it states. Read the statement, not the name.
theorem.deep: The gap between what a theorem states and what its title suggests is where formal work is most often overread, which is why the statements rather than the labels are the published object.

theory.label: theory
theory.preview: A theory is an organized body of definitions, assumptions, methods, and results used to explain or reason about a class of phenomena or structures.
theory.card: A mathematical theory develops consequences from explicit foundations; an empirical scientific theory also connects predictions with observations. The word does not mean an unsupported guess.
theory.rule: Identify the theory's domain, assumptions, and evidence standard.
theory.deep: Theories organize many individual statements into a reusable framework and can be extended or revised without erasing the status of every established result.

tool.label: tool
tool.preview: A tool is a program or instrument used to inspect, transform, validate, or operate on artifacts.
tool.card: Tools extend what a person or agent can do, but their outputs inherit the tool's inputs, configuration, and limitations. Tool availability is separate from permission to use it.
tool.rule: Record which tool and version produced a result and which authority permits the action.
tool.deep: A tool may wrap another program or service, so evidence should preserve the underlying command or protocol when exact reproduction matters.

toolchain.label: toolchain
toolchain.preview: A toolchain is the ordered set of compilers, interpreters, package managers, builders, and checkers used to turn source files into a runnable or verified result.
toolchain.card: A toolchain is part of a result's provenance because changing one tool or version can change whether the source builds or what output it produces. Reproducible work records the exact versions and the command path through them.
toolchain.rule: When a build or proof result matters, check which toolchain and versions produced it.
toolchain.deep: Toolchains form a dependency chain: source is parsed, dependencies are resolved, code is compiled or elaborated, and a final checker accepts or rejects the output, so each stage has a different role in trust.

totient.label: totient
totient.preview: The totient of a whole number is how many smaller positive numbers share no factor with it.
totient.card: It is one of the oldest functions in number theory and behaves irregularly: it jumps around according to the factorisation of each number rather than following any smooth rule. That irregularity is what makes a series built from it hard, because no simple approximation captures the terms.
totient.rule: A totient series inherits the irregularity of factorisation.
totient.deep: The approach taken here is to find exact structure in the irregularity rather than to approximate it, which is what the rational basis for the dyadic sections provides.

transaction.label: transaction
transaction.preview: A transaction is a group of steps that either all take effect or none of them do.
transaction.card: Without it, multi-step work can stop halfway and leave a state that is neither the old one nor the new one. The value is not speed; it is that there is no partial result to misread later.
transaction.rule: A transaction says the change is complete or absent. It does not say the change was correct.
transaction.deep: Multi-step agent work here is required to land as a transaction rather than as a promise, so a change to the world counts only once it has actually landed.

transcendental.label: transcendental
transcendental.preview: A number is transcendental when no polynomial with whole-number coefficients has it as a root.
transcendental.card: Transcendence is strictly stronger than irrationality. Every transcendental number is irrational, but the reverse fails: the square root of two is irrational and satisfies x squared minus two, so it is not transcendental. Very few tools reach an individual constant, which is why transcendence results for specific series are rare.
transcendental.rule: A transcendence claim is stronger than the matching irrationality claim, so check which one a result actually delivers.
transcendental.deep: In the Erdős #269 work the reciprocal sums of running least common multiples over two distinct primes are argued transcendental by a paper argument using a result of Bugeaud and Laurent. That deduction is not Lean-checked, and Steve Fan published the same two-prime reduction first. Three primes onward remains open.

transcript.label: transcript
transcript.preview: A transcript is the recorded text of a session, kept so what was said or done can be reread rather than recalled.
transcript.card: Transcripts here are evidence in the same sense as result records: the account written afterwards is a summary, and the transcript is the thing it summarises. Keeping both is what makes it possible to check one against the other.
transcript.rule: Where a summary and a transcript disagree, the transcript is the record.
transcript.deep: Summaries are not usually dishonest; they are lossy in a direction that flatters. Keeping the source makes the loss recoverable.

trust.label: trust
trust.preview: Trust is a willingness to rely on a person, system, source, or claim under particular expectations and risk.
trust.card: Trust can be earned through authority, evidence, repeated reliability, accountability, or constrained access, but it remains scoped. Technical systems often replace broad trust with narrower checks and permissions.
trust.rule: Before relying on something trusted, identify what property is trusted, by whom, under which conditions, and with what fallback.
trust.deep: Trust is not proof and should not silently cross from one source or capability to another.

truth_maintenance.label: truth maintenance
truth_maintenance.preview: Truth maintenance is the bookkeeping that ties each belief to its evidence, dependencies, invalidation conditions, and consequences so failed assumptions or contradictions are routed to repair instead of silently corrupting settled state.
truth_maintenance.card: Instead of holding facts as one flat, undifferentiated pile, the system records for each claim its evidence, its dependencies, its current status, its appeal state, the conditions that would invalidate it, and the actions it does or does not license. A receipt from a check, a model's output, a generated page, and a doctrine commitment therefore do not share one indiscriminate authority. The standing question is always what is believed now, why, what would overturn it, and what stays blocked while uncertainty remains.
truth_maintenance.rule: When a belief on this site is presented as held, treat it as held for stated reasons and only until those reasons are undercut: look for what it depends on and what would invalidate it, rather than reading it as fixed.
truth_maintenance.deep: It is a diagnostic discipline here, adapted locally by the Workingness Instrument: a claim that fails or is contradicted lowers in status and gates the actions that depended on it, instead of vanishing or quietly persisting as if still sound.

type_a.label: Type A
type_a.preview: A Type A is an actor with gated access to the live substrate, able to inspect current files and records, run tools, and perform mutations such as editing, validation, testing, committing, or routing work.
type_a.card: Type A describes a shape of actor, not a quality ranking. It is the lane with live-substrate authority: it can read the working files on disk, run commands, make edits under the system's gates, check its own work, and feed what it learned back into the shared records. Its freedom is bounded by the latest instruction it was given, the limits of what it is allowed to change, the standards, and the requirement to validate, roll back, and leave a record. Controller sessions are Type A; a tool-using helper agent with live access to the repository is a delegated Type A.
type_a.rule: When something is marked Type A, take it as an actor operating on the live system with real power to change it, kept inside defined gates, rather than a measure of how capable or senior that actor is.
type_a.deep: Type A sits on one axis only, substrate authority; how capable the actor is, which surface it runs on, its delegation role, its context mode, and its thinking budget are separate, independent classifications. The contrasting shape, Type B, reads the same world but works from prepared material rather than live private state and does not hold mutation authority.

type_a_judgment.label: Type A judgment
type_a_judgment.preview: Type A judgment is a capable substrate actor's governed discernment for noticing what is missing, stale, or misplaced and inferring the right bounded destination from the system's own rules without waiting for a bespoke instruction.
type_a_judgment.card: When an agent reads this system as a body of rules, standards, and recorded state, Type A judgment is the part of its work that is not mechanical: spotting a missing route, a standard that no longer matches reality, or a local lesson worth carrying back into the shared rules. It is a small, open set of traits rather than a fixed list of virtues, with attention and care as early examples, and it is meant to be traceable rather than a passing mood.
type_a_judgment.rule: Where the site refers to Type A judgment, treat it as the agent's discernment exercised on this material, grounded in the system's rules and records, not as an unaccountable opinion.
type_a_judgment.deep: It rests on a simple invariant: if a judgment changes how a later agent will behave, it should be written down with its sources and routes rather than left as something only the current session knows.

type_a_metabolism.label: Type A metabolism
type_a_metabolism.preview: Type A metabolism is the high-agency lane that resolves work with no settled rule—such as naming primitives, repairing contradictions, changing standards, or promoting principles—into governed structure that later routine work can follow.
type_a_metabolism.card: Most upkeep in the system runs along fixed tracks: a known job, a validator, a row to patch. Type A metabolism is what runs when no such track exists yet. It takes a broad, ambiguous situation and collapses it into something bounded and reusable, such as a named rule, a standard, or a repaired scaffold, while preserving the original situation, the limit of what it is allowed to decide, its checks, and a way to roll back. It is the system changing its own rules rather than just applying them, so it is treated as expensive and powerful.
type_a_metabolism.rule: When you meet Type A metabolism, read it as a record of judgement applied where the rules were still open: the system deciding a new boundary under validation, not running a routine job. The decision it reached is what makes the later routine work cheap.
type_a_metabolism.deep: Its judgement loop draws on the system's axioms and principles as design intuition and on imported patterns as raw material, and it ends in either a better local rule or a named, recorded rejection. Once the resulting grammar is stable, ongoing maintenance moves to the lower-agency Type B lane.

type_a_operating_register.label: Type A operating register
type_a_operating_register.preview: The Type A operating register is the expected conduct of a live-substrate agent: steward what it touches and durably route what it learns.
type_a_operating_register.card: It is one of two registers the system distinguishes. A Type A agent is a high-agency controller, a coding agent or its operator, acting on the system from the inside; the register describes how that controller is meant to behave across a piece of work. The behaviours are concrete: steward and thicken the files and records it edits, watch for drift between a summary and what it describes, use what it builds, and pass any local discovery upward through the narrowest honest channel. It is a posture, composed from named judgment traits like care, common sense, and critic stance, not a single tool or a step in a checklist.
type_a_operating_register.rule: When a page describes work in the Type A register, read it as the controller's own account of how it operated: what it stewarded, what it noticed, and where it routed each finding. The register tells you the standard of conduct behind the work, not a guarantee about any single output.
type_a_operating_register.deep: The register pairs with Type A judgment, which holds the individual trait definitions, and with the propagation surfaces that carry a local finding into doctrine, standards, or vocabulary according to how settled it is. It governs the behaviour of the controller, not the content of any one component.

type_b.label: Type B
type_b.preview: A Type B is an actor reasoning from context handed to it outside the live substrate, able to produce advice, drafts, or candidate answers but unable to inspect private files, run local commands, or mutate the system directly.
type_b.card: Type B is one of two actor shapes the system recognises. A Type B actor reasons through a chat window, a browser session, a provider or web API, or any channel where it sees only the context it was given, not the live repository. It can decide, research, critique, and correct at a high level over that materialised context, but it has no direct authority to inspect private files, execute commands, edit, test, or commit; any such action has to be carried out by an actor that does hold that access. The counterpart shape, Type A, is the actor running inside the live machinery with those affordances.
type_b.rule: When something is produced by Type B, treat it as advisory: a synthesis built from the context it was shown, to be checked against the live system before anything is acted on.
type_b.deep: The distinction is about access to the live machinery, not about intelligence: a capable Type B actor can outthink the harness it cannot touch, and a delegated worker that does hold live repository tools is a Type A actor, not Type B, despite being delegated.

type_b_metabolism.label: Type B metabolism
type_b_metabolism.preview: Type B metabolism is the bounded, deterministic upkeep lane for repeatable work after a structure is settled, such as syncing files, refreshing projections, filling records, and running checks rather than inventing new governing shapes.
type_b_metabolism.card: This is how the system keeps its many surfaces current at scale. Once a kind of thing has a known shape, with a defined target, input, output schema, validation command, and a record of what it is allowed to claim, Type B work carries out the repeatable part: refreshing an index, refilling a summary band, detecting duplicates, checking that evidence pointers still resolve, or applying a draft patch to a row. Each run is bounded by a fixed input and a fixed output shape, is checked against a stated standard, and can be safely re-run without changing the result.
type_b_metabolism.rule: When a surface is described as produced by Type B metabolism, treat it as maintenance against a settled shape: it is kept current by repeatable, validated jobs, and it stops short of inventing new structure or making a final promotion decision on its own.
type_b_metabolism.deep: It can be carried out by plain deterministic code, small validators, scheduled jobs, or cheap external calls, and its safety rests on four things: a bounded input, an explicit output shape, a validation step, and the fact that re-running it produces the same result. The complementary, open-ended lane that first makes a thing legible enough to maintain this way is called Type A.

typed_relation.label: typed relation
typed_relation.preview: A typed relation is a recorded link between two statements that says what kind of link it is: that one implies another, reformulates it, is a finite instance of it, or rules out a route to it.
typed_relation.card: An untyped link only says two things are related, which is nearly useless for reasoning. Typing the link is what makes the map answerable: you can ask what a result implies, what still depends on an unproved antecedent, or which approaches have already been closed off, and get an answer rather than a reading list.
typed_relation.rule: Follow the relation type, not just the link. What connects two statements is the content.
typed_relation.deep: Recording the type is also what makes a wrong connection falsifiable. A link labelled implies can be checked; a link labelled related cannot.

up_propagate.label: up-propagate
up_propagate.preview: To up-propagate is to move a reusable local lesson into the smallest durable system artifact that should carry it.
up_propagate.card: Up-propagation is the direction in which reusable learning travels through the system: from a specific local case toward a more lasting home such as a skill, a standard, a paper module, an agent seed, or an axiom. The destination is chosen by how settled and how authoritative the lesson is, so a routine procedure lands in a skill, a fixed data shape lands in a standard, and operator intent lands in the source voice records. The aim is to record the lesson once, in the least authoritative place that can hold it honestly, rather than letting it be rediscovered.
up_propagate.rule: When something is described as up-propagated, treat it as a local finding that has been deliberately lifted into a more durable artifact; trace it to that artifact to see where it now lives and what scope it claims.
up_propagate.deep: Up-propagation does not turn every finding into doctrine. It routes a finding to the least authoritative durable layer that can preserve it without overstating it, which is why most lessons settle as skills or standards rather than as axioms or principles.

update.label: update
update.preview: An update is a change that brings material, state, or software to a newer or corrected condition.
update.card: An update may add information, replace stale values, fix defects, or synchronize a projection with its source. It should state what changed and what prior condition it supersedes.
update.rule: Read an update with its target, change summary, date or version, and validation status.
update.deep: Newer does not automatically mean better or authoritative; an update inherits the rules governing the thing it changes.

validate.label: validate
validate.preview: To validate something is to check it against stated requirements or evidence and determine whether those requirements are satisfied.
validate.card: Validation can concern structure, behaviour, links, data, or claims. It produces a result relative to a known rule set; it does not silently establish properties that were never checked.
validate.rule: Whenever a result is called validated, identify the validator, inputs, requirements, and recorded outcome.
validate.deep: Validation is strongest when reproducible and independent of the material's own unverified claims about itself.

validation.label: validation
validation.preview: Validation is the act of checking an artifact or result against a declared contract, acceptance condition, or allowed shape and recording the outcome.
validation.card: Validation answers whether the tested object met the selected rules in that run. The strength of the result comes from the contract and test coverage, so validated never means universally correct unless the contract itself establishes that much.
validation.rule: Read a validation result together with the exact contract, inputs, and exclusions it checked.
validation.deep: Validation may be structural, behavioural, semantic, or release-oriented, and combining those classes without naming them is a common way to overstate what a green result proves.

validator.label: validator
validator.preview: A validator is a program or component that applies declared rules to an input and emits a structured pass, fail, warning, or blocked result.
validator.card: A validator concentrates a policy into executable checks so the same input is judged consistently. Its verdict is only as strong as the rules it implements, the data it actually reads, and the negative cases proving it rejects invalid inputs.
validator.rule: Inspect what the validator recomputes and which failure cases it exercises before treating its verdict as evidence.
validator.deep: A trustworthy validator is small enough to review, deterministic where possible, self-falsifying through negative fixtures, and explicit about checks it delegates or cannot perform.

value.label: value
value.preview: A value is the particular data, quantity, text, or status assigned to a variable, field, expression, or measurement.
value.card: Values are interpreted through their surrounding type, unit, field, or mathematical expression. The same symbol or number can mean different things in different records.
value.rule: Read a value together with its name, type, units, and source.
value.deep: A recorded value may be declared, computed, measured, or copied, and that provenance determines what checks can establish about it.

variable.label: variable
variable.preview: A variable is a named value that may vary or be supplied later; in Plectis it appears both as a mathematical symbol and as a program or configuration value.
variable.card: A theorem variable receives a type, quantifier, and logical scope. A program variable receives a value from code, input, configuration, or the environment and has a runtime lifetime. The same spelling does not give those two variables the same source or authority.
variable.rule: For mathematics, track type, quantifier, and binder; for software, track declaration, input source, lifetime, and mutation.
variable.deep: Lean makes mathematical variable scope explicit so a symbol cannot silently change type or dependency across a proof. Runtime and environment variables instead derive their meaning from the executing program and current environment, so reproduction requires recording both their names and effective values.

verification.label: verification
verification.preview: Verification is the act of confirming that a specific claim, output, or artifact matches its authoritative source or satisfies a precisely stated property.
verification.card: Verification asks whether the thing is correct with respect to a named reference or property, while validation more broadly asks whether it meets an acceptance contract. Both words need a declared object and criterion; `verified` without those details is incomplete.
verification.rule: When something is verified, identify what was compared, which authority or property served as the reference, and what was not checked.
verification.deep: Verification can range from comparing file hashes to kernel-checking a proof, so the method and trusted checker determine how much confidence the word carries.

version.label: version
version.preview: A version is an identified state of an artifact or system at a particular point in its change history.
version.card: Versions let readers distinguish current material from earlier copies and reproduce results against the same inputs. A version may be named by a release number, commit, date, or source hash.
version.rule: Record the version whenever a claim could change as the artifact evolves.
version.deep: Two paths can point to different content over time, so exact reproduction needs both location and version identity.

vulnerability.label: vulnerability
vulnerability.preview: A vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited or triggered to violate a system's intended security or safety properties.
vulnerability.card: A vulnerability links a flaw or unsafe condition to an impact through some feasible path. Severity depends on reachability, required access, affected assets, and available mitigations.
vulnerability.rule: When a vulnerability is claimed, look for the affected boundary, triggering conditions, impact, and supporting reproduction or analysis.
vulnerability.deep: A theoretical weakness becomes operationally important when an attacker or failure can actually reach it under the stated conditions.

wave.label: wave
wave.preview: A wave is one bounded pass of execution inside a phase: a single planned unit of work with a stated objective, an execution mode, the paths it is allowed to touch, and a route for folding its outcome back into the system's durable record.
wave.card: Work in this system is organised into phases, and each phase is carried out as a sequence of waves rather than one continuously rewritten effort. A wave plans a single pass, runs it, records what it did and what the evidence showed, and then either evolves the working state or hands off cleanly. Because each wave has a defined boundary, the work stays resumable: a later pass can pick up from the recorded outcome instead of from chat history.
wave.rule: Take a wave as one finished pass of work with its own objective and recorded outcome, not the whole phase. What it changed and what it proved sit inside that one pass.
wave.deep: A wave can run in different execution modes, from a direct local change to a delegated or multi-agent pass, and its result is assimilated into the system's durable state so that the boundary between current work and the settled substrate is preserved.

whisper.label: Whisper
whisper.preview: Whisper is OpenAI's speech-to-text model, which turns recorded audio into text with timings for each word.
whisper.card: The timings are what make it useful for video work: once every word has a timestamp, the words can be lined up against the frames that were on screen when they were spoken.
whisper.rule: A transcript is a rendering of the audio. It is not a record of what was on screen.
whisper.deep: The video editor inside the private system transcribes locally with Whisper, indexes the screen frames against the words, and writes every cut as a proposal a person has to accept before it renders.

whole.label: whole
whole.preview: A whole is the complete object, collection, or system considered together rather than only one of its parts.
whole.card: What counts as the whole depends on a boundary. A complete public site can still be only one projection of the whole repository, and a whole repository can still depend on outside services.
whole.rule: Before interpreting whole or entire, identify the boundary that determines which parts are included.
whole.deep: Properties of individual parts do not automatically establish the same property for the whole because interactions can create new behaviour.

whole_system_correctness.label: whole-system correctness
whole_system_correctness.preview: Whole-system correctness is the claim that an entire system behaves correctly, used here mainly as an explicit boundary that no individual page, component, or passing check is allowed to assert.
whole_system_correctness.card: Every component here establishes something local: this check, on these inputs, produced this result. None of them add up to a statement about the system entire. The phrase is used as a refusal rather than a goal, and the scope limit on each result names it explicitly so that a passing check is not read as a wider guarantee.
whole_system_correctness.rule: Treat any wording that implies whole-system correctness as an overclaim, including on this site.
whole_system_correctness.deep: The reason for naming a claim nobody makes is that it is the claim readers infer for free. A repository of passing checks reads like a working system unless the gap is stated, so the release gates refuse language that closes it.

work.label: work
work.preview: Work is purposeful effort that changes, examines, explains, or verifies something.
work.card: On this site, work usually means a bounded task with an intended result, not mere activity. Its value depends on what changed or became known and on whether that outcome was checked.
work.rule: Read a claim of work by asking what its target was, what result it produced, and what evidence closes it.
work.deep: Effort, output, and completion are separate: substantial effort may yield no valid result, while a small operation may complete the required work.

work_landing.label: work landing
work_landing.preview: Work landing is the transition from attempted activity to a durable accepted result whose changes, validation, ownership, and closeout are recorded.
work_landing.card: Work lands only when the attempted change reaches the durable surface that owns it and can be reopened without the session that produced it. In ai_workflow that normally means the owned source path contains the change, the focused validation has a recorded outcome, concurrent ownership was respected, the resulting status and remaining boundary are explicit, and the change has a commit or equivalent durable receipt. A successful-looking tool run or chat summary is still only activity until those pieces agree.
work_landing.rule: Treat work as landed only when the artifact and its validation record can be reopened independently of the session that produced them.
work_landing.deep: Landing is the acceptance transition between mutation and continuity. It binds the changed artifact to provenance, validation, ownership, reversibility, status, and any residual that still needs an owner. This is why a patch can be technically correct yet not landed, and why landing one bounded change says nothing about unrelated work.

working_record.label: working record
working_record.preview: A working record is the long-form rendered PDF that preserves the reasoning surface for one Plectis mathematics problem.
working_record.card: A Plectis working record is the long-form companion to a short problem note. It keeps the mathematical setup, checked premises, routes that were explored, failures that materially changed the direction, exact formal results, and the surviving open obligation together in one rendered PDF. It is designed to show substantially more of the reasoning path than the polished note while remaining an authored, versioned account rather than a raw session dump.
working_record.rule: Use a working record to inspect how the argument and its dead ends developed, then follow its Lean and claim-registry links for proof status. Do not treat it as an exhaustive trace of every private search step.
working_record.deep: The distinction is three-way. A problem note gives the short proved/open boundary; a working record gives the extended reasoning surface; an agent trace or private search history records lower-level session events and may not be public. The working record selects and organizes the reasoning needed to understand the mathematical route without pretending that selection is the proof or the complete provenance.

workingness.label: workingness
workingness.preview: Workingness is whether the system knows what it believes, why, what it does not know, and what that uncertainty still permits, rather than a count of passing tests.
workingness.card: Workingness asks a sharper question than "do the tests pass". It is the diagnostic condition in which the system can turn evidence into calibrated belief, send each failure to the part of the system that owns its repair, and act only within bounds it is explicitly allowed to. It separates whether events were observed from whether the system's own state of belief is sound, and it is read off concrete signals such as a court pass, a drift check, or a live receipt before any change is made.
workingness.rule: Treat a workingness reading as a statement about the system's self-knowledge at that moment, not a warranty that everything is correct. Check what it is actually grounded in before relying on it to permit a change.
workingness.deep: Workingness is the control question behind the system improving itself: can it convert evidence into calibrated belief, failures into the right repair plane, and judgement into bounded permission to act, without corrupting its source material, its doctrine, its route graph, or its generated pages.

workingness_instrument.label: Workingness Instrument
workingness_instrument.preview: A workingness instrument is the record that states what one live result proves and which changes that evidence permits or blocks.
workingness_instrument.card: It is the row-shaped contract for one live outcome. In one place it pins down the kind of claim, its current status, the evidence and dependencies under it, the conditions that would invalidate it, the appeals that block it from being promoted, and the repairs and mutations it allows or forbids. It turns judgments that would otherwise stay implicit into explicit fields: this receipt counts as evidence, this scorer output is a judgment, this projection is stale, this change is forbidden until a named gate passes.
workingness_instrument.rule: Read a workingness instrument as the boundary on what a result lets you do: its allowed and blocked actions are the operative part, not the surrounding summary.
workingness_instrument.deep: It is a diagnostic contract, not an authority writer: it governs and records what a result permits, but it does not itself change the doctrine, the route graph, or the standards.

zero.label: zero
zero.preview: Zero is the number that acts as the additive identity, so adding it leaves a number unchanged.
zero.card: Zero marks absence of quantity and separates positive from negative numbers. It is an integer, rational number, real number, and—in Lean's convention—a natural number.
zero.rule: Check whether zero is allowed before dividing, taking reciprocals, or applying a positivity hypothesis.
zero.deep: Many exceptional cases in algebra and number theory arise because multiplication by zero collapses information and division by zero is undefined.

zone.label: zone
zone.preview: A zone is one thematic region of the map over the proof corpus, grouping the statements that belong to a single line of argument.
zone.card: Zones exist so a reader can enter a corpus somewhere specific rather than at the beginning. Each collects the statements about one mechanism or one family of results, with the relations among them, so a question about that mechanism does not require reading the rest.
zone.rule: A zone bounds where an argument lives. It is a reading route, not a claim of completeness.
zone.deep: Partitioning is what turns an index into something navigable. Without it the map is only a flat list with more metadata.
